NET-001.prerequisites: Written scope/rules-of-engagement authorization that explicitly covers reflection/amplification traffic, since even a controlled test generates unsolicited bulk traffic — any destination address used in a spoofed-source test must be a host you own or control, never a real third party. A Linux host with root access for raw-socket packet crafting (scapy or hping3). A network path to the resolver under test that does not sit behind egress source-address filtering (BCP38/BCP84) — most cloud/VPS providers block spoofed packets, so this specific step usually requires an on-prem lab network. dig, nmap, and Wireshark/tcpdump installed for verification.
NET-001.whatItIs: DNS amplification lets an attacker turn a small amount of their own bandwidth into a much bigger flood aimed at a victim. They send a tiny DNS request to a resolver, but fake the sender's address to be the victim's — so the resolver sends its (much bigger) answer to the victim instead of back to the attacker. Certain DNS record types are favored because their answers can be 50-100x bigger than the original request, multiplying the attack's power.
NET-001.rootCause: Two things combine to make this possible: DNS normally runs over a connectionless protocol with no way to verify the sender's address is real, so an attacker can fake it. And the resolver is set up to answer these large lookups for anyone who asks, rather than only for its own known users — so anyone on the internet can use it as an amplifier.
NET-001.impact: A sustained amplification flood can saturate the victim's inbound bandwidth entirely, taking down public-facing services — websites, VPN concentrators, mail gateways — for as long as the attack continues, with recovery often requiring upstream ISP-level scrubbing rather than anything the victim alone can do. Because the traffic's apparent source is the resolver rather than the true attacker, initial incident response is misdirected toward the resolver's owner. An organization that operates an abusable resolver also bears its own cost — bandwidth and CPU consumed servicing the flood — plus reputational and, in some regulatory contexts, liability exposure for being an unwitting participant in an attack against a third party.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every DNS resolver in scope, internal and internet-facing, with a UDP service sweep: nmap -sU -p53 --open against the target range.

For each resolver found, test from a vantage point outside its expected client base whether it answers recursive queries at all (cross-reference the related 'Open DNS Resolver' finding, which covers this check in depth).
Measure the realized amplification ratio per record type by comparing query size to response size for ANY, TXT, DNSKEY, and RRSIG against a zone known to carry large records.

Send a rapid burst of identical queries to see whether Response Rate Limiting (RRL) is enabled — a resolver that starts truncating or dropping repeat queries within a few requests is meaningfully harder to abuse at scale.

If host/config access is available, review the allow-recursion, allow-query, and rate-limit directives directly in the resolver's configuration rather than inferring them from black-box probing alone.

Cross-check the resolver's public IP against Shodan/Censys and public open-resolver project listings — if it's already indexed there, it's likely already being abused by third parties independent of your own test.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the rules of engagement explicitly authorize reflection/amplification testing, and nominate a destination address you own before crafting any spoofed packet — never a real third-party address.

Stand up a packet-crafting host with root/raw-socket access and confirm your own network path does not perform egress source-address filtering, since most commercial cloud/VPS providers silently drop spoofed packets.
Send a normal, non-spoofed query first to record the baseline response size for the record type you intend to use, so the amplification ratio you calculate later is accurate.
Craft a single UDP/53 query to the resolver with the source IP field set to your own monitoring host's address and the query set to the high-ratio record type identified during discovery.
On the monitoring host, capture inbound traffic to confirm the amplified response arrived and calculate the realized ratio (response bytes divided by original query bytes).

Repeat the single-packet test against each in-scope resolver individually — one packet per resolver is sufficient evidence; do not loop, flood, or scale the technique, since that shifts the activity from a controlled proof-of-concept into an actual denial-of-service condition.
Record whether RRL activated during testing, the resolver's response latency under the minimal load applied, and the calculated amplification factor for the final report.

examplePayloads.label: Baseline (non-spoofed) amplification-ratio check — ANY record
Amplification-ratio check — DNSSEC DNSKEY record (often a higher ratio)
Automated open-recursion check across a range
Direct query/answer byte-size comparison
Single spoofed-source packet to your OWN monitoring host only (lab use, authorized scope only)
examplePayloads.command: sudo python3 -c "from scapy.all import *; send(IP(src='<address-you-own>', dst='<resolver-ip>')/UDP(sport=33333, dport=53)/DNS(rd=1, qd=DNSQR(qname='isc.org', qtype='ANY')))"

examplePayloads.label: Test RRL behavior with a small repeated-query burst (5 requests only)
examplePayloads.command: for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do dig @<resolver-ip> target-zone.com TXT +noall +stats | grep 'Query time'; done

variants: Amplification via DNSSEC-signed zones specifically (DNSKEY/RRSIG), which tend to produce a higher ratio than unsigned equivalents because of the embedded key/signature material.
Chained amplification, where the attacker first uses one reflection vector (e.g., NTP monlist) to reach the resolver, then pivots to DNS amplification from the same vantage point.

Amplification via a resolver's own EDNS0 buffer size setting — some resolvers advertise a large buffer size (4096 bytes) by default, which can be requested explicitly to maximize response size regardless of record type.

Distributed reflection using many discovered open resolvers simultaneously against a single victim — the real-world attack pattern, only ever demonstrated conceptually via the single-resolver single-packet method in an authorized test, never executed at scale.

Related application-layer reflection using other UDP-based protocols with similar characteristics (NTP monlist, memcached, SSDP, CLDAP), which should be checked as related findings rather than assuming DNS is the only reflector present.
mitigation: Restrict recursive resolution (allow-recursion) to the organization's own client IP ranges; public-facing authoritative servers should serve authoritative answers only, with recursion disabled entirely.
Enable Response Rate Limiting (RRL) on all resolvers so repeated identical queries are throttled automatically.
Disable or restrict ANY-query support where the resolver software allows it.

Implement BCP38/BCP84 egress source-address filtering at the network edge so spoofed-source packets can't leave the network in the first place — this is the most durable fix and helps against every reflection technique, not just DNS.
Deploy upstream DDoS scrubbing/anycast capacity for any internet-facing resolver so a real amplification flood can be absorbed rather than reaching the origin.

Monitor egress/ingress volumetric anomalies on UDP/53 specifically, since a sudden spike in outbound DNS responses not matched by a corresponding spike in legitimate inbound queries is a strong indicator of resolver abuse in progress.

Periodically re-scan your own address space for newly-exposed resolvers after infrastructure changes, and register internet-facing resolvers with community open-resolver remediation services if found.

NET-002.prerequisites: A network position capable of observing and injecting packets on the path between a target client and the DNS resolver it queries (e.g. the same local network segment, or an on-path position via a separate ARP-spoofing/rogue-DHCP finding). Scapy or a dedicated DNS-spoofing tool (dnsspoof, Ettercap's dns_spoof plugin) and Wireshark for capture verification.
NET-002.whatItIs: An attacker who can see a victim's outgoing DNS lookup (because they're on the same network, or otherwise positioned to intercept it) races the real DNS answer with a fake one of their own — crafted to look just like a real reply — hoping their fake answer arrives first. If it does, the victim's computer accepts it and remembers the wrong, attacker-controlled address for that website.
NET-002.rootCause: Standard DNS lookups have no cryptographic proof that a response is genuine — the only thing protecting against forgery is a couple of numbers that a real response has to match. If an attacker can already see the original request, they already know those numbers, turning this into a simple race instead of requiring any real guesswork.
NET-002.impact: Once a poisoned response is accepted and cached, every subsequent request for that hostname from the affected client (or, if the poisoning targets a shared recursive resolver's cache, every client using that resolver) resolves to the attacker-controlled IP for the cache's TTL duration, enabling transparent traffic interception, credential phishing via a spoofed but correctly-named service, or malware delivery disguised as a legitimate software update.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether DNSSEC is deployed and actually validated by the resolver/client in scope, since a validating resolver rejects a forged response lacking a valid signature chain regardless of transaction-ID/source-port guessing.
Where DNSSEC isn't in play, assess the resolver's source-port randomization behavior (a resolver using a fixed or narrow source-port range is significantly easier to race successfully).

With authorization, position as an on-path observer of a nominated test client's DNS queries and confirm the ability to see the outgoing query's transaction ID before the legitimate resolver's response arrives.
Check whether the client/resolver validates the response's source IP strictly matches the queried server, since some poisoning techniques also spoof the source address.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active DNS response forgery against a nominated test client on the target network segment.
Position to observe the test client's outgoing DNS query for a chosen test hostname.
Craft a forged DNS response matching the observed transaction ID, source port, and queried name, with an attacker-controlled answer IP, and race it against the legitimate resolver's real response.
Confirm the test client accepts and caches the forged answer by having it resolve the test hostname and observing it point to the attacker-controlled IP.
Demonstrate impact via a benign redirect (a test page) rather than an actual phishing/malware payload, and document the poisoning technique and cache-acceptance evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Capture DNS query traffic to observe transaction ID and timing
Craft and race a forged DNS response with Scapy
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from scapy.all import *
send(IP(dst='<victim-ip>', src='<real-resolver-ip>')/UDP(sport=53, dport=<observed-client-port>)/DNS(id=<observed-txid>, qr=1, aa=1, qd=DNSQR(qname='test-target.example.com'), an=DNSRR(rrname='test-target.example.com', rdata='<attacker-controlled-ip>')))
"

examplePayloads.label: Automated tool alternative for local-segment DNS spoofing

variants: On-path spoofing of an individual client's query (requires observing that specific query) versus off-path cache poisoning of a shared recursive resolver (the classic Kaminsky-style attack, requiring transaction-ID/source-port guessing rather than direct observation, and affecting every client behind that resolver).
Poisoning combined with a prior rogue-DHCP/ARP-spoofing finding to first achieve the on-path position needed to observe the victim's queries in the first place.
mitigation: Deploy DNSSEC and ensure resolvers/clients actually validate signatures, which prevents an unsigned or improperly-signed forged response from being accepted regardless of transaction-ID/timing.

Ensure resolvers randomize both transaction ID and source port fully, and consider 0x20 encoding (randomizing query-name letter case) as an additional anti-spoofing layer for resolvers that support it.
Prefer DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS for client-to-resolver communication, which provides transport-layer authentication and encryption closing the on-path forgery vector at that hop.

Address the underlying on-path-positioning vector (ARP spoofing, rogue DHCP) as the root enabler, since a well-secured resolver still doesn't help if the attacker can simply become the DNS server the victim talks to at the network layer.

NET-003.prerequisites: A domain you control (or a subdomain delegation) for hosting an authoritative DNS-tunneling endpoint, and a DNS-tunneling toolkit (iodine, dnscat2) installed on both a test client and the controlled authoritative-side listener. Network access from the test client to any DNS resolver the target environment permits outbound queries to.
NET-003.whatItIs: DNS lookups get used as a hidden communication channel to sneak data out of a network, by encoding stolen data into what looks like unusual website subdomain names, sent to a server the attacker controls — and getting instructions back the same way, hidden in the DNS response. This works because DNS traffic is almost always allowed out of a network with no restriction, even in otherwise tightly locked-down environments.
NET-003.rootCause: DNS has to work everywhere for the internet to function, so it's rarely blocked or closely inspected at the network's edge. And since a subdomain name can technically be almost anything, there's no built-in way to tell a legitimate, oddly-named subdomain apart from one secretly carrying stolen data.
NET-003.impact: An attacker who has gained code execution on an internal host, but who is blocked from direct outbound HTTP(S)/other protocols by egress filtering, can still exfiltrate data or maintain command-and-control communication via DNS queries, since this channel is typically permitted through even a fairly restrictive firewall policy, and detecting the abuse requires DNS-specific traffic analysis rather than generic port/protocol blocking.
stepsToIdentify: Review the network's egress-filtering policy specifically for whether DNS queries are restricted to only the organization's designated internal resolvers, or whether any host can query arbitrary external DNS servers directly.
With authorization, attempt to establish a DNS-tunneling session from a test host using a standard toolkit, and measure whether it succeeds and at what throughput.

Review DNS query logs (if accessible) for anomalies characteristic of tunneling — unusually long subdomain labels, high query volume to a small number of unusual domains, or a high proportion of TXT/NULL record-type queries.

Check whether DNS traffic is inspected by any security tooling (a DNS-specific IDS/analytics product) capable of flagging tunneling-characteristic patterns, versus being entirely unmonitored once it leaves the organization's resolver.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes establishing a DNS-tunneling channel from a designated test host to an attacker-controlled domain.
Set up the authoritative-side listener (iodine/dnscat2 server) for the controlled test domain.
From the test host, establish the tunnel and confirm connectivity through it, measuring achievable throughput.
Demonstrate a benign, bounded data-exfiltration proof-of-concept (transferring a small, clearly-labeled test file) through the tunnel, without accessing or exfiltrating any real, sensitive data.
Document whether the tunnel was detected by any monitoring in place during the test, and the achieved throughput/reliability characteristics.

examplePayloads.label: Start the iodine server on the attacker-controlled authoritative side
Establish the tunnel from the test client
Confirm connectivity and measure throughput through the established tunnel
examplePayloads.command: ping -c5 10.0.0.1  # over the iodine interface, then transfer a small test file to measure throughput

variants: Data-exfiltration-focused tunneling (moving stolen data out) versus full interactive command-and-control tunneling (a reverse shell or agent check-in channel) — both abuse the same underlying protocol characteristic but serve different attacker objectives.
Tunneling via standard A/TXT record queries versus via less common record types (NULL, CNAME chains) that may evade simpler, signature-based tunneling-detection rules.
mitigation: Restrict outbound DNS queries to only the organization's designated internal resolvers, blocking direct external DNS queries from general-purpose hosts at the network egress point.

Deploy DNS-specific monitoring/analytics capable of detecting tunneling-characteristic patterns (query-length distribution anomalies, high-volume queries to a small set of unusual domains, elevated TXT/NULL record-type query proportions).
Apply DNS response-rate and query-rate limiting per host, which raises the cost of high-throughput tunneling even where the channel itself can't be entirely blocked.
Where feasible, use a DNS firewall/RPZ (response policy zone) capability to block resolution of newly-registered or reputation-flagged domains commonly associated with tunneling infrastructure.

NET-004.prerequisites: A network position on the same local multicast domain as the target (mDNS operates only within a single link-local segment). A multicast-capable network interface and a tool for crafting/injecting mDNS responses (Scapy, or a purpose-built mDNS-spoofing tool like Responder's mDNS module).
NET-004.whatItIs: A local device-discovery protocol (used by things like AirPlay-style discovery) lets any device on the network answer 'that's me' when asked about a specific name — with nothing verifying the responder actually owns that name. An attacker can respond first, claiming to be whatever device or service the victim is looking for, and since the answer usually gets trusted and remembered without double-checking, redirect the victim's future traffic to themselves.
NET-004.rootCause: This protocol was built for convenience on small, trusted home networks, where any device answering for a name was assumed to be legitimate — there's no built-in way to actually prove ownership of a name. That assumption falls apart completely on any shared network, like a corporate guest WiFi, where an attacker can simply answer first or more consistently than the real device.
NET-004.impact: An attacker can cause a victim's device to cache a poisoned mDNS resolution redirecting a legitimate local-service hostname (a printer, a file share, an IoT device advertised via mDNS) to an attacker-controlled address, enabling traffic interception or a credential-harvesting man-in-the-middle position for whatever service the victim believed they were reaching.
stepsToIdentify: Passively capture mDNS traffic (multicast address 224.0.0.251, port 5353) on the target network segment to inventory legitimate `.local` names in active use.
With authorization, send a crafted mDNS response claiming ownership of a nominated test `.local` hostname and observe whether a test client's cache accepts and uses it.

Assess whether any client-side verification (checking response consistency across multiple queries, or requiring DNSSEC-like validation which mDNS doesn't natively support) provides any compensating protection.
Determine the network segment's trust level (a fully internal, access-controlled LAN versus a shared guest/public network) to correctly scope the finding's real-world risk.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active mDNS response spoofing against a nominated test client on the target network segment.
Observe the test client's mDNS query for a chosen test `.local` hostname.
Respond with a crafted mDNS answer claiming ownership of that hostname, pointing to an attacker-controlled test address.
Confirm the test client's subsequent connection to that hostname reaches the attacker-controlled address instead of the legitimate service.
Document the poisoning technique and cache-acceptance evidence, without intercepting genuine production traffic beyond the test scenario.

examplePayloads.label: Passively capture mDNS traffic to inventory active .local names
Craft and send a spoofed mDNS response claiming a test hostname
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from scapy.all import *
send(IP(dst='224.0.0.251')/UDP(sport=5353, dport=5353)/DNS(qr=1, aa=1, an=DNSRR(rrname='test-printer.local', type='A', rdata='<attacker-test-ip>')))
"

variants: mDNS response spoofing on IPv4 versus the IPv6 multicast equivalent (using ff02::fb rather than 224.0.0.251), which some spoofing tools/detections handle inconsistently.
Spoofing used purely for traffic redirection versus combined with a subsequent credential-harvesting captive-portal-style interception once traffic is redirected.
mitigation: Restrict mDNS traffic to trusted network segments only, disabling or firewalling it on guest/public/shared networks where zero-configuration discovery isn't a genuine requirement.

Where feasible, use network-level multicast isolation/client-isolation features to prevent one client's mDNS traffic from being observable or spoofable by another untrusted client on the same segment.
Monitor for anomalous or conflicting mDNS responses (the same `.local` name being answered by multiple, inconsistent source addresses) as a detection signature for active spoofing.
For genuinely sensitive local services, prefer an authenticated discovery/connection mechanism over relying on mDNS resolution alone as a trust anchor.

NET-005.prerequisites: A network position on the same local IPv6 segment as the target. An IPv6-capable interface and Scapy (or a dedicated tool like the THC-IPv6 suite) for crafting MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery) packets.
NET-005.whatItIs: A protocol routers use to figure out which devices want which multicast traffic (used with IPv6) has no way to verify that a message claiming to register interest is actually legitimate. An attacker can fake these messages to manipulate what multicast traffic gets forwarded, falsely register or unregister interest on someone else's behalf, or flood the router with fake requests to overload its tracking table.
NET-005.rootCause: This protocol, like much of IPv6's original local-network toolkit, was designed assuming a friendly, cooperative network with no built-in message verification. Any device on the network can send these messages, and a normal router will act on them without checking whether the sender is actually who they claim to be.
NET-005.impact: An attacker can manipulate multicast traffic forwarding on the segment (potentially intercepting or disrupting multicast-dependent applications), or exhaust router resources via a flood of forged listener reports for many distinct groups, denying legitimate multicast service to the segment.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm IPv6 and multicast usage is active on the target segment, and identify what multicast-dependent applications/services are in use, to scope realistic impact.
With authorization, craft and send a forged MLD report claiming (or disclaiming) listener status for a test multicast group and observe whether the router's forwarding behavior changes accordingly.

Test MLD-flood resilience by sending a bounded, agreed volume of forged reports for many distinct groups and monitoring router resource impact (if observable/authorized) or the associated MLD-state table size.
Check whether SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery) or an equivalent IPv6-layer authentication mechanism is deployed, which would meaningfully mitigate this class of spoofing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active MLD spoofing/flooding against the target IPv6 segment's router, with an agreed, bounded approach given the potential for genuine multicast-service disruption.
Send a forged MLD listener report for a nominated test multicast group and confirm the router's forwarding behavior changes to match the forged claim.
Where authorized, send a bounded flood of forged reports for many distinct groups and observe resource-impact indicators.
Document the confirmed spoofing/flooding impact and stop well before genuinely disrupting shared network availability.

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send a forged MLD listener report with Scapy
THC-IPv6 suite alternative for MLD-related attacks

variants: Forged reports manipulating multicast-traffic forwarding for a specific group versus a broad flood targeting router MLD-state-table exhaustion.
MLDv1 versus MLDv2-specific message-format abuse, relevant to which protocol version the target router/segment actually runs.
mitigation: Deploy SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery, RFC 3971) or an equivalent IPv6-layer message-authentication mechanism where router/switch support allows, closing the unauthenticated-message gap.
Apply multicast-related rate limiting on router/switch ports to bound the resource impact of any MLD-flood attempt.
Restrict which network segments/ports are permitted to send MLD messages that the router will act on, where switch-level filtering capability supports it.
Monitor for anomalous MLD message volume/patterns as a detection signature for active spoofing/flooding attempts.

NET-006.prerequisites: Network access to the target service's listening port. Standard banner-grabbing tools (nmap, netcat, telnet) capable of retrieving an unauthenticated service-identification banner.
NET-006.whatItIs: When you connect to a network service — SSH, a mail server, a web server — it responds with a greeting message revealing the exact software and version it's running, more detail than it actually needs to share. That gives an attacker a precise, effortless starting point to go look up known vulnerabilities for that exact version.
NET-006.rootCause: A lot of services show this detailed greeting by default, since it's genuinely handy for administrators troubleshooting a connection. Turning it off or making it generic is a separate hardening step that doesn't affect how the service actually works, so it's easy to just never get done.
NET-006.impact: An attacker can precisely fingerprint the exact software version running on a target service without any active exploitation attempt, then cross-reference that version against public vulnerability databases to identify a specific, known exploit — significantly narrowing and accelerating the reconnaissance phase of an attack compared to having to fingerprint the service through less direct, more effortful means.
stepsToIdentify: Connect to each in-scope service's listening port and capture the initial banner/response using a service-appropriate connection method.

Compare the disclosed detail level against what's operationally necessary — a generic "SSH" identifier is reasonable, whereas a specific vendor, product, and exact patch-level version string is excessive.

Cross-reference any disclosed specific version against public CVE databases to confirm whether the finding also enables identification of a concrete, exploitable vulnerability (in which case this becomes a lead-in to that more specific finding).
Repeat across every network service in scope, since banner verbosity is frequently inconsistent across different services on the same host/estate.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes banner-grabbing reconnaissance against the target services.
Connect to each service and capture its banner/identification response.
Document the exact disclosed version/build detail for each service.
Where a disclosed version maps to a known CVE, note this as a compounding, escalation-worthy finding and consider further, separately-scoped exploitation testing for that specific CVE.

examplePayloads.label: Automated banner-grabbing service scan
Manual banner grab via netcat
Manual banner grab for a web server via curl headers

variants: Verbose banner disclosed at the network-protocol level (SSH/FTP/SMTP greeting) versus at the HTTP application layer (a `Server` response header revealing web-server and framework version).

Banner disclosure on an internal-only service (lower real-world exploitability, since it requires prior network access) versus on an internet-facing service (immediately usable by any remote attacker).
mitigation: Configure services to present a generic, minimal banner that doesn't disclose specific product/version/build detail, where the service supports this configuration option.
Remove or genericize the `Server` (and equivalent) HTTP response header at the web-server/reverse-proxy layer.

Prioritize this as a defense-in-depth, reconnaissance-slowing measure rather than a primary control — patch management addressing the underlying versions remains the more important, direct mitigation for any specific CVE the banner might reveal.
Periodically re-audit banner configuration across the estate, since default configurations are sometimes restored during a service upgrade/reinstall.

NET-007.prerequisites: Network access to the target's SMB service (TCP 445/139). Standard SMB enumeration tools (smbclient, enum4linux, CrackMapExec/NetExec, rpcclient).
NET-007.whatItIs: The target's file-sharing service (SMB) allows someone to connect with no username or password at all — a 'null session' — and depending on how it's set up, that connection can still be used to list shared folders, usernames, group memberships, and password policy settings, all without ever providing a real credential.
NET-007.rootCause: Older versions of this service used to allow this kind of anonymous connection by default, to support certain legitimate background operations. While modern defaults are much stricter, a specific server can still have this setting explicitly turned back on — often to keep some old, legacy application working — leaving this door open.
NET-007.impact: An attacker gains detailed reconnaissance information without needing any valid credential at all — a full username list is a direct input to a subsequent password-spraying/brute-force attack, share names reveal potentially sensitive data-storage locations worth targeting, and password-policy detail informs how aggressive a credential attack can be before triggering lockout.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt to establish a null SMB session against the target and, if successful, enumerate available shares, local users, and groups.

Test specifically for anonymous share enumeration (`IPC$` access) and anonymous user/SID enumeration via RPC calls, since these can sometimes be independently enabled/disabled from the null session itself.
Where a share list is obtained, attempt to connect to each share anonymously to determine whether any additionally permit anonymous read/write access (a compounding, more severe finding).
Confirm the SMB protocol version in use, since this finding is most commonly associated with older SMBv1 configurations but can persist on later versions if specific settings are misconfigured.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes null-session enumeration testing against the target SMB service.
Establish a null/anonymous SMB session and enumerate available shares.
Enumerate local user accounts and groups via the null session, using a purpose-built enumeration tool.
Retrieve password-policy details (lockout threshold, minimum length) if exposed via the same null-session access.
Document every category of information successfully enumerated without credentials, as evidence for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Attempt a null session and enumerate shares
Comprehensive null-session enumeration (users, groups, policy)
Modern alternative using NetExec/CrackMapExec

variants: Null-session share enumeration only, versus full null-session user/group/password-policy enumeration via RPC, the latter providing significantly more attack-planning value.
Null session permitted on a legacy SMBv1 configuration specifically, versus a modern SMB version with a specific misconfigured anonymous-access setting.
mitigation: Disable null-session/anonymous access entirely (`RestrictAnonymous` set to its most restrictive value on Windows, or the equivalent Samba configuration) unless a specific, documented legacy compatibility need exists.

Disable SMBv1 entirely where not required for legacy compatibility, since it's both this finding's most common context and carries its own separate, more severe vulnerabilities (see the related SMBv1/EternalBlue-class finding).
Restrict anonymous share (`IPC$` and others) access explicitly, independent of the general null-session setting.
Periodically re-test null-session access as part of routine internal network assessments, since this setting can regress during system reimaging or a legacy-application-driven configuration change.

NET-008.prerequisites: Network access to the local multicast segment where target devices announce services via mDNS/DNS-SD. Standard mDNS/DNS-SD browsing tools (avahi-browse on Linux, dns-sd on macOS, or a Python script using zeroconf).
NET-008.whatItIs: Devices on the local network automatically broadcast what services they offer (used for things like AirPlay/Chromecast-style discovery), and often reveal more than intended in the process — device names that hint at internal naming schemes, exactly what software and version each device is running, and sometimes extra details like a device's model number or firmware version.
NET-008.rootCause: This broadcasting is unauthenticated and unencrypted by design — the entire point of the protocol is to make devices trivially discoverable to each other. But that same design means anyone else quietly listening on the network sees exactly the same operational details meant only for legitimate local device discovery.
NET-008.impact: An attacker on the local network segment (or one who has gained a foothold there) can passively build a detailed inventory of devices, their services, versions, and naming conventions with zero active probing or authentication required — this reconnaissance directly feeds targeted attack planning (identifying specific device models/versions with known vulnerabilities) and, where naming conventions reveal internal organizational structure, supports social-engineering pretexts.
stepsToIdentify: Passively browse mDNS/DNS-SD advertisements on the target segment for an agreed observation window.
Catalog every advertised device/service, its hostname, and any TXT-record metadata disclosed.

Assess whether any disclosed detail (a specific firmware version, an internal asset-naming pattern, a service type suggesting a sensitive function) constitutes excessive operational disclosure beyond what local discovery genuinely requires.
Cross-reference any disclosed device/firmware version against known CVEs as a potential escalation lead.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes passive mDNS/DNS-SD browsing on the target network segment.
Run a browsing tool for an agreed observation window and capture the full set of advertised services/devices.
Document each device's hostname, advertised service types, and any TXT-record metadata.
Where a specific device/firmware version is identified, note it for potential cross-referencing against known vulnerabilities as a compounding finding.

examplePayloads.label: Browse all advertised mDNS/DNS-SD services on the segment (Linux)
Browse all advertised services (macOS)
Python-based enumeration with zeroconf for scripted analysis

variants: Disclosure via device hostname/naming convention (organizational-structure reconnaissance value) versus via TXT-record firmware/model metadata (direct vulnerability-research value).
mDNS advertisement on a fully internal, access-controlled segment versus on a shared guest/public network where any visitor can passively observe the same detail.
mitigation: Restrict mDNS/DNS-SD traffic to trusted network segments, disabling or firewalling it on shared/guest/public networks where zero-configuration discovery isn't operationally required.
Adopt neutral, non-descriptive device-naming conventions for anything advertised via mDNS/DNS-SD, avoiding internal asset-tagging patterns or organizationally-revealing names.
Minimize TXT-record metadata to only what's genuinely required for service discovery, avoiding disclosure of specific firmware/model version detail where possible.

Periodically conduct the organization's own passive mDNS/DNS-SD survey to understand what an external observer on a shared segment would learn, informing naming-convention and segmentation improvements.

NET-009.prerequisites: A network position on the target's local segment capable of racing DHCP or DNS responses against legitimate ones. Scapy or a dedicated tool (Yersinia for DHCP-related attacks) for crafting and timing race-condition packets. A precise packet-timing capability, since this attack class depends on winning a genuine race window.
NET-009.whatItIs: There's a small window of time between when a device asks for something (like a network address, or a DNS lookup) and when the real, official answer arrives — and during that window, an attacker on the same network can inject a fake answer of their own. If the fake answer gets there first, the device accepts it instead of waiting for the real one.
NET-009.rootCause: Both of these request types just accept whichever answer arrives first as the real one, with no way to detect or reject a genuine answer that shows up a moment too late. It comes down entirely to which response the device happens to process first — something an attacker positioned on the same network can influence just by answering faster and more reliably than the real server.
NET-009.impact: Depending on which protocol's race is won, an attacker can assign a victim a malicious DHCP lease (setting themselves as the default gateway/DNS server, establishing a durable man-in-the-middle position for all the victim's subsequent traffic) or poison a specific DNS resolution — both outcomes stem from the same underlying race-condition weakness and grant the attacker a position to intercept, redirect, or manipulate the victim's network traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target network segment lacks DHCP snooping (for the DHCP-race variant) or DNSSEC validation (for the DNS-race variant), since either compensating control substantially closes the specific race window this finding covers.

With authorization, measure the typical response-time window between a test client's request and the legitimate server's response, to assess how feasible winning the race is for an attacker positioned on the same segment.
Attempt to win the race with a forged response in a controlled test, and confirm whether the client accepts the forged answer.
Assess switch-level protections (DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection) that specifically target this race-condition class at the network-infrastructure layer.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active race-condition exploitation against a nominated test client's DHCP/DNS request on the target segment.
Position to observe the test client's request and prepare a forged response crafted to match the expected reply format.
Race the forged response against the legitimate server's response and confirm which one the test client accepts.

Where the forged response wins, demonstrate the resulting impact (a malicious DHCP-assigned gateway, or a poisoned DNS resolution) using only the test client and non-destructive proof-of-concept actions.
Document the confirmed race-condition outcome and the specific protocol/timing characteristics that made it winnable.

examplePayloads.label: Measure legitimate DHCP/DNS response timing as a baseline
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 67 or udp port 53' -w timing_baseline.pcap

examplePayloads.label: Race a forged DHCP ACK against the legitimate server
examplePayloads.command: yersinia dhcp -attack 3  # rogue DHCP server / discovery race attack mode

examplePayloads.label: Race a forged DNS response (see the dedicated DNS-spoofing finding's payload for a full example)

variants: DHCP-response race (establishing a rogue gateway/DNS assignment) versus DNS-response race (poisoning a specific name resolution) — both share the same underlying timing-race root cause but differ in protocol and resulting impact.

Race won via pure response-speed on an otherwise-unprotected segment versus won by first suppressing/delaying the legitimate server's response (a denial-of-service-assisted race, increasing the attacker's timing advantage).
mitigation: Deploy DHCP snooping on network switches, which drops DHCP server responses from any port not explicitly designated as a trusted uplink, closing the DHCP-race variant at the switch-infrastructure layer.
Deploy DNSSEC validation, closing the DNS-race variant by rejecting an unsigned/improperly-signed forged response regardless of race timing.
Deploy Dynamic ARP Inspection alongside DHCP snooping for comprehensive protection against this broader class of local-segment race/spoofing attacks.
Segment and restrict which hosts can reach client segments directly, reducing the population of potential on-path attackers capable of attempting these races at all.

NET-010.prerequisites: Network access to the target DNS resolver's UDP/53 port from an external (non-client) vantage point. dig or nmap's dns-recursion script for confirmation.
NET-010.whatItIs: A DNS resolver will look things up on behalf of literally anyone on the internet, instead of only its own organization's users. That means anyone can use it to look up any domain they want — and the resolver itself becomes a target for abuse and reconnaissance, separate from whether it's specifically used for the amplification attack described elsewhere.
NET-010.rootCause: The setting controlling who's allowed to use this resolver was left at a permissive default — answer anyone — rather than being explicitly restricted to the organization's own network. This often happens because the resolver was never given a proper hardening pass, or a setting that was once appropriately narrow got loosened at some point to fix an access problem and was never tightened back up.
NET-010.impact: Beyond the amplification-DDoS-specific risk covered by the related finding, an open resolver can be abused for cache-snooping reconnaissance (revealing which domains the organization's users have recently visited by checking whether specific domains are already cached), can be used as a stepping stone to obscure the true source of other DNS-based abuse, and represents a persistent, unnecessary attack-surface exposure regardless of the specific abuse vector chosen.
stepsToIdentify: From a vantage point outside the resolver's expected client base, send a recursive query for a domain the resolver shouldn't have cached and confirm whether it returns an answer (indicating recursion is permitted) versus refusing the query.

Test cache-snooping specifically by querying (non-recursively) for a domain the target's own users are known/suspected to visit, and checking whether a cached answer is returned, revealing recent browsing activity.
Cross-reference this finding against the related DNS-amplification finding, since an open resolver confirmed here is the prerequisite condition for that separate, amplification-specific exploitation.
Check the resolver's public IP against open-resolver-project listings (if already indexed there, it's likely already being abused by third parties).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes open-resolver testing against the target DNS resolver.
Send a recursive query from outside the expected client base and confirm the resolver answers it.
Perform a cache-snooping test query for a plausible, client-relevant domain and check for a cached (non-recursive, immediately-answered) response.
Document the confirmed open-recursion behavior and any cache-snooping findings as evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Test for open recursion from an external vantage point
examplePayloads.command:
dig @<resolver-ip> isc.org A +norecurse
dig @<resolver-ip> isc.org A  # compare recursive vs non-recursive behavior

examplePayloads.label: Automated open-recursion scan across a range
Cache-snooping test for a specific domain

variants: Open recursion combined with high amplification-ratio record types (covered in depth by the dedicated DNS-amplification finding) versus open recursion alone without a notable amplification angle, still valuable for cache-snooping and abuse-obscuring purposes.
Fully open (any internet host) versus open to a broader-than-intended but not fully public range (e.g. an entire ISP's address block rather than the organization's own).
mitigation: Restrict recursive resolution to the organization's own documented client IP ranges via the resolver's `allow-recursion` configuration; public-facing authoritative servers should serve authoritative answers only, with recursion disabled entirely.
Register any internet-facing resolver found open with community open-resolver remediation services/projects to accelerate remediation visibility.
Enable Response Rate Limiting (RRL) as a complementary control, per the related amplification finding.
Periodically re-scan the organization's own address space for newly-exposed open resolvers after infrastructure changes.

NET-011.prerequisites: Network access to a workstation or an installed application capable of configuring its own DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) resolver, independent of the OS/network's configured DNS settings. Wireshark or an equivalent monitoring tool positioned at the network egress/monitoring point to confirm detection gaps.
NET-011.whatItIs: An app or a device setting lets someone route their DNS lookups through an encrypted connection to a resolver of their choice, instead of the organization's own. Because that traffic looks just like ordinary encrypted web browsing from the network's perspective, it completely bypasses whatever DNS-based monitoring, filtering, or logging the organization normally relies on.
NET-011.rootCause: This encrypted DNS feature was specifically designed to protect user privacy from anyone watching the network — which is a genuinely good thing for individual privacy, but directly conflicts with an organization's need to inspect and filter DNS traffic for security. Since many devices now let users pick their own resolver with no central policy stopping them, any endpoint that hasn't been explicitly locked down can quietly route around the organization's DNS-based security controls.
NET-011.impact: Malware or a malicious insider can use a rogue DoH configuration to resolve command-and-control or exfiltration-related domains that the organization's DNS-based blocklist/monitoring would otherwise catch, entirely bypassing that control since the DNS resolution now travels as opaque HTTPS traffic rather than plaintext (or organization-monitored) DNS — this significantly weakens DNS-layer security monitoring as a detection/prevention control across the estate.
stepsToIdentify: Check organizational policy/configuration (via group policy, MDM, or browser enterprise-configuration) for whether DoH is explicitly disabled or locked to only the organization's own DoH-capable resolver.
With authorization, attempt to configure a non-organizational DoH resolver on a test endpoint (via browser settings or OS-level configuration) and confirm whether the change is permitted.
Where permitted, generate DNS queries via the rogue DoH configuration and confirm whether the organization's DNS-monitoring/security tooling has any visibility into or ability to block them.
Assess whether network-level blocking of known public DoH resolver endpoints (as a compensating control) is in place.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes DoH-bypass testing against a designated test endpoint.
Configure a rogue, non-organizational DoH resolver on the test endpoint.
Perform DNS resolution for a test domain via the rogue DoH configuration and confirm it succeeds.
Check whether the organization's DNS security monitoring/logging captured or could act on this resolution.
Document the confirmed bypass and the resulting gap in DNS-layer security visibility.

examplePayloads.label: Configure a rogue DoH resolver in a Chromium-based browser (test endpoint)
examplePayloads.command: # Browser settings -> Privacy and Security -> Security -> Use secure DNS -> With: Custom -> https://dns.example-public-resolver.com/dns-query

examplePayloads.label: Confirm DNS resolution via the rogue DoH configuration is functioning
examplePayloads.command: # perform a test domain lookup through the browser and confirm resolution succeeds

examplePayloads.label: Check for network-level blocking of known public DoH endpoints

variants: User-configured rogue DoH via browser settings (requires only standard user privilege) versus a malware-configured rogue DoH resolver embedded directly in malicious code, bypassing any user-facing configuration UI entirely.
DoH bypass affecting only a specific application's DNS resolution (browser-only DoH) versus a system-wide DoH configuration affecting every application on the endpoint.
mitigation: Explicitly disable or lock DoH configuration via enterprise policy (browser group policy, MDM configuration profiles) to prevent endpoints from using an unauthorized DoH resolver.

Where DoH is desired for its privacy/integrity benefits, deploy and mandate the organization's own DoH-capable resolver, preserving DNS-layer visibility while still gaining DoH's transport protections.
Block known public DoH resolver endpoints at the network egress level as a compensating control for any endpoint that isn't fully centrally managed.
Monitor for HTTPS traffic patterns characteristic of DoH usage to unexpected/non-approved resolver endpoints as a detection signature.

NET-012.prerequisites: Access to Certificate Transparency log query tools (crt.sh, or the CT Search API of a major log operator) and the target organization's known domain names.
NET-012.whatItIs: Public logs that record every legitimately-issued website security certificate can reveal gaps in an organization's own oversight — certificates issued for subdomains the security team never even knew existed, or certificates issued by a provider that shouldn't have been allowed to issue them at all, because the DNS setting meant to restrict that wasn't properly configured.
NET-012.rootCause: Every publicly trusted certificate has to be logged in these public records — which is a good security feature overall — but an organization that never actually checks its own log entries has no visibility into certificates being issued for its own domains by anyone capable of passing the issuer's verification process, including a compromised internal process or an unauthorized team.
NET-012.impact: An unmonitored, unauthorized certificate issuance for the organization's domain — whether from an internal shadow-IT source or an external party who's somehow satisfied domain validation improperly — can go undetected indefinitely, and if the certificate falls into the wrong hands, enables a highly convincing phishing or man-in-the-middle setup using a certificate that browsers will trust completely, since it's genuinely valid and CT-logged.
stepsToIdentify: Query CT logs (via crt.sh or an equivalent) for every certificate ever issued for the organization's registered domains and subdomains.
Cross-reference the resulting certificate list against the organization's own asset inventory/known subdomains, flagging any certificate for a subdomain not in the documented inventory.

Check the organization's DNS for CAA records restricting which CAs are authorized to issue certificates for its domains, and confirm whether any logged certificate was issued by a CA outside that authorized list.
Assess whether the organization has any active, ongoing CT-log-monitoring process (versus this being a one-time, point-in-time check performed only during this assessment).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes CT-log reconnaissance against the target organization's domains — this is a purely passive, externally-observable data-source review requiring no direct interaction with the target's infrastructure.
Query CT logs for the full historical certificate-issuance record across all in-scope domains.
Compile the list of certificates for undocumented/unexpected subdomains and any issued by an unauthorized CA (per CAA records).
For any suspicious certificate found, attempt to determine (via passive means — WHOIS, historical DNS records) whether the corresponding subdomain is still active and what it hosts.
Document each finding as evidence of a gap in either certificate-issuance authorization control (CAA) or asset-inventory/monitoring completeness.

examplePayloads.label: Query CT logs for all certificates issued for the organization's domain
Check for CAA records restricting authorized certificate issuers
Cross-reference discovered subdomains against known DNS records
examplePayloads.command: for sub in $(cat ct_discovered_subdomains.txt); do dig +short $sub; done

variants: Certificate issued for a genuinely forgotten/shadow-IT subdomain (an internal governance gap) versus one issued by a CA outside the organization's CAA-authorized list (a potential domain-validation-control failure worth deeper investigation).
A single, historical, likely-benign certificate anomaly versus an ongoing pattern of unauthorized issuance suggesting a systemic gap in the organization's certificate-request process.
mitigation: Implement active, ongoing CT-log monitoring (via a dedicated service or a scheduled automated query) for the organization's domains, alerting on any newly-logged certificate for an unrecognized subdomain or unauthorized CA.

Publish CAA DNS records explicitly restricting which CAs are authorized to issue certificates for the organization's domains, closing the gap that allows an unexpected CA to issue a valid certificate at all.
Maintain a complete, current asset inventory of subdomains (overlapping with the general improper-inventory-management finding) to make CT-log cross-referencing meaningful and actionable.

Establish a clear, centralized certificate-request process so legitimate certificate issuance is always expected and traceable, making any CT-log anomaly easier to immediately recognize as unauthorized.

NET-013.prerequisites: Network access to the target's SIP/VoIP infrastructure. SIPVicious (svmap/svwar/svcrack) or a similar SIP-enumeration toolkit, and a softphone/SIP client for manual verification.
NET-013.whatItIs: A phone system's signaling setup lets someone figure out which internal phone extensions are real, just by watching for differences in how the system responds to valid versus made-up extension numbers — and where extensions are protected by a weak or default PIN, an attacker can brute-force their way into one, letting them make fraudulent calls or eavesdrop on call setup.
NET-013.rootCause: Phone systems are often set up with a focus on call quality and easy interoperability rather than security, and default settings frequently allow this kind of anonymous probing — meant for legitimate network health checks — to be abused for reconnaissance. That's often paired with short, easy-to-remember numeric PINs used for convenience.
NET-013.impact: Toll fraud (an attacker registering as a valid extension and placing expensive international/premium-rate calls billed to the organization) is the most immediately monetizable impact, alongside eavesdropping on call setup metadata and, in unencrypted deployments, potential media-stream interception (see the related SIP/RTP eavesdropping finding) — VoIP toll fraud specifically has caused substantial real-world financial losses for under-secured deployments.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for SIP services (typically UDP/TCP 5060) across the target's network range.
Enumerate valid extension numbers by observing differing SIP response codes/timing for existing versus non-existing extensions via OPTIONS or REGISTER probing.
For enumerated extensions, attempt to determine authentication strength by testing a small, bounded set of common/default PIN values against a nominated test extension.
Assess whether the SIP infrastructure is reachable from the internet directly (significantly higher risk) versus only from an internal/VPN-connected position.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SIP enumeration and credential-testing against the target VoIP infrastructure, using a nominated test extension for any credential-testing step.
Scan for and confirm the SIP service's presence and version/vendor via banner/OPTIONS response.
Enumerate valid extensions using a SIP-enumeration tool.
Attempt authentication against the nominated test extension using a bounded, agreed set of weak/default PIN candidates.
Where a weak credential is found, demonstrate impact via a benign test call/registration rather than an actual toll-fraud call, and document the finding.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for SIP services across the target range
Enumerate valid extensions on a discovered SIP server
Test a bounded set of weak PINs against a nominated test extension

variants: Extension enumeration and credential brute-force enabling toll fraud, versus a call-eavesdropping/interception angle if the SIP signaling and media (RTP) streams are also unencrypted (overlapping with the dedicated SIP/RTP eavesdropping finding).

SIP infrastructure exposed directly to the internet (severe, remotely exploitable) versus reachable only from an internal network position (still a significant finding but requiring prior network access).
mitigation: Require strong, non-default authentication credentials for every SIP extension, avoiding short numeric PINs in favor of longer, more complex values where the endpoint hardware/softphone supports it.
Restrict SIP service reachability to only expected, authorized network sources (internal segments, a specific trunk provider's IP range) rather than leaving it broadly reachable.
Implement account lockout/rate limiting on failed SIP authentication attempts to prevent unbounded credential brute-forcing.

Enable call-detail-record monitoring/alerting for anomalous call patterns (unusual destinations, unusual call volume/timing) as a detective control against toll fraud that slips past preventive measures.

NET-014.prerequisites: A network position on the same local multicast segment as the target (identical prerequisite set to NET-004's cache-poisoning finding, since both exploit the same fundamental mDNS trust gap). Scapy or a purpose-built mDNS-spoofing tool.
NET-014.whatItIs: This is the more active version of the local device-discovery spoofing described elsewhere: instead of targeting one specific device name, an attacker responds to every single local discovery request on the network, impersonating whatever's being asked for — positioning themselves as a man-in-the-middle across a wide range of local services like file sharing, printing, or smart-device control.
NET-014.rootCause: Same root cause as the more targeted version: this discovery protocol has no built-in way to verify a response is genuine, so any device on the network can answer for any name, and devices generally just trust whichever answer arrives first.
NET-014.impact: Broad, opportunistic man-in-the-middle positioning across every mDNS-dependent service on the segment simultaneously, rather than a single, targeted hostname — this can affect file-sharing protocols, printer communications, media-casting protocols, and IoT device-control channels all at once, giving the attacker a wide surface for credential harvesting or traffic manipulation across many different applications and users on the shared segment.
stepsToIdentify: Passively observe mDNS query volume and diversity on the target segment to characterize how many distinct services/hostnames are being actively queried (indicating the breadth of potential opportunistic-spoofing impact).
With authorization, respond to every observed mDNS query on the segment with a forged answer pointing to an attacker-controlled test address, rather than targeting a single, pre-selected name.
Confirm the breadth of impact by observing how many distinct clients/services accept the forged responses across the observation window.

Assess whether client isolation (see the related wireless/wired network-isolation findings) is in place, which would limit this broad spoofing technique's reach even if mDNS itself remains unauthenticated.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes broad, opportunistic mDNS spoofing against the target network segment, agreeing a bounded test window given the potential for widespread, if benign, disruption.
Run a tool that responds to every mDNS query observed on the segment with a forged answer directing to an attacker-controlled test endpoint.
Observe and document which services/clients accept the forged responses across the test window.
Demonstrate impact via a benign redirect for one representative, nominated test scenario (rather than actually intercepting real production traffic across every affected client).
Stop the broad spoofing promptly once the finding is proven, given its potential for widespread disruption if left running.

examplePayloads.label: Passively observe mDNS query volume/diversity as a baseline
Respond to all observed mDNS queries with a forged answer (bounded test window)

variants: Broad, opportunistic spoofing across all observed queries (this finding) versus targeted spoofing of one specific, pre-selected hostname (the related NET-004 cache-poisoning finding) — the underlying protocol weakness is identical, but the exploitation breadth and typical attacker objective differ.

Spoofing on a segment lacking client isolation (broad, multi-client impact) versus one with client isolation in place (limiting the practical reach even though the mDNS weakness itself is unaddressed).
mitigation: Restrict mDNS traffic to trusted, isolated network segments, disabling it on guest/shared/public networks.
Apply client isolation on shared segments to limit the practical reach of any broad spoofing attempt even where mDNS remains technically unauthenticated.

Monitor for anomalous or high-volume conflicting mDNS responses across many distinct queried names as a detection signature for this broader spoofing pattern, distinct from a single targeted poisoning attempt.
For genuinely sensitive local services, avoid relying on mDNS-based discovery/connection as a trust anchor at all.

NET-015.prerequisites: Network access to a target service using DTLS (WebRTC, VPN, IoT) or QUIC (HTTP/3). A TLS/QUIC-analysis tool (nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers adapted for DTLS where supported, or a dedicated QUIC-analysis tool/library) and Wireshark for capture-based inspection.
NET-015.whatItIs: A service using one of the newer, UDP-based encrypted connection protocols (used for things like video calls or newer web traffic) is set up with weak encryption settings, an outdated version, or skips properly checking the other side's certificate — the same kind of TLS weaknesses covered elsewhere in this list, just showing up in these newer transport protocols instead of classic web traffic.
NET-015.rootCause: Securing these newer protocols is a less mature, less well-trodden area compared to decades of established practice around classic web encryption. It's common for a service adopting one of these newer transports to end up with weaker default settings, simply because far less organizational attention and tooling has been built up around auditing them.
NET-015.impact: Depending on the specific weakness, impact mirrors the classic TLS equivalents — weak cipher suites enabling practical decryption, missing certificate validation enabling a man-in-the-middle position, or an outdated protocol version carrying known vulnerabilities — but occurring in DTLS/QUIC-based services (WebRTC media streams, VPN tunnels, HTTP/3 web traffic) that may not have received the same routine hardening review as the organization's classic HTTPS endpoints.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all in-scope services using DTLS (WebRTC-based applications, certain VPN products) or QUIC/HTTP/3.

For each, attempt to enumerate supported cipher suites and protocol versions using DTLS/QUIC-aware tooling, since standard TCP-based TLS scanners often don't handle these UDP-based protocols correctly.
Capture a sample handshake with Wireshark and manually inspect the negotiated parameters where automated tooling support is limited.

Confirm whether certificate validation is genuinely enforced (attempt a connection with a certificate the client shouldn't trust) rather than merely assumed present because the classic TLS equivalent enforces it correctly.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes DTLS/QUIC configuration testing against the target service.
Enumerate supported cipher suites/protocol versions using available tooling, supplementing with manual Wireshark capture analysis where needed.
Where a weak cipher suite or outdated protocol version is confirmed supported, assess practical exploitability using the same techniques applicable to the classic TLS equivalent weakness.
Test certificate validation enforcement by attempting a connection with an untrusted/self-signed test certificate.
Document the exact weak configuration confirmed and its practical exploitability for the specific DTLS/QUIC-based service.

examplePayloads.label: Capture a DTLS/QUIC handshake for manual configuration analysis
Inspect negotiated parameters in the capture with Wireshark's protocol dissectors
Test certificate validation enforcement with an untrusted test certificate

variants: Weak cipher-suite/protocol-version configuration on a WebRTC-based media service (DTLS) versus on an HTTP/3 web service (QUIC) — both share the same root-cause hardening gap but affect different service types.
Missing certificate validation specifically, versus a supported-but-not-mandated weak cipher suite that a downgrade attempt could still force even if a strong default is otherwise negotiated.
mitigation: Apply the same TLS-hardening rigor to DTLS/QUIC configuration as to classic TLS — disable weak/outdated cipher suites and protocol versions, and enforce strict certificate validation.
Use current, well-maintained DTLS/QUIC libraries that default to strong configurations, rather than manually configuring cipher suites where avoidable.
Include DTLS/QUIC-based services explicitly in routine TLS-configuration audits, rather than assuming coverage from classic HTTPS-focused scanning tools/processes alone.
Stay current with DTLS/QUIC-specific hardening guidance as it matures, since this is a faster-evolving area than classic TLS best practice.

NET-016.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Grafana instance (typically port 3000 or fronted by a reverse proxy). A web browser or curl for testing default credentials.
NET-016.whatItIs: A monitoring dashboard tool is reachable with its factory-default admin username and password still active — meaning it was never changed during or after setup, giving full administrative control to anyone who finds and reaches it.
NET-016.rootCause: This tool ships with a well-known default login specifically to make initial setup easier, and changing it afterward is a manual step that's easy to skip — especially for something that started as a quick test or internal tool and just never got a proper hardening pass.
NET-016.impact: Full administrative access to the monitoring platform, which frequently has read access configured to numerous backend data sources (databases, cloud metrics APIs, internal services) — an attacker with Grafana admin access can not only view all dashboarded metrics/data (a significant information-disclosure risk on its own) but in many configurations can also add new data-source connections or execute queries against existing ones, potentially pivoting into the underlying data sources themselves.
stepsToIdentify: Identify Grafana instances in scope via port/service scanning or subdomain enumeration (a distinctive login page, or a `/api/health` endpoint disclosing the product).
Attempt login with the documented default credential (`admin`/`admin`).
Where successful, review the instance's configured data sources to assess the scope of backend access the compromised admin session provides.
Check the Grafana version for any additional known CVEs that might compound the impact beyond just the default-credential access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes default-credential login testing against the identified Grafana instance.
Attempt login with the default admin credential.
Where successful, enumerate configured data sources and dashboards to document the scope of accessible backend systems/data.
Demonstrate impact via a benign, read-only action (viewing a dashboard, listing data sources) rather than modifying configuration or querying sensitive backend data beyond what's needed as evidence.
Document the confirmed default-credential access and the resulting scope of exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Identify a Grafana instance via its health endpoint
Attempt login with default credentials
Enumerate configured data sources using the authenticated session

variants: Default credential never changed at all, versus changed to another common/weak value (a variant of the same underlying weak-credential-hygiene gap).
Default-credential access to Grafana alone, versus combined with a further, known Grafana CVE (several plugin- or path-traversal-related CVEs have affected various versions) compounding the impact.
mitigation: Change the default administrative credential immediately upon deployment, as a mandatory, enforced first-run step rather than an optional recommendation.
Integrate Grafana authentication with the organization's SSO/identity provider where feasible, removing standalone local-credential risk entirely.
Restrict network reachability of monitoring dashboards to internal/VPN-only access rather than exposing them directly to the internet.
Include default-credential checks for all monitoring/observability tooling in routine internal vulnerability scanning.

NET-017.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Zabbix or Nagios monitoring server (typically a web interface on port 80/443, or a dedicated port depending on deployment). A web browser or curl for testing default credentials.
NET-017.whatItIs: A network-monitoring server is reachable using its documented, well-known default admin credentials, still unchanged — giving full administrative access to the entire monitoring platform to anyone who finds it.
NET-017.rootCause: This platform ships with default credentials specifically to help with initial setup, and changing them afterward is easy to forget, especially for internal monitoring tools that don't get the same security attention as customer-facing systems.
NET-017.impact: Full administrative access to the network-monitoring platform, which typically has extensive visibility into the organization's entire infrastructure inventory (every monitored host, its IP address, running services, and often stored credentials for agent-based or remote-check authentication) — an attacker with this access gains a comprehensive, ready-made reconnaissance map of the internal network, and in many configurations can also execute remote checks/scripts against monitored hosts, providing a potential pivot point into the broader environment.
stepsToIdentify: Identify Zabbix/Nagios instances in scope via port/service scanning, a distinctive login page, or product-specific default paths.
Attempt login with the documented default credential for the identified product/version.
Where successful, review the monitored-host inventory and any stored credentials/check configurations to assess the scope of exposure.
Check whether the platform is configured to execute remote scripts/checks against monitored hosts, which would compound the impact into a potential lateral-movement vector.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes default-credential login testing against the identified monitoring platform.
Attempt login with the default administrative credential.
Where successful, enumerate the monitored-host inventory as evidence of the reconnaissance-value impact.
Where remote-check/script execution capability is confirmed, demonstrate a benign, non-destructive proof-of-concept action against a designated test host rather than a production monitored asset.
Document the confirmed default-credential access and the resulting scope of exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Identify a Zabbix instance and attempt default-credential login
Enumerate monitored hosts using the authenticated session

variants: Zabbix's specific documented default credential versus a Nagios deployment with a weak, guessable custom credential rather than a true vendor-shipped default — both represent the same underlying weak-credential-hygiene gap.
Read-only default-credential access (dashboard/inventory viewing) versus access that also permits remote check/script execution against monitored hosts, the latter being materially more severe.
mitigation: Change default administrative credentials immediately upon deployment, enforced as a mandatory first-run step.
Integrate authentication with the organization's SSO/identity provider where the platform supports it.
Restrict network reachability of the monitoring platform to internal/VPN-only access.
Apply least privilege to any remote-check/script-execution capability, and audit which hosts/scripts are reachable from the monitoring platform's administrative interface.

NET-018.prerequisites: Network access to a configuration-management server's control interface (Ansible Tower/AWX API, Salt master's port 4505/4506, Puppet master's port 8140). Standard HTTP/API tooling (curl) and, where authentication is confirmed absent, the ability to submit a job/command through the exposed interface.
NET-018.whatItIs: A configuration-management server — a tool specifically designed to push commands and settings out to every server it manages — is reachable over the network with no login required at all, or is exposed more broadly than it should be.
NET-018.rootCause: Tools like this are inherently some of the highest-trust, highest-impact systems in an environment, since they're built to run commands across an entire fleet of machines. That exact power makes any gap in their login or network exposure extremely serious — yet they're sometimes set up quickly for internal convenience without the same careful access review given to customer-facing systems.
NET-018.impact: An attacker who reaches an unauthenticated configuration-management control interface can push a malicious configuration/command to every host under that server's management in one action — this is among the most severe possible findings in any network environment, since it provides a direct path to compromise the entire managed fleet simultaneously, not just a single host.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for configuration-management service ports/interfaces across the target's network range.
For each discovered instance, attempt to access its control interface/API without providing any credential.
Where access succeeds, enumerate the scope of managed hosts (without executing any command) to establish the potential blast radius.
Assess whether the interface is reachable from a broader network scope than its intended, restricted management-network boundary.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes interacting with the discovered, unauthenticated configuration-management interface — given the severity and blast radius, this needs unambiguous authorization and an agreed, tightly-bounded action plan.
Access the interface without credentials and enumerate the managed-host inventory as the primary evidence of scope.

Where authorized to demonstrate command-execution impact, submit a single, clearly-labeled, entirely benign command/job (e.g. writing a uniquely-named marker file) targeted at one specific, nominated test host only — never a fleet-wide action.
Confirm the benign action executed successfully on the nominated test host, then immediately stop, given the severity of what broader access would represent.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated access, the managed-host inventory scope, and the demonstrated command-execution capability.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for configuration-management service ports
Attempt unauthenticated access to a discovered Ansible Tower/AWX API
Enumerate managed hosts via an unauthenticated Salt master (if reachable)

variants: Fully unauthenticated control-plane access (no credential barrier at all) versus authentication present but the interface reachable from a far broader network scope than its intended management-only segment.
Read-only enumeration access versus full command/job-execution capability — the latter is categorically more severe.
mitigation: Require strong authentication (and ideally mutual TLS/certificate-based authentication) on every configuration-management control interface, with no exceptions.
Restrict network reachability of the control interface to a dedicated, tightly-controlled management network/VLAN, never exposing it to general internal network segments or the internet.
Apply the principle of least privilege to which users/roles can submit jobs/commands, and audit/log every job execution for accountability.
Treat configuration-management infrastructure as a top-tier, highest-priority asset in security review and monitoring, given its inherent fleet-wide blast radius.

NET-019.prerequisites: A network position on a segment participating in PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) or IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) signaling. Scapy or a dedicated multicast-testing tool for crafting IGMP/PIM messages.
NET-019.whatItIs: Protocols that manage multicast traffic (used for things like streaming to many devices at once) aren't set up to restrict which parts of the network are actually trusted to participate. An attacker on an untrusted part of the network can inject fake join/leave messages to manipulate which devices receive multicast traffic, or in some setups, even influence how that traffic gets routed.
NET-019.rootCause: These protocols were designed assuming a cooperative, trusted network of routers and devices, and real authentication for them is rarely actually turned on in practice. Combined with no restriction on which network segments are trusted to send these messages, any device reachable on a participating part of the network can typically influence multicast behavior across the whole network.
NET-019.impact: An attacker can disrupt legitimate multicast-dependent services (video distribution, financial market-data feeds, some VoIP/paging systems) by manipulating group membership or routing-tree state, or in some scenarios redirect multicast traffic to an unintended destination, potentially exposing or disrupting sensitive multicast-distributed content.
stepsToIdentify: Identify multicast-dependent applications/services in scope and confirm PIM/IGMP is actively used to support them.
Review router/switch configuration for interface-level trust restrictions on which segments are permitted to send PIM/IGMP signaling that's acted upon.
