With authorization, craft and send a forged IGMP join/leave message for a test multicast group and observe whether the router's group-membership state changes accordingly.
Where PIM specifically is in scope, assess whether IPsec or an equivalent authentication mechanism is deployed for PIM signaling.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active IGMP/PIM signaling manipulation against the target network segment, with a bounded, agreed approach given the potential for genuine multicast-service disruption.
Send a forged IGMP join/leave message for a nominated test multicast group and confirm the resulting group-membership state change.
Where authorized, test PIM-specific manipulation and observe any resulting routing-tree impact.
Document the confirmed manipulation and stop well before genuinely disrupting shared multicast services.

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send a forged IGMP join message with Scapy
Check router multicast group-membership state after injection
examplePayloads.command: show ip igmp groups  # on a Cisco-style device, with authorization

variants: IGMP join/leave manipulation affecting local group membership, versus PIM-level manipulation affecting the broader multicast routing tree across multiple hops.

Manipulation causing a denial-of-service (disrupting legitimate multicast delivery) versus a traffic-redirection angle (routing multicast content to an unintended, potentially attacker-observable destination).
mitigation: Restrict which interfaces/segments are trusted to participate in PIM/IGMP signaling via switch/router-level configuration (IGMP snooping with appropriate trust boundaries, PIM neighbor filtering).
Deploy IPsec or an equivalent authentication mechanism for PIM signaling where router support allows.
Apply rate limiting on IGMP/PIM message processing to bound the impact of any injection/flooding attempt.
Segment multicast-dependent, sensitive traffic onto dedicated, access-controlled network infrastructure separate from general-purpose segments.

NET-020.prerequisites: Network access to a target NTP server configured with Autokey authentication. Wireshark for capturing Autokey exchange traffic, and knowledge of Autokey's documented cryptographic weaknesses.
NET-020.whatItIs: An older method for cryptographically securing time-synchronization traffic (meant to stop an attacker from spoofing what time it is) relies on a scheme with well-documented, long-standing weaknesses — so much so that current best-practice guidance recommends against using it at all in favor of a newer replacement. Simply still using it is itself the finding, regardless of the exact configuration.
NET-020.rootCause: This method was designed in an earlier, less rigorous era of security engineering, and it's accumulated enough publicly known weaknesses over time that even its own broader community has moved on to a more modern, better-designed replacement. An organization still using it is relying on something its own designers and the wider security community have already abandoned.
NET-020.impact: Depending on the specific weakness exploited, an attacker may be able to defeat Autokey's intended authentication, enabling NTP spoofing (see the related NTP-spoofing finding) despite Autokey nominally being in place specifically to prevent that — undermining time-synchronization integrity, which can cascade into problems for any time-sensitive security control (certificate validity checking, Kerberos ticket lifetimes, log-correlation accuracy) that depends on accurate system time.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether Autokey is the authentication mechanism in use for NTP on the target's time-synchronization infrastructure, versus NTS or simple symmetric-key authentication.
Capture Autokey's identity/key-exchange traffic and review it against publicly-documented weaknesses in the specific protocol version/implementation.
Assess the practical impact of accurate time synchronization being compromised, given what other security controls in the environment depend on it.
Confirm whether the NTP server/client software in use has received patches for known Autokey-specific CVEs, if any apply to the specific version.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes NTP Autokey configuration review and, where a specific technical weakness applies, exploitation testing against the target infrastructure.
Capture and analyze the Autokey exchange to identify the specific implementation/version in use.

Where a documented, exploitable weakness applies to that specific version, assess feasibility of using it to defeat Autokey's authentication, potentially chaining into the related NTP-spoofing finding.
Document the confirmed use of the deprecated Autokey mechanism as a standalone finding regardless of whether a specific further weakness was successfully chained.

examplePayloads.label: Capture NTP Autokey exchange traffic for analysis
Query the NTP server for its configured authentication scheme

variants: Autokey in use with no further, additional exploitable weakness confirmed (still a valid finding given its deprecated status) versus Autokey combined with a confirmed, exploitable implementation-specific weakness enabling a practical spoofing bypass.

Autokey's own protocol design was found to have cryptographic weaknesses independent of implementation bugs, meaning even a fully-patched Autokey deployment carries residual protocol-level risk that symmetric-key or NTS-based authentication does not.
mitigation: Migrate from NTP Autokey to NTS (Network Time Security), the current, TLS-based, actively-maintained authentication mechanism for NTP.
Where NTS isn't yet supported by the deployed NTP software, use simple symmetric-key authentication as an interim, better-understood alternative to Autokey.
Track and apply patches for the specific NTP software version in use, since Autokey-related and other NTP CVEs continue to be disclosed periodically.

Treat accurate, authenticated time synchronization as a security-relevant dependency across the environment, prioritizing its remediation given how many other controls (certificate validation, Kerberos, log correlation) rely on it.

NET-021.prerequisites: Network access to the target RADIUS/TACACS+ authentication server or a position on the path between a network device and that server. Wireshark for capture and analysis, and, where PAP/weak shared-secret conditions are found, a password-cracking tool (hashcat/John the Ripper) or a RADIUS-specific tool (radsniff, eapmd5pass).
NET-021.whatItIs: The systems that centrally manage logins for network devices are set up with outdated, weak protections — using an old, crackable method to secure shared secrets, an old scheme that only lightly obfuscates traffic instead of properly encrypting it, or transmitting passwords in a form that's effectively as readable as plain text.
NET-021.rootCause: These login systems were designed in an earlier era with weaker cryptography than would be chosen today. Stronger, modern options do exist for both, but an organization can still be running them in their older, weaker configuration mode — especially the systems used for device administration, which tend to get less security attention than the ones users interact with directly.
NET-021.impact: An attacker who can observe RADIUS/TACACS+ traffic (via a position on the network path, or a compromised network device) may be able to recover the shared secret via offline cracking (if it's weak) or, for TACACS+'s classic weak-obfuscation scheme, decrypt captured packet bodies directly — either outcome can expose network-device administrative credentials or enable forging further authentication requests, potentially compromising the broader network-device administrative-access control plane.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the RADIUS/TACACS+ server(s) and review their configuration for shared-secret strength, PAP usage, and, for TACACS+, whether classic weak obfuscation or a newer, properly-encrypted mode is in use.
With authorization, capture authentication traffic between a network device and the RADIUS/TACACS+ server.
For RADIUS, attempt to crack the shared secret offline from the captured response-authenticator material if it appears weak.
For TACACS+, attempt to decrypt the captured packet body using its classic (weak) obfuscation scheme if that mode is confirmed in use.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes RADIUS/TACACS+ traffic capture and offline cracking/decryption against the target infrastructure.
Capture authentication traffic during a test authentication event (using a nominated test network device/account where possible).
Attempt offline cracking of a weak RADIUS shared secret, or direct decryption of TACACS+'s classic obfuscation scheme.
Where successful, confirm the recovered secret/credential by using it to construct and validate a forged authentication exchange in a controlled test.
Document the specific weakness confirmed and the resulting credential/secret exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Capture RADIUS/TACACS+ authentication traffic
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 'udp port 1812 or tcp port 49' -w authn_capture.pcap

examplePayloads.label: Attempt offline RADIUS shared-secret cracking
examplePayloads.command:
radsniff -i eth0 -f 'udp port 1812' -O pcap_perror
hashcat -m 22300 radius_hash.txt wordlist.txt  # mode number varies by RADIUS hash type extracted

examplePayloads.label: Decrypt captured TACACS+ traffic using its classic weak obfuscation (with the shared key, if separately obtained, or via cracking)

variants: Weak RADIUS shared secret enabling offline cracking of the response-authenticator material, versus TACACS+'s classic obfuscation scheme being directly (not just weakly) reversible given the shared key.
PAP-based inner authentication (cleartext-equivalent credential transport) versus a stronger EAP-TLS/PEAP-based method for RADIUS specifically.
mitigation: Use long, high-entropy, randomly generated shared secrets for both RADIUS and TACACS+, rotated periodically.
Migrate TACACS+ to a properly-encrypted transport variant where the vendor/implementation supports it, rather than the classic weak-obfuscation mode.
For RADIUS-based 802.1X, use EAP-TLS or PEAP rather than PAP for the inner authentication method.
Restrict network reachability of the RADIUS/TACACS+ traffic path to trusted management-network segments, reducing the population of potential on-path observers.

NET-022.prerequisites: Network access to the target's SNMP service (UDP 161). snmpwalk or an equivalent SNMP client, and Wireshark to capture and confirm the actual security level negotiated.
NET-022.whatItIs: The device supports a properly encrypted mode for its monitoring protocol (SNMP), but it's configured to only authenticate — not actually encrypt — the traffic, or sometimes neither. That means monitoring data, which often includes detailed device configuration and status information, travels across the network in plain, readable text even though the device is fully capable of encrypting it.
NET-022.rootCause: This encryption setting has to be turned on separately from the authentication setting, and it's common for administrators to set up authentication (to stop unauthorized access) while overlooking the separate step of actually turning on encryption — especially if the device was upgraded from an older protocol version that never had encryption as an option at all.
NET-022.impact: Anyone with network-path visibility (a shared segment, a compromised intermediate device) can passively capture and read SNMP traffic in full, exposing device configuration detail, interface/routing state, and any other MIB data queried — this is primarily an information-disclosure risk, but the disclosed configuration detail can meaningfully aid further network reconnaissance and attack planning.
stepsToIdentify: Query the target device's SNMPv3 configuration (where administrative access allows) or capture live SNMP traffic to determine the actual security level in use.
Confirm whether authPriv is configured and actually negotiated for the specific user/community in use, versus authNoPriv or noAuthNoPriv.
Where cleartext SNMP traffic is captured, inspect its content for the specific data disclosed (interface tables, routing info, system description).
Check whether SNMPv1/v2c (which have no meaningful security at all) remain enabled alongside SNMPv3, since either protocol version being reachable independently negates SNMPv3's protections.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SNMP traffic capture and querying against the target device.
Capture SNMP traffic during a normal query/poll cycle and confirm the negotiated security level.
Where cleartext (authNoPriv/noAuthNoPriv) traffic is confirmed, extract and document the specific MIB data disclosed.
Separately query the device to check whether SNMPv1/v2c remains enabled and reachable, which would represent a more severe, independent finding.

examplePayloads.label: Capture SNMP traffic to determine actual security level
Inspect the security level negotiated in the capture
Check whether SNMPv1/v2c remains independently reachable

variants: authNoPriv (authenticated but no encryption) versus noAuthNoPriv (neither authentication nor encryption) — both share the missing-encryption root cause but noAuthNoPriv is materially more severe given the absence of any access control at all.
SNMPv3 misconfigured to authNoPriv while SNMPv1/v2c is simultaneously still enabled and reachable, providing an even easier bypass of whatever SNMPv3 protection was intended.
mitigation: Configure SNMPv3 with authPriv (both authentication and encryption/privacy) for every user/community, rather than authNoPriv or noAuthNoPriv.
Disable SNMPv1/v2c entirely wherever SNMPv3 is deployed, since their continued availability undermines any SNMPv3 hardening regardless of its own configuration.
Restrict SNMP reachability to a dedicated management network/VLAN rather than leaving it reachable from general-purpose segments.
Periodically re-audit SNMP security-level configuration across the device estate, since this setting can be inconsistently applied across a large fleet.

NET-023.prerequisites: Network access to the target's SSH service. nmap's ssh2-enum-algos script or ssh-audit for enumerating supported algorithms and configuration weaknesses.
NET-023.whatItIs: The target's SSH server (used for secure remote administration) still supports old, weak cryptographic methods — legacy key-exchange methods, weak ciphers, weak integrity checks, or in the worst case, an entirely outdated version of the SSH protocol itself — alongside, or instead of, the strong, modern options current systems support.
NET-023.rootCause: SSH's recommended settings have evolved a lot as cryptography has advanced, but a lot of long-running servers were configured once and never revisited to remove old, legacy options that were originally kept around just for compatibility with clients that may not even be in use anymore.
NET-023.impact: An attacker positioned to negotiate the connection (or in some legacy-algorithm scenarios, one who can force a downgrade) may be able to exploit the specific weak algorithm's known cryptographic weakness to recover session key material or otherwise weaken the connection's confidentiality/integrity guarantees — while full practical exploitation varies by exact algorithm and attacker position, the continued presence of legacy, deprecated algorithms is itself an indicator of inadequate configuration hardening warranting remediation regardless of an immediately demonstrable full break.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the SSH server's supported key-exchange, cipher, and MAC algorithms using an SSH-specific audit tool.
Cross-reference the enumerated list against current hardening guidance (Mozilla's OpenSSH guidelines, or an equivalent current standard) to flag any deprecated/weak algorithm still offered.
Confirm whether SSH protocol version 1 is still enabled at all, which would be a severe, standalone finding given its comprehensively broken cryptographic design.
Assess the server's host-key algorithm and size as well, since a weak host key undermines server-authentication integrity independent of the session-level algorithm negotiation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SSH algorithm enumeration against the target service.
Run an SSH-audit tool to enumerate the complete supported algorithm set.
Document every deprecated/weak algorithm still offered, cross-referenced against current hardening standards.
Where a specific, practically-exploitable weakness applies to one of the confirmed weak algorithms, assess and document its real-world exploitability in this specific deployment context.

examplePayloads.label: Comprehensive SSH configuration audit
Enumerate supported algorithms via nmap's SSH script
Confirm whether SSH protocol version 1 is still supported

variants: Weak key-exchange algorithm (diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, offering insufficient key strength) versus a weak cipher/MAC combination — both contribute to the same overall weak-configuration finding but represent distinct algorithm categories.
SSH protocol version 1 still enabled (a severe, standalone legacy-protocol finding) versus only weak algorithm options within an otherwise SSHv2-only configuration.
mitigation: Remove support for all deprecated/weak key-exchange, cipher, and MAC algorithms from the SSH server configuration, retaining only current, strong algorithm suites (current guidance from Mozilla's OpenSSH hardening guide or an equivalent authoritative source).
Disable SSH protocol version 1 entirely if still enabled — there is no legitimate reason to retain it in a current environment.
Use a strong, modern host-key algorithm (Ed25519 or RSA at a sufficient key size) rather than a legacy DSA or undersized RSA key.

Periodically re-audit SSH configuration across the device estate as part of routine hardening review, since legacy algorithm support can be reintroduced by a firmware/OS upgrade resetting to vendor defaults.

NET-024.prerequisites: Network access to the target HTTPS web service. curl or a browser's developer tools to inspect response headers.
NET-024.whatItIs: A website that serves HTTPS doesn't send the specific instruction telling browsers 'always use HTTPS for this site from now on.' Without it, if someone ever accesses the site over plain, unencrypted HTTP even once — through an old bookmark, a mistyped address, or a stale link — that specific connection attempt is vulnerable to being intercepted or downgraded before it even has a chance to switch to HTTPS.
NET-024.rootCause: This is a specific instruction that has to be explicitly turned on — it's not automatic just because HTTPS is available, and it's a common thing to overlook even on a site that correctly redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS. That redirect alone still requires one initial, unprotected HTTP request to happen first — which is exactly the gap this missing instruction leaves open.
NET-024.impact: An attacker positioned on the network path (a malicious Wi-Fi access point, an on-path position via ARP spoofing) can intercept a victim's initial HTTP request (before any redirect to HTTPS occurs) and either serve a spoofed HTTP response directly or use an SSL-stripping technique to keep the entire session downgraded to HTTP, capturing credentials and session data in cleartext — HSTS specifically closes this window by ensuring the browser never issues that initial unprotected HTTP request in the first place, for any domain it has previously received the header from.
stepsToIdentify: Request the target application over HTTPS and inspect the response headers for the presence of `Strict-Transport-Security`.
Where present, check its `max-age` value (should be a substantial duration, commonly one year or more) and whether `includeSubDomains` is set if the protection should extend to subdomains.
Separately confirm whether the site correctly redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS at the server level, since this is a related but distinct control from HSTS itself.

Check whether the domain is submitted to the HSTS preload list (via a preload-list-lookup tool), which provides protection even for a user's very first visit, before any HSTS header could have been received.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes HSTS-configuration testing and, if demonstrating the downgrade risk, a controlled network-position test against a nominated test client.
Request the application over HTTPS and confirm the presence/absence of the HSTS header.

Where absent, demonstrate the practical risk by simulating a network position that intercepts a test client's initial HTTP request (a controlled SSL-stripping proof-of-concept) and confirming the interception succeeds due to the missing HSTS protection.
Document the missing header and the demonstrated downgrade-interception risk.

examplePayloads.label: Check for the HSTS header in the HTTPS response
Confirm HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect behavior separately
Check HSTS preload-list status

variants: HSTS header entirely absent versus present but with an insufficient `max-age` value (too short to provide meaningful ongoing protection) or missing `includeSubDomains` where subdomains also serve sensitive content.
HTTP-to-HTTPS server-side redirect present but HSTS absent (still leaves the initial-request downgrade window open) versus both missing entirely.
mitigation: Add the `Strict-Transport-Security` header to every HTTPS response, with a substantial `max-age` (commonly at least one year) and `includeSubDomains` where appropriate.
Submit the domain to the browser HSTS preload list for protection even on a user's first-ever visit, closing the gap that HSTS's own header-based mechanism can't cover.
Ensure the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect is also correctly configured as a complementary, defense-in-depth control alongside HSTS.
Apply HSTS configuration consistently across every subdomain/service under the organization's control, not just the primary domain.

NET-025.prerequisites: Network access to the target's NFS service (typically port 2049). showmount and the standard NFS client mount tooling.
NET-025.whatItIs: A shared network file system is set up too permissively — open to any client instead of a specific, trusted list, allowing a remote 'root' user to access it with full administrative rights, or granting write access where read-only would have been enough. This lets an unauthorized device connect to it and read, or even change, its contents.
NET-025.rootCause: These sharing permissions have to be explicitly and carefully scoped when the file system is set up, and a broad, permissive configuration is a straightforward oversight — sometimes put in place to quickly fix an access problem and then never properly locked back down afterward.
NET-025.impact: Any client that can reach the NFS service can mount the export and access its full contents, potentially including sensitive files, and where root-squash is disabled, a client presenting a root UID gets full root-level file-system access to the export regardless of the actual client-side user's real privilege — this can expose or corrupt significant amounts of data depending on what's exported.
stepsToIdentify: Query the target NFS server for its list of exports and their configured access restrictions.
Attempt to mount each discovered export from a test client and confirm whether access succeeds without prior authorization.

Check whether root-squash is enabled by attempting a file operation as root (UID 0) on the mounted export and observing whether root-level access is honored or correctly mapped down to an unprivileged user.
Review the actual content exposed via the mounted export for sensitivity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes NFS export enumeration and mounting testing against the target service.
Query the export list via showmount.
Mount a discovered export from a test client and confirm access.
Test root-squash behavior by attempting a root-level file operation on the mount.
Document the exact export path, its permissive configuration, and the confirmed access/privilege level achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate NFS exports on the target server
Mount a discovered export from a test client
Test root-squash behavior

variants: Export reachable by any client (`*`) versus scoped to a broader-than-intended but not fully open IP range.

Root-squash disabled (`no_root_squash`), granting remote root-level access, versus root-squash correctly enabled but the export still granting write access more broadly than necessary for legitimate use.
mitigation: Restrict NFS exports to an explicit, minimal allowlist of specific, trusted client IP addresses rather than exporting to any client.
Enable root-squash (map remote root UID 0 to an unprivileged user) on every export unless there's a specific, well-understood, documented reason not to.
Grant read-only access by default, applying write access only where genuinely required.
Consider NFSv4 with Kerberos-based authentication (rather than NFSv3's IP-based trust model alone) for environments requiring stronger access-control guarantees.

NET-026.prerequisites: Network access to the target VPN endpoint (IPsec, OpenVPN, or an equivalent). ike-scan for IPsec/IKE enumeration, or openvpn's own diagnostic/verbose connection logging for OpenVPN-specific configuration review.
NET-026.whatItIs: The VPN's encryption setup uses outdated, weak options — old, crackable encryption methods, weak integrity checks, or a weak key-exchange strength that doesn't meet current standards.
NET-026.rootCause: Once a VPN is deployed and working, it often gets left untouched for years to avoid breaking existing client connections. Security best practices have moved on considerably since many of these were first set up, and without a periodic review, a VPN can keep using settings that were fine at the time but are now considered weak.
NET-026.impact: Depending on the specific weak algorithm, an attacker with sufficient resources and network position may be able to weaken or defeat the VPN's confidentiality/integrity guarantees, potentially exposing the traffic the VPN was specifically deployed to protect — for a VPN carrying genuinely sensitive traffic (remote administrative access, sensitive business data), this represents a significant erosion of the protection the organization believes it has in place.
stepsToIdentify: For IPsec/IKE-based VPNs, enumerate the offered Phase 1/Phase 2 proposals (encryption algorithm, integrity algorithm, Diffie-Hellman group) using ike-scan.
For OpenVPN, review the server configuration file (where accessible) or the negotiated cipher visible in verbose client-connection logs.
Cross-reference the confirmed algorithm choices against current hardening guidance (NIST SP 800-77 for IPsec, or current OpenVPN hardening documentation).
Flag any deprecated/weak algorithm still offered or negotiated by default.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes VPN cryptographic-configuration enumeration against the target endpoint.
Run the appropriate enumeration tool/technique for the specific VPN technology in use.
Document every weak/deprecated algorithm confirmed offered or negotiated.
Where a specific, practically-exploitable weakness applies to a confirmed weak algorithm, assess and document its real-world exploitability in this deployment.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate IKE Phase 1 proposals offered by an IPsec VPN endpoint
Aggressive-mode-specific enumeration (also relevant to the related PSK finding)
Review negotiated OpenVPN cipher from a verbose test connection log

variants: Weak IKE Phase 1 encryption/integrity algorithms and DH group (IPsec-specific) versus a deprecated cipher configuration in OpenVPN — both share the same root-cause outdated-hardening pattern but affect different VPN technologies.
Weak algorithm offered as one option among several (client could still negotiate a strong one) versus configured as the server's only/default option, forcing every client onto the weak choice.
mitigation: Configure IPsec VPNs to offer only current, strong algorithm suites (AES-GCM encryption, SHA-256 or stronger integrity, DH group 14 or higher) and remove legacy weak options entirely.
Configure OpenVPN to use AES-GCM (or an equivalent current AEAD cipher) rather than deprecated CBC-mode or Blowfish ciphers.
Periodically re-audit VPN cryptographic configuration against current hardening guidance, since this area evolves and a long-lived, unreviewed deployment tends to fall behind.

Plan and communicate any necessary client-side update requirements when tightening VPN cryptographic configuration, to avoid breaking legitimate connectivity for clients that only support the older algorithms.

NET-027.prerequisites: Read/administrative access to the target's WireGuard or OpenVPN static-key configuration (for a white-box review), or knowledge that a static (non-per-session) key is in use across a fleet of devices/sites. A comparison capability across at least two separate deployments/devices to test for key reuse.
NET-027.whatItIs: A VPN setup uses the exact same private key across many different devices or locations, instead of giving each one its own unique key. That means if an attacker extracts the key from just one device, they can impersonate or decrypt traffic for every other device sharing that same key.
NET-027.rootCause: Generating and distributing a unique key for every single device takes more ongoing effort than just reusing one central key across an entire fleet. That shortcut is sometimes taken during initial rollout without fully realizing it collapses what should be many separate points of trust into one single point of failure.
NET-027.impact: Extraction of the shared key from any single compromised device (a stolen laptop, a compromised branch-office router) grants the ability to decrypt traffic from, or impersonate, every other device sharing that same key — turning what should be a contained, single-device compromise into a fleet-wide VPN-trust compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Review the VPN deployment's key-provisioning process/documentation to determine whether keys are generated uniquely per device/site or from a single, shared source.
Where accessible, extract the configured key from two or more separate devices/sites and directly compare them for identity.
Assess how many devices/sites share the same key, to correctly scope the finding's real-world blast radius.
Confirm whether any key-rotation process exists at all, since a shared key that's also never rotated compounds the risk further.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes key-extraction and comparison testing across multiple test devices/sites in the target's VPN deployment.
Extract the configured static key from a first test device/site.
Extract the configured key from a second, independent test device/site.
Confirm the two extracted keys are identical, proving shared-key reuse across the fleet.
Document the confirmed key-reuse pattern and the number of devices/sites sharing the same key, as evidence of the blast-radius impact.

examplePayloads.label: Extract a WireGuard private key from a device's configuration
Compare extracted keys from two separate devices for identity
Extract an OpenVPN static key from a client configuration file

variants: Shared static key across an entire fleet of remote-access client devices, versus shared only across a smaller subset (e.g. all branch-office site-to-site tunnels using one common key) — the blast radius differs but the root cause is the same.
Key reuse with no rotation at all, versus a shared key that is periodically rotated but still distributed identically to every device at each rotation, never becoming genuinely per-device unique.
mitigation: Generate a unique keypair per device/site during provisioning, using an automated, scalable key-generation and distribution process to keep the operational overhead manageable at fleet scale.
Maintain a per-device key inventory enabling targeted revocation of a single compromised device's key without needing to rotate the entire fleet's shared secret.
For OpenVPN specifically, prefer a full TLS-based configuration (per-client certificates) over a static pre-shared-key model wherever the deployment scale/tooling allows it.
Establish a regular key-rotation cadence regardless of the per-device-uniqueness fix, as defense in depth.

NET-028.prerequisites: Network access to the target's container-registry service (typically port 5000 for Docker Registry v2). curl or the Docker CLI configured to interact with an insecure/unauthenticated registry.
NET-028.whatItIs: A private repository storing container images is reachable over the network with no login required to download — and sometimes even upload — images. Anyone who finds it can download the organization's private images, which often contain source code, configuration, and sometimes hardcoded credentials. If uploads are also unprotected, they could plant a malicious image that ends up running in the organization's own deployment pipeline.
NET-028.rootCause: This kind of registry sometimes gets set up quickly for internal convenience without login protection from the start, or protection gets added for uploads (used by the build process) while downloads are left open under the assumption that only internal systems would ever find it — an assumption that breaks down if it's actually reachable more broadly than intended.
NET-028.impact: Anyone who discovers the registry can pull and reverse-engineer the organization's private application images, extracting embedded source code, configuration files, and any credentials/secrets baked into image layers (overlapping with the general hardcoded-secrets risk, but at the container-image layer specifically) — and where push access is also unauthenticated, an attacker can poison the registry with a malicious image that the organization's own deployment automation might subsequently pull and run.
stepsToIdentify: Identify container-registry services in scope via port/service scanning.
Attempt to list and pull images from the registry without providing any authentication credential.
Where pull access succeeds, extract and inspect a representative image's layers for embedded secrets/source code as impact evidence.
Test push access separately (using a benign, clearly-labeled test image) to determine whether the registry permits unauthenticated uploads as well, which represents a more severe, additional finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated registry interaction against the target service.
Attempt to list the registry's repository catalog without authentication.
Pull a representative image and extract its layers for content inspection.
Where push access also succeeds, upload and then remove a benign, clearly-labeled test image to confirm write access without actually poisoning the registry with anything used in a real deployment.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated pull (and, if applicable, push) access and the specific sensitive content found in extracted images.

examplePayloads.label: List the registry's repository catalog without authentication
Pull an image without authentication using the Docker CLI
Extract and inspect a pulled image's layers for embedded secrets
examplePayloads.command: docker save <target-ip>:5000/<discovered-repo>:latest -o image.tar && tar -xf image.tar && grep -r 'password\|api_key' .

variants: Unauthenticated pull access only (information-disclosure risk) versus unauthenticated push access as well (a supply-chain-poisoning risk if the organization's deployment pipeline trusts the registry implicitly).
Registry reachable from the internet directly (severe) versus reachable only from an internal network position (still significant, but requiring prior network access).
mitigation: Require authentication for both pull and push operations on every container registry, with no unauthenticated access permitted.

Restrict network reachability of the registry to the organization's internal network/build infrastructure, never exposing it directly to the internet unless there's a specific, deliberate, hardened public-registry use case.
Scan container images for embedded secrets as part of the CI/CD pipeline before they're pushed to any registry, reducing the impact of any future access-control gap.
Apply image-signing and signature-verification in the deployment pipeline, so even an unauthenticated push of a malicious image couldn't be trusted/deployed without a valid signature.

NET-029.prerequisites: Network access to the target's management/administrative VPN endpoint, and either valid (test) credentials or knowledge that only a single authentication factor is required. A VPN client appropriate to the technology in use.
NET-029.whatItIs: A VPN specifically used for privileged, administrative access — reaching management tools and internal admin systems — only requires a username and password, with no second factor required, even though what it grants access to is far more sensitive than a typical, general-purpose VPN.
NET-029.rootCause: Multi-factor login sometimes gets rolled out for the organization's main, broadly-used VPN — since it's visible and gets attention — while a separate, smaller VPN used only by IT staff gets overlooked, under the mistaken idea that a smaller, more technical user base means lower risk. In reality, the elevated access this VPN grants makes it, if anything, a higher priority for extra protection.
NET-029.impact: A compromised single-factor credential (via phishing, password reuse, or credential stuffing) is sufficient on its own to gain access to the organization's most sensitive management network segment, providing a direct path to compromise network infrastructure, administrative interfaces, and any jump-host-reachable internal systems — this represents an outsized risk relative to the narrow population of legitimate users, precisely because of what the access grants.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the specific VPN endpoint(s) used for privileged/management network access, distinct from the organization's general-purpose remote-access VPN.
Confirm the authentication requirement for this specific VPN — whether MFA is enforced, or only a single factor is required.
With authorization, attempt to authenticate using only a valid test credential (no MFA step) and confirm whether access is granted.
Assess what network segments/systems become reachable once VPN access is established, to correctly scope the finding's severity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes authentication testing against the target management-VPN endpoint using provided test credentials.
Attempt authentication using only the single-factor credential.
Confirm whether access is granted without any additional MFA challenge.
Where access is granted, document what network segments/systems are reachable as the impact evidence, without further exploiting that access beyond what's needed to confirm the finding.

examplePayloads.label: Attempt VPN authentication with only a single-factor test credential
Confirm reachable network scope once connected
examplePayloads.command: ip route  # inspect routes pushed by the VPN to understand the accessible network scope

variants: Complete absence of MFA on the management VPN, versus MFA present but with a bypassable fallback path (a "remember this device" setting with an excessively long trust duration).

Management VPN granting broad, flat network access versus properly segmented access limited to only the specific management systems a given administrator role requires — the MFA gap compounds whichever access-scope condition is also present.
mitigation: Require multi-factor authentication for every privileged/management-access VPN, treating it as at least as high a priority as the general-purpose user-facing VPN, given the elevated sensitivity of what it grants.
Apply the principle of least privilege to what network segments/systems are reachable once management-VPN access is established, limiting the impact of any single compromised session.
Monitor and alert on management-VPN authentication events specifically, given the sensitivity of this access path.
Periodically audit every VPN/remote-access entry point in the environment for consistent MFA enforcement, since a narrower, less-visible VPN is an easy one to miss during a broader MFA rollout.

NET-030.prerequisites: Network access to the target's IPMI/BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) service (UDP 623). ipmitool or metasploit's IPMI-related auxiliary modules for testing the specific authentication-bypass techniques applicable to the IPMI protocol version in use.
NET-030.whatItIs: A widely-used protocol for remotely managing servers at the hardware level (power control, remote console access) has some well-documented flaws in its authentication — including a setting that allows connecting with no authentication at all, and a separate flaw in its login handshake that leaks enough information to crack the password offline, regardless of how strong that password actually is.
NET-030.rootCause: The login handshake for this protocol was specified in a way that reveals a scrambled version of the password to anyone who starts the handshake, even before they've actually logged in — a flaw baked into the protocol's own design, not just a specific product's bug. On top of that, many devices ship with the 'no authentication at all' option turned on by default.
NET-030.impact: An attacker can extract the BMC's password hash without any prior authentication and crack it offline (defeating even a strong password given enough time/compute, since the protocol discloses the hash to any requester), or, where cipher-suite-0 remains enabled, bypass authentication entirely — either path grants full out-of-band management access to the underlying server, including power control, virtual media mounting, and remote KVM console access, independent of and unconstrained by the host OS's own security controls.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for IPMI services (UDP 623) across the target's network range.
Test whether cipher-suite-0 (no authentication) is accepted by the discovered BMC.
Where cipher-suite-0 isn't available, attempt the RAKP password-hash-disclosure technique to extract the BMC's password hash without authenticating.
Where a hash is extracted, attempt offline cracking against a representative wordlist to assess practical crackability within the engagement's time budget.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes IPMI authentication-bypass and hash-extraction testing against the target BMC.
Test for cipher-suite-0 acceptance and, if successful, confirm unauthenticated management access.
If cipher-suite-0 isn't available, use the RAKP technique to extract the BMC's password hash.
Attempt offline cracking of the extracted hash against a representative wordlist.

Where either technique succeeds, confirm the resulting management-access scope (power control, console access) via a benign, non-destructive action, and document the specific bypass/extraction technique used.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for IPMI services
Test for cipher-suite-0 authentication bypass
Extract the RAKP password hash for offline cracking
examplePayloads.command: metasploit-framework/msfconsole -q -x 'use auxiliary/scanner/ipmi/ipmi_dumphashes; set RHOSTS <target-ip>; run; exit'

examplePayloads.label: Offline-crack the extracted hash

variants: Cipher-suite-0 authentication bypass (complete absence of authentication) versus the RAKP hash-disclosure vulnerability affecting even a properly-configured, authentication-enabled BMC.
IPMI reachable from the internet directly (severe, since BMCs are sometimes inadvertently exposed) versus reachable only from an internal management network position.
mitigation: Disable cipher-suite-0 on every BMC, requiring a proper authenticated cipher suite for all IPMI access.

Set a long, high-entropy BMC password, understanding this mitigates but doesn't eliminate the RAKP hash-disclosure design flaw's cracking risk given enough time/compute — network isolation remains the more fundamental fix.
Restrict IPMI/BMC network reachability to a dedicated, isolated out-of-band management network, never exposing it to general-purpose network segments or the internet.
Where the BMC firmware supports it, migrate to a more modern out-of-band management protocol/configuration with stronger authentication guarantees than classic IPMI 2.0 RAKP.

NET-031.prerequisites: Physical or network access to a switch port protected by 802.1X Network Access Control with MAC Authentication Bypass (MAB) configured as a fallback. A device/laptop with the ability to spoof its MAC address, and a means to observe a legitimate device's MAC address on the same segment (passively sniffing traffic, or physical observation of a connected device's label).
NET-031.whatItIs: A switch port that normally requires proper login credentials falls back to a weaker check for devices that can't do a full login — like printers or IP phones — just checking whether the device's network address is on an approved list. Since that address is trivial to fake, an attacker can copy a legitimate device's address and get the same network access without ever passing a real login check.
NET-031.rootCause: This fallback exists specifically to accommodate devices that genuinely can't do a full login, trading real security for compatibility — but a device's network address travels in plain sight on every packet it sends and can be changed in software on almost any device. So this 'authentication' is really just an easily-copied allowlist check, not real proof of identity.
NET-031.impact: An attacker can gain the same network access level as a legitimate, MAB-authenticated device (which sometimes places these devices on trusted internal VLANs given their operational necessity) simply by spoofing an observed MAC address, potentially bypassing NAC entirely to reach network segments that should otherwise require proper 802.1X credentials.
stepsToIdentify: Identify switch ports/segments using MAB as a fallback authentication mechanism, via documentation review or observed behavior (a non-802.1X-capable device successfully connecting).
Passively observe traffic on the segment to identify the MAC address of a legitimate MAB-authenticated device.
With authorization, disconnect (or use a separate test port) and reconnect a test device with its MAC address spoofed to match the observed legitimate device.
Confirm whether the switch grants the same network access to the spoofed-MAC test device as it would to the genuine one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes MAC-spoofing testing against the target MAB-protected switch port/segment.
Passively observe and record a legitimate, MAB-authenticated device's MAC address on the segment.
Configure a test device with the observed MAC address spoofed onto its network interface.
Connect the test device to the network and confirm it receives the same MAB-based network access.
Document the confirmed bypass and the resulting network access level achieved via the spoofed identity.

examplePayloads.label: Passively observe traffic to identify a legitimate device's MAC address
Spoof the observed MAC address onto a test interface (Linux)
examplePayloads.command:
ip link set eth0 down
ip link set eth0 address <observed-legitimate-mac>
ip link set eth0 up

examplePayloads.label: Confirm network access after connecting with the spoofed MAC
examplePayloads.command: dhclient eth0 && ip addr show eth0

variants: MAC spoofing to gain access to a segment hosting IoT/printer-appropriate resources only (lower impact) versus a segment where MAB-authenticated devices are inadvertently granted broader, more sensitive network access than their operational function requires.
MAC observed via passive sniffing on the same segment versus obtained via physical inspection of a device's asset label (many devices print their MAC address on an external label).
mitigation: Minimize reliance on MAB wherever possible, migrating devices to genuine 802.1X authentication (via a supplicant or a certificate-based EAP method) as device capability allows.

Where MAB must remain for legitimate device-compatibility reasons, restrict MAB-authenticated devices to a tightly-scoped, low-privilege VLAN with access only to the specific resources those device types genuinely require, never the same trust level as fully 802.1X-authenticated devices.

Combine MAB with additional device-fingerprinting signals (DHCP fingerprinting, traffic-pattern profiling) to raise the bar beyond a simple MAC-address check, understanding this remains a weaker control than genuine authentication.
Monitor for MAC-address conflicts (the same MAC appearing on multiple physical ports/locations in a short window) as a detection signature for spoofing attempts.

NET-032.prerequisites: Network access to an in-scope SSH service (TCP/22 or non-standard). nmap with the ssh2-enum-algos NSE script, or ssh -vv against the target for manual negotiation inspection. No credentials required — this is a pre-authentication configuration check.
NET-032.whatItIs: When connecting to an SSH server, the server tells the client which encryption methods it's willing to use. If a server still offers old, weak options — even alongside good, modern ones — a connection can still end up using the weak option, opening the door to attacks that can forge signatures, recover plaintext, or exploit padding flaws.
NET-032.rootCause: SSH servers often keep old, weak options around for compatibility with older client software, and these settings rarely get revisited once a server's initially set up. Since the client and server just agree on whatever weak option they both happen to support, an attacker positioned to interfere with that negotiation can sometimes influence which one gets chosen.
NET-032.impact: A weak SSH algorithm configuration does not grant immediate access on its own, but it materially lowers the bar for a sufficiently resourced, on-path attacker to forge a host key signature or recover session content, undermining the confidentiality and integrity guarantees administrators rely on when using SSH for privileged remote management. Because SSH is almost universally the primary administrative access path for servers and network devices, any weakening of its cryptographic guarantees disproportionately affects the organization's most sensitive access channel.
stepsToIdentify: Run nmap --script ssh2-enum-algos against the target port to enumerate every key-exchange, host-key, cipher, and MAC algorithm the server currently offers.
Cross-reference the returned algorithm list against the current weak/deprecated set (ssh-rsa/SHA-1 host keys, ssh-dss, diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, arcfour, any CBC-mode cipher, hmac-md5/hmac-sha1).

Attempt a manual connection with ssh -oHostKeyAlgorithms=ssh-rsa -oKexAlgorithms=diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 (or the specific weak algorithm found) to confirm the server actually accepts and completes a handshake using it, not just advertises it.

Check the SSH server version banner against known CVEs for that specific version (e.g., older OpenSSH builds with regreSSHion or algorithm-negotiation flaws) to determine if a weak algorithm is exploitable beyond a configuration-hardening finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers the SSH service and that active MITM/downgrade testing (if attempted) is authorized, since it may require positioning between a real client and the server.

Where the weak algorithm is a diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 key exchange, demonstrate feasibility by noting the reduced key size makes a Logjam-style precomputed discrete-log attack tractable for a well-resourced attacker.

Where ssh-rsa/SHA-1 host keys are offered, document that SHA-1 collision research materially weakens the trust guarantee of host-key verification, even though full forgery remains impractical for most attackers today.

If positioned as an on-path attacker in an authorized red-team exercise, attempt to strip the modern algorithms from the negotiation packet in transit and confirm whether the client silently falls back to a weak algorithm.

Report the specific weak algorithms confirmed reachable, distinguishing configuration-hardening findings (offered but not the primary risk) from directly exploitable ones (accepted despite modern alternatives being available).

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate all SSH algorithms with nmap NSE
Force a specific weak key-exchange algorithm
Force legacy ssh-rsa host-key algorithm

variants: CBC-mode ciphers still enabled, which are theoretically susceptible to plaintext-recovery attacks in specific SSH implementations (analogous to the TLS BEAST-class issue).
Weak MAC algorithms (hmac-md5, hmac-sha1) retained alongside modern hmac-sha2 options, weakening integrity guarantees without disabling the connection outright.
mitigation: Explicitly configure the SSH daemon's HostKeyAlgorithms, KexAlgorithms, Ciphers, and MACs directives to include only modern options (ed25519/ecdsa host keys, curve25519-sha256 key exchange, chacha20-poly1305/aes-gcm ciphers), removing legacy entries entirely rather than merely deprioritizing them.
Regenerate any RSA host key still in use as an ed25519 key where client compatibility allows, since ed25519 avoids the SHA-1 signature concern entirely.
Standardize SSH hardening configuration via a management baseline (Ansible/Puppet template) applied fleet-wide, rather than relying on per-host manual configuration.
Periodically re-run algorithm enumeration against the fleet as new weaknesses are published, since today's acceptable algorithm can become tomorrow's deprecated one.

NET-033.prerequisites: Physical access to an available network jack/switch port in the target facility. A standard laptop/device with a wired network interface, no special tooling required beyond basic network configuration.
NET-033.whatItIs: The organization's wired network has no real check on who's allowed to connect — on some or all switch ports, anyone who physically plugs into an available network jack (in a conference room, an empty desk) gets full network access immediately, with no login or verification of any kind.
NET-033.rootCause: Setting up and maintaining proper network-connection checks takes real, ongoing effort — configuring every kind of device, setting up a backend login system, handling exceptions for devices that can't do a full login. That effort sometimes gets skipped, especially in older buildings or networks where physical building security (badge access) was assumed to be protection enough on its own.
NET-033.impact: Anyone who can gain brief physical access to the facility — a visitor, a delivery person, a social-engineering pretext, or simply an unlocked/unmonitored space — can plug in a device and immediately reach the internal network with whatever access level that network segment grants, entirely bypassing any expectation that only authorized corporate devices/users would ever be network-connected.
stepsToIdentify: With physical-access authorization, connect a test device to an available network jack in a representative location (a conference room, a common area).
Observe whether any authentication challenge (802.1X) occurs before network connectivity is established, or whether an IP address/network access is granted immediately.
Where access is granted, assess what internal network segments/resources are reachable from that jack's connected VLAN.
Repeat across a representative sample of different physical locations/jack types, since NAC coverage can be inconsistent across a large facility/estate.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes physical network-jack connectivity testing at the target facility.
Connect a test device to an available jack in each sampled location.
Confirm whether network access is granted without any authentication challenge.
Where access is granted, perform a benign reconnaissance action (a ping sweep of the local subnet, a check for reachable internal services) to document the scope of accessible resources.
Document each tested location's NAC status and the resulting network-access scope achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Connect and check for immediate, unauthenticated network access
examplePayloads.command: ip addr show eth0  # check whether DHCP assigned an address without any 802.1X challenge

examplePayloads.label: Perform a benign reconnaissance sweep of the reachable local subnet

variants: Complete absence of NAC across the facility, versus NAC deployed inconsistently (present in server-room/data-center areas but absent in general office/conference-room jacks).

Unauthenticated jack granting access to a general corporate VLAN versus, in the most severe case, directly to a sensitive internal segment (a server VLAN accidentally reachable from a general-access jack).
mitigation: Deploy 802.1X-based NAC across all wired network access points, with a MAB-based fallback (scoped narrowly per the related MAB finding) only for genuinely non-802.1X-capable devices.
Where full 802.1X deployment is a longer-term project, apply interim compensating controls — disabling unused switch ports entirely, and applying basic port-security/MAC-limiting on active ports.

Segment the network so that even an unauthenticated connection (where NAC gaps remain during a phased rollout) reaches only a minimal, internet-only guest-equivalent VLAN rather than the general corporate network.
Periodically physically audit network-jack accessibility and NAC coverage across representative facility locations, since gaps can be introduced during office moves/renovations.

NET-034.prerequisites: A network position capable of responding to DHCP requests on the target segment (an on-path position, or a rogue DHCP server if the segment lacks DHCP snooping — see the related findings covering that prerequisite condition). Scapy or a rogue-DHCP tool (dnsmasq configured maliciously, or Yersinia) for crafting DHCP responses with malicious option values.
NET-034.whatItIs: When a device connects to the network, it normally gets basic settings like its address and gateway — but it can also be told extra routing or proxy instructions. A rogue device pretending to be the network's real address-assignment service can abuse these extra instructions to redirect some or all of a victim's traffic through a server the attacker controls, or point them at a malicious proxy configuration.
NET-034.rootCause: These extra network instructions are trusted completely, with nothing verifying they actually came from the legitimate network service. A device has no way to tell a real instruction apart from a fake one sent by a rogue device on the same network — and some of these instructions can even override the normal default settings, taking priority over them.
NET-034.impact: An attacker can redirect specific victim traffic (for a chosen destination range, via option 121) or the victim's proxy configuration (via option 252/WPAD) through an attacker-controlled intermediary without needing to alter the client's default gateway or DNS server at all, enabling a targeted, potentially less-noticeable interception of specific traffic flows.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target segment lacks DHCP snooping (a prerequisite for a rogue DHCP server to operate at all, or relevant to the race-condition variant if snooping is partial).

With authorization, operate a rogue DHCP server (or race a legitimate one) issuing option 121 with a crafted, more-specific static route directing a chosen test destination range through an attacker-controlled test host.
Confirm the test client's routing table reflects the injected, more-specific route and that traffic to the chosen test range is redirected accordingly.
Separately test option 252/WPAD abuse by pointing the client at an attacker-controlled proxy-autoconfiguration file and confirming the client fetches and applies it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes rogue-DHCP option-injection testing against a nominated test client on the target segment.
Configure a rogue DHCP server (or race a legitimate one) to issue option 121 with a malicious static route for a chosen test destination range.
Confirm the test client's routing table and subsequent traffic reflect the injected route.
Demonstrate impact via a benign redirect (a test page) for traffic to the chosen range, and separately test the option 252/WPAD variant.
Document the confirmed option-injection technique and its traffic-redirection impact.

examplePayloads.label: Configure a rogue DHCP server with a malicious option 121 static route
Confirm the injected route on the test client
Test option 252 (WPAD proxy-autoconfig) abuse

variants: Option 121 static-route injection redirecting specific traffic ranges, versus option 252/WPAD abuse redirecting proxy configuration and thus all HTTP(S) traffic through an attacker-controlled proxy.
Injection via a fully rogue DHCP server on an unprotected segment, versus via winning a race against the legitimate server (overlapping with the dedicated DHCP/DNS race-condition finding).
mitigation: Deploy DHCP snooping on network switches to prevent unauthorized DHCP servers (and their option values) from being accepted on any port not designated as a trusted uplink.

Disable WPAD auto-discovery entirely where not genuinely required, or ensure the legitimate WPAD configuration is served from an authenticated, trusted source rather than relying on client-side DHCP-option/DNS-based discovery alone.
Monitor for unexpected DHCP servers or unusual option values on the network as a detection signature.
Apply Dynamic ARP Inspection alongside DHCP snooping for comprehensive protection against this broader class of local-segment spoofing attacks.

NET-035.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Microsoft SQL Server port (TCP 1433, or a dynamic port discovered via the SQL Server Browser service on UDP 1434). nmap and a MSSQL-capable client (sqlcmd, or Impacket's mssqlclient.py) for connection testing.
NET-035.whatItIs: A Microsoft SQL Server database is directly reachable from a much broader part of the network than it should be — sometimes even the internet — instead of being limited to only the specific application servers that actually need to talk to it. That gives anyone with network access a direct path to attempt a login or exploit a database-level flaw, completely bypassing whatever access controls exist at the application level.
NET-035.rootCause: Database servers sometimes get deployed without deliberate planning around network isolation — ending up on the same broad network segment as everything else, or worse, directly reachable from the internet for remote-management convenience — instead of being locked down behind a firewall that only allows the specific systems that genuinely need to connect.
NET-035.impact: Direct network reachability to the database engine enables credential brute-forcing/spraying against SQL authentication, exploitation of any known CVE affecting the specific SQL Server version and patch level, and, if weak/default credentials are found, direct data access entirely bypassing the application's own access-control and business-logic layer.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for the MSSQL port (and the SQL Server Browser service) across the target's network range, including from an external, internet-facing vantage point if the organization's perimeter is in scope.
For each discovered instance, attempt to determine the version/patch level via the service's own banner/version-disclosure behavior.
Assess whether the discovered instance is reachable from a broader scope than the specific application servers that should be its only legitimate clients.
Where authorized, test for default/weak SQL authentication credentials as a separate, compounding finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes direct MSSQL port connectivity testing against the target instance.
Confirm the instance is reachable and identify its version/patch level.
Where authorized, attempt authentication using a bounded, agreed set of default/weak credential candidates.
Document the confirmed network-exposure scope (which source locations can reach the port) and any additional weak-credential finding.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for the MSSQL port and browser service
Attempt to determine version via the SQL Server Browser service
Attempt connection with a bounded set of default/weak credentials (with authorization)

variants: Database port reachable from a broader internal network segment than intended (moderate-to-high severity) versus directly internet-facing (severe, immediately remotely exploitable).
Exposed port alone (a network-segmentation finding) versus exposed port combined with weak/default credentials (a compounding, more directly exploitable finding).
mitigation: Restrict network reachability of the database engine port to only the specific application server(s) that genuinely require direct database connectivity, via firewall rules/security groups.
Never expose a database engine port directly to the internet; require any remote administrative access to go through a VPN or bastion host instead.
Disable the SQL Server Browser service where dynamic-port discovery isn't genuinely needed, reducing reconnaissance surface.
Apply strong, unique credentials and keep the database engine patched to its current version regardless of network-exposure remediation, as defense in depth.

NET-036.prerequisites: Network access to the target's MySQL (TCP 3306) or PostgreSQL (TCP 5432) port. nmap and the respective database client (mysql, psql) for connection testing.
NET-036.whatItIs: This is the exact same problem as with Microsoft SQL Server, just affecting MySQL or PostgreSQL databases instead — the database port is directly reachable from a much broader part of the network than it should be.
NET-036.rootCause: Same root cause as the SQL Server version: the database was deployed without deliberate network isolation, ending up reachable from a much broader part of the network, or the internet, instead of being locked down to only the specific systems that need it.
NET-036.impact: Direct network reachability enables credential brute-forcing/spraying, exploitation of any known CVE affecting the specific engine version, and, if weak/default credentials are found, direct data access bypassing the application's own access-control layer entirely — MySQL/PostgreSQL exposure is a particularly common finding given how frequently these engines are deployed in cloud/containerized environments where a security-group misconfiguration can inadvertently expose the port publicly.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for MySQL/PostgreSQL ports across the target's network range, including from an external vantage point if the organization's perimeter is in scope.
For each discovered instance, determine version/patch level via the connection banner.
Assess whether the instance is reachable from a broader scope than its legitimate application-server clients.
Where authorized, test for default/weak database credentials as a compounding finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes direct database-port connectivity testing against the target instance.
Confirm reachability and identify version/patch level.
Where authorized, attempt authentication using a bounded, agreed set of default/weak credential candidates.
Document the confirmed network-exposure scope and any additional weak-credential finding.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for MySQL/PostgreSQL ports
Determine MySQL version via connection banner
Attempt connection with a bounded set of default/weak credentials (with authorization)

variants: Database port reachable from an internal network segment (moderate-to-high) versus directly internet-facing (severe) — frequently the result of a cloud security-group misconfiguration for either engine.
MySQL specifically versus PostgreSQL specifically — same root cause, but the exact credential-testing/exploitation tooling differs by engine.
mitigation: Restrict network reachability of the database engine port to only the specific application server(s) requiring direct connectivity, via firewall rules/security groups.
Never expose a database engine port directly to the internet.
For cloud-hosted instances specifically, audit security-group/network-ACL configuration explicitly for this port, since it's a common source of accidental public exposure in cloud environments.
Apply strong, unique credentials and keep the database engine patched to its current version as defense in depth.

NET-037.prerequisites: A network position on the path between a client and a mail/other STARTTLS-capable server (an on-path position via a separate ARP-spoofing/rogue-infrastructure finding, or a lab test setup). Scapy or a purpose-built STARTTLS-stripping tool for crafting/manipulating the plaintext response preceding the TLS upgrade.
NET-037.whatItIs: Some email and messaging protocols start their conversation in plain text and only switch to encryption partway through, after a specific upgrade signal. Bugs in how that upgrade happens have historically let an attacker sneak extra plain-text commands in right before the switch, which then get treated as if they arrived after encryption started — or trick the client into thinking encryption was never available at all, keeping the whole session unencrypted.
NET-037.rootCause: This 'start plain, then upgrade' design creates a tricky transition moment where data received just before the upgrade can, due to implementation mistakes, get mixed up with data that should only be trusted after encryption began. This class of bug comes down to not properly clearing out that in-between data at the exact moment encryption kicks in.
NET-037.impact: Depending on the specific implementation bug and protocol, an attacker can inject commands that execute in the authenticated, post-TLS session context (potentially manipulating mailbox state or exfiltrating data), or can strip the TLS upgrade entirely, downgrading the entire session to plaintext and exposing credentials and message content to passive interception.
stepsToIdentify: Identify STARTTLS-capable services in scope (SMTP, IMAP, POP3 servers) and their exact software/version.

Cross-reference the identified version against published STARTTLS-injection CVEs for that specific software (several mail-server and library implementations have had specific, disclosed instances of this bug class).
With authorization, position as an on-path observer/injector for a test client's connection to the service and attempt the specific injection/stripping technique documented for the identified CVE.
Confirm whether the client either processes an injected command as authenticated, or is downgraded to a fully plaintext session.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes on-path STARTTLS manipulation testing against the target service using a nominated test client/account.
Position on-path for the test client's connection to the STARTTLS-capable service.
Apply the specific injection/stripping technique matching the identified software's known vulnerability.
Confirm the resulting impact — an injected command executing in the authenticated context, or a full plaintext downgrade — using only benign, non-destructive test actions.
Document the exact software/version, the specific technique used, and the confirmed impact.

examplePayloads.label: Identify the target STARTTLS service's exact software/version
Test for a buffered-command injection immediately preceding STARTTLS (protocol/version-specific PoC)

variants: Command-injection variant (a plaintext command buffered and later processed as authenticated) versus a full STARTTLS-stripping variant (the client is tricked into never upgrading to TLS at all).
Vulnerability affecting SMTP specifically versus IMAP/POP3 — each protocol's specific implementations have had distinct, separately-disclosed instances of this bug class.
mitigation: Apply vendor patches addressing the specific STARTTLS-injection CVE for the mail/protocol server software in use.

Where supported, prefer implicit TLS (a dedicated, always-encrypted port such as SMTPS/993-IMAPS) over STARTTLS's plaintext-then-upgrade model, eliminating this entire class of transition-point vulnerability.
Ensure the server implementation correctly discards/resets any buffered pre-TLS data at the moment of the TLS handshake, per current protocol-implementation best practice.
Periodically re-test STARTTLS implementations after any server software upgrade, since this bug class has recurred across multiple, independently-discovered implementation issues over time.

NET-038.prerequisites: Network access to the target TLS service. nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script or testssl.sh for enumerating supported cipher suites, including anonymous variants.
NET-038.whatItIs: The target's encrypted connection (TLS) supports a specific mode that encrypts the data but never actually verifies who's on the other end. A client connecting this way has no cryptographic guarantee it's actually talking to the real server rather than an attacker — defeating one of the two things encryption is supposed to guarantee.
NET-038.rootCause: This particular mode exists in the encryption standard for rare situations where both sides already trust each other some other way, so verifying identity isn't needed. Its presence on a normal, general-purpose server is almost always accidental — a broad, unreviewed list of allowed encryption options that was never trimmed down to exclude something clearly inappropriate for this context.
NET-038.impact: A client that negotiates (or is forced, via a downgrade attempt, to negotiate) an anonymous cipher suite establishes an encrypted connection with absolutely no server-identity verification, making it trivial for an on-path attacker to transparently proxy/replace the connection with a MITM position — the encryption itself provides essentially no real security benefit in this scenario since the attacker can simply also encrypt their own intercepted traffic to the same anonymous cipher suite.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the target TLS service's supported cipher suites using an SSL/TLS-scanning tool that specifically flags anonymous variants.

Confirm whether an anonymous cipher suite can actually be successfully negotiated in practice (rather than merely appearing supported in a broad server configuration but being unreachable due to client-side restrictions).
Where negotiable, demonstrate the practical MITM risk with an authorized, controlled interception test using the anonymous cipher suite.

Check whether the affected service actually allows a client to select an anonymous cipher suite in practice, since some stacks list it in the offered set but reject it if a client insists on no-authentication mode.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cipher-suite enumeration and, if demonstrating impact, a controlled MITM test against the target TLS service.
Enumerate supported cipher suites and confirm anonymous variants are present.
Attempt to establish a connection explicitly requesting an anonymous cipher suite and confirm successful negotiation.

Where authorized, demonstrate the MITM risk by transparently intercepting a test connection using the anonymous cipher suite, confirming no client-side certificate warning is triggered (since none would be, given the absence of a certificate to validate at all).
Document the confirmed anonymous-cipher-suite support and the demonstrated MITM feasibility.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate cipher suites including anonymous variants
Comprehensive TLS configuration scan flagging anonymous ciphers
Explicitly attempt to negotiate an anonymous cipher suite

variants: Anonymous cipher suite supported alongside strong, authenticated options (an attacker must force its selection, e.g. via a cipher-downgrade attempt) versus, in a severe misconfiguration, being the server's negotiated default.

Anonymous DH cipher suites (offering no server authentication at all) are a distinct, more severe variant than merely-weak-but-authenticated suites, since they permit a trivial MITM with no certificate spoofing required whatsoever.
mitigation: Remove all anonymous cipher suites (ADH/AECDH) from the server's TLS configuration entirely — there is essentially no legitimate general-purpose deployment scenario justifying their inclusion.
Adopt a current, well-vetted TLS cipher-suite configuration baseline (Mozilla's SSL Configuration Generator or equivalent) rather than a broad, unreviewed cipher list.
Periodically re-scan TLS configuration after any server software update, since a default configuration reset during an upgrade can sometimes reintroduce broader cipher support than intended.

NET-039.prerequisites: Network access to the target HTTPS/TLS service. openssl or curl for retrieving and inspecting the presented certificate.
NET-039.whatItIs: The security certificate a service presents doesn't actually match the address being connected to — it lists a different domain, an old former name, or a pattern that doesn't cover the address in use. A properly checking client should refuse the connection or show a warning.
NET-039.rootCause: This usually happens when a service gets renamed or moved to a new address without getting a matching new certificate, when one certificate gets reused across several differently-named services it was never actually issued to cover, or when something serving multiple backend systems uses just one certificate that doesn't actually cover all of them.
NET-039.impact: Beyond simply generating end-user certificate warnings (which erode trust and can train users to habitually click through security warnings, weakening the practical value of certificate validation across the board), a hostname mismatch specifically indicates the client cannot cryptographically confirm it's connecting to the intended, correct service — a client or automated system that's configured to skip hostname validation to work around the warning becomes vulnerable to a straightforward MITM using any valid certificate for a different domain.
stepsToIdentify: Connect to the target service and retrieve the presented certificate.
Compare the certificate's Common Name and Subject Alternative Names against the exact hostname used to establish the connection.

Confirm whether the mismatch is present across the service's full lifecycle (every connection) or only under specific conditions (a specific load-balancer backend, a specific virtual-host configuration).

Assess whether any client/automated system in the environment has been configured to skip hostname validation specifically to work around this mismatch, which would represent a compounding, more severe finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes certificate inspection against the target service.
Retrieve the presented certificate and document the exact mismatch between its listed names and the connection hostname.
Where feasible, identify the root cause (a renamed service, a shared certificate, a load-balancer misconfiguration) via further passive investigation.
Document the confirmed mismatch and any evidence of validation being bypassed elsewhere in the environment as a result.

examplePayloads.label: Retrieve and inspect the presented certificate's subject/SAN fields
Quick curl-based mismatch check

variants: Certificate for an entirely different, unrelated domain (indicating a significant configuration error or a stale/misassigned certificate) versus a near-miss (missing a specific subdomain from an otherwise-correct wildcard/SAN list).
