Mismatch on a customer-facing service (high visibility, erodes user trust in certificate warnings broadly) versus on an internal-only service (lower visibility but potentially indicating the same underlying certificate-management process gap).
mitigation: Issue and deploy a certificate whose Subject Alternative Names correctly and completely cover every hostname the service is actually reachable under.
Establish a certificate-management process that reissues/updates certificates automatically whenever a service is renamed or a new hostname alias is added.
Never configure a client or automated system to skip hostname validation as a workaround for a mismatch; fix the underlying certificate instead.
Include certificate-hostname-match verification in routine, automated certificate-monitoring/expiry-tracking tooling.

NET-040.prerequisites: Network access to the target HTTPS/TLS service. openssl or curl for retrieving and inspecting the certificate's validity period.
NET-040.whatItIs: The certificate a service presents has passed its expiration date. A properly checking client should refuse to connect at all — this is usually the result of a missed manual renewal, or an automated renewal process that quietly failed without anyone noticing.
NET-040.rootCause: Renewing a certificate is a recurring task that depends on either someone remembering to do it manually, or an automated system working correctly every time. A manual process is easy to miss amid other priorities, and an automated one can silently break — a permissions issue, a changed setting, an expired credential used by the renewal tool itself — with nobody finding out until connections actually start failing.
NET-040.impact: Client connections are either outright rejected (for strict-validating clients/automated systems, causing a genuine service outage for that integration) or, for end-user browsers, present a prominent security warning that erodes trust and, if users are trained to click through it, weakens the practical value of certificate validation as a security control across the board.
stepsToIdentify: Connect to the target service and retrieve the presented certificate's validity period (notBefore/notAfter dates).
Confirm whether the current date falls outside that validity window.

Where expired, assess the operational impact — whether any automated system/integration depending on this service has already failed as a result, versus the expiration having occurred very recently with impact not yet fully manifested.
Investigate (where access allows) whether an automated-renewal process exists and why it failed, versus the certificate having always been manually managed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes certificate-validity inspection against the target service.
Retrieve the certificate and confirm its expiration status.
Document the exact expiration date and how long the certificate has been expired.
Where feasible, assess and document the operational impact already observed (failed integrations, user-facing warnings) as evidence for prioritizing remediation.

examplePayloads.label: Check the certificate's validity dates
Quick curl-based expiration check

variants: Certificate expired very recently (impact may still be limited/not yet fully manifested) versus expired for an extended period (suggesting a completely broken renewal process with no one monitoring for it at all).
Manually-managed certificate lapsing due to a missed reminder, versus an automated-renewal (ACME-based) process that silently failed.
mitigation: Implement automated certificate renewal (an ACME client for Let's Encrypt or an equivalent CA-integrated automation) wherever the CA/infrastructure supports it, removing dependency on manual process entirely.
Deploy certificate-expiration monitoring/alerting with a sufficient lead time (30+ days before expiration) so any renewal failure is caught and remediated well before actual expiration.

Where automated renewal fails, ensure the failure itself generates an alert (not just silent retry) so the underlying cause (a changed validation path, an expired renewal-automation credential) can be fixed promptly.

Maintain a complete inventory of every certificate in the environment (overlapping with the general asset-inventory-management finding) so none are managed outside the monitoring/renewal process's visibility.

NET-041.prerequisites: Network access to the target CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) service, typically UDP port 5683. A CoAP client tool (coap-client from libcoap, or Copper for Firefox) and Wireshark for capture verification.
NET-041.whatItIs: An IoT device uses a lightweight communication protocol built for small, low-power devices, but without its encrypted version turned on — meaning everything it sends, including sensor readings, control commands, or configuration values, travels across the network in plain, readable text.
NET-041.rootCause: Encryption adds processing overhead that's sometimes deliberately left off on genuinely limited, battery-powered IoT hardware for performance reasons, or it's simply not turned on by default out of the box. This whole area of IoT security also just gets less routine attention than more mature web-security practices.
NET-041.impact: Anyone with network-path visibility can passively capture and read CoAP traffic in full, exposing sensor readings, device state, and control commands, and — since CoAP has no built-in authentication independent of DTLS — can also actively inject forged requests to manipulate device behavior (turning off a sensor, issuing an unauthorized control command) with no cryptographic barrier at all.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for CoAP services (UDP 5683, and 5684 for the DTLS-secured variant, CoAPS) across the target's IoT network segment.
Where a plain CoAP (5683) service is found, confirm whether a DTLS-secured (5684) alternative is also offered but simply not used by clients, versus DTLS being entirely unsupported by the device.
Capture CoAP traffic and confirm requests/responses are readable in cleartext.
With authorization, attempt to send a forged CoAP request (a GET/PUT to a discovered resource path) and observe whether the device processes it without any authentication challenge.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes CoAP traffic capture and request-forgery testing against the target IoT device/gateway.
Capture CoAP traffic during normal device operation and extract a sample of sensor data/control commands in cleartext as evidence.
Enumerate available CoAP resources on the device (many CoAP implementations support a `.well-known/core` resource-discovery endpoint).
Attempt to send a forged, unauthenticated request to a discovered resource and confirm whether the device processes it.
Document the confirmed cleartext exposure and any successful unauthenticated request-forgery impact.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for CoAP services
Enumerate available CoAP resources via well-known discovery
Capture CoAP traffic for cleartext content inspection
Send a forged, unauthenticated request to a discovered resource

variants: Cleartext data exposure only (passive eavesdropping risk) versus unauthenticated control-command injection (active device-manipulation risk) — both stem from the same missing-DTLS root cause but differ in exploitation technique and impact severity.
CoAP deployed with no DTLS support at all in the device firmware, versus DTLS supported but simply not enabled/enforced in the current configuration.
mitigation: Enable and enforce DTLS (CoAPS, port 5684) for all CoAP communication, using pre-shared keys, raw public keys, or certificate-based authentication as appropriate to the device's capability and deployment scale.

Where a device genuinely cannot support DTLS due to hardware constraints, isolate it on a dedicated, restricted IoT network segment with no access to sensitive resources, treating the segment itself as untrusted.
Apply resource-level access control on the CoAP server (where the implementation supports it) so that even an unauthenticated request is restricted to only genuinely non-sensitive resources.

Include CoAP/IoT-protocol security explicitly in the organization's IoT-device procurement and security-review criteria, since this class of protocol receives less routine hardening attention than mainstream web protocols.

NET-042.prerequisites: Network access to the target's internal management interface (a switch/router admin web UI, an out-of-band management port). nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script or testssl.sh, and openssl s_client for manual protocol-version testing.
NET-042.whatItIs: An internal-only management console — like a network device's admin webpage — still supports very old, deprecated versions of TLS encryption with known weaknesses, often left unfixed specifically because the interface is internal-only and got a lower priority for hardening than anything customer-facing.
NET-042.rootCause: Internal management interfaces often run on device firmware that ships with old protocol support kept around for compatibility with older management tools. Because these interfaces never face the public internet, they typically get reviewed and hardened far less often than internet-facing systems, letting old, weak protocol support linger long after it's been cleaned up elsewhere.
NET-042.impact: An attacker who has gained a foothold on the internal network (via any other vector) and can reach the management interface can exploit the specific weaknesses of SSLv3/TLS 1.0 (a POODLE-style padding-oracle attack, or other CBC-mode-related weaknesses) to potentially decrypt session content or downgrade the connection, compromising the confidentiality of administrative credentials and session data for what is typically among the most sensitive interfaces in the environment.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate internal management interfaces in scope and test each for SSLv3/TLS 1.0 support using a protocol-version-aware scanning tool.
Confirm whether the legacy protocol is merely offered as one option (a modern client would negotiate a stronger version by default) versus being the interface's only/default supported version.
Where SSLv3 specifically is confirmed, assess practical POODLE exploitability given the interface's actual traffic patterns and reachability.
Prioritize findings by the sensitivity of the specific management interface (a core network-device admin console is higher priority than a less-critical internal tool).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes legacy-protocol testing and, where applicable, exploitation against the target management interface.
Confirm SSLv3/TLS 1.0 support via protocol-version enumeration.
Where SSLv3 is confirmed, assess and, if authorized and safe to do so in a controlled test, demonstrate the POODLE padding-oracle technique against a representative session.
Document the confirmed legacy-protocol support and, if applicable, the demonstrated cryptographic weakness.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate supported TLS/SSL protocol versions
Comprehensive legacy-protocol and cipher scan
Manually confirm SSLv3 acceptance

variants: SSLv3 support specifically (directly POODLE-vulnerable) versus TLS 1.0 support (weaker but with a less immediately practical, well-known exploit path in most modern client configurations).

Legacy protocol as the interface's default/preferred version (higher risk, since ordinary connections may actually use it) versus offered only as a fallback option that a modern client would never select absent a forced downgrade.
mitigation: Disable SSLv3 and TLS 1.0 entirely on all management interfaces, requiring TLS 1.2 or 1.3 as the minimum supported version, consistent with the same standard applied to customer-facing services.
Apply the organization's TLS-hardening standard uniformly across all interfaces regardless of internal/external exposure, rather than deprioritizing internal-only systems.
Restrict network reachability of management interfaces to a dedicated, access-controlled management network/VLAN as a complementary control.
Include internal management interfaces explicitly in routine, periodic TLS-configuration scanning rather than assuming lower external visibility implies lower priority.

NET-043.prerequisites: Network access to the target's iSCSI (TCP 3260) or unencrypted SMB traffic path. Wireshark for capture and content inspection, and an iSCSI initiator/SMB client for interaction testing.
NET-043.whatItIs: A protocol used to share network storage (remote hard drives, or shared file access) sends its entire data payload — potentially including sensitive files, databases, or entire virtual machine images — across the network completely unencrypted, readable by anyone who can passively observe that network traffic.
NET-043.rootCause: Storage networking protocols were historically designed assuming they'd run on a fully separate, physically secured network built just for storage traffic, where encryption seemed like unnecessary overhead. That assumption often doesn't hold anymore, since storage traffic increasingly shares the same general-purpose network as everything else — without a matching decision to actually turn on the encryption options that are available.
NET-043.impact: Anyone with passive access to the network segment carrying storage traffic can capture and reconstruct the complete data being transferred — an entire disk volume, database file, or set of shared documents — representing a very high-volume, high-sensitivity data-exposure risk given that storage traffic often carries bulk copies of an organization's most valuable data assets.
stepsToIdentify: Identify storage-protocol traffic (iSCSI, unencrypted SMB) traversing shared or otherwise non-isolated network segments in scope.
Confirm whether iSCSI is using its optional IPsec-based encryption, or SMB is using SMB3 encryption/signing, versus running entirely in the clear.
With authorization, capture a sample of storage traffic and confirm the actual file/block content is reconstructable from the capture.
Assess the network segment's isolation level (a genuinely dedicated, physically-separate SAN fabric versus a shared, converged network) to correctly scope real-world exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes storage-traffic capture and content-reconstruction testing on the target network segment.
Capture traffic during a representative storage operation (a test file transfer, a test iSCSI read/write).
Reconstruct and inspect the captured content to confirm plaintext data recovery.
Document the confirmed lack of encryption and the specific data type/volume recoverable from the capture.

examplePayloads.label: Capture iSCSI traffic for content inspection
Extract and reconstruct file content from unencrypted SMB traffic
Check whether SMB encryption/signing is negotiated for a given share

variants: iSCSI traffic unencrypted (no IPsec applied) versus SMB traffic without encryption/signing enabled — both represent the same missing-transport-encryption root cause across different storage protocols.

Storage traffic on a genuinely isolated, dedicated fabric (lower real-world risk despite the technical finding) versus on a shared, converged network segment reachable by a broader population of hosts/users.
mitigation: Enable IPsec for iSCSI traffic where the storage infrastructure supports it, or migrate to a storage protocol/transport with built-in encryption.
Enable and enforce SMB3 encryption (and signing) for all SMB shares carrying sensitive data.

Where feasible, isolate storage-network traffic onto a genuinely dedicated, access-controlled fabric separate from general-purpose network segments, reducing the population of potential passive observers even if encryption enablement is a longer-term project.
Include storage-protocol encryption status explicitly in routine network security assessments, since this traffic is easy to overlook relative to more visible, user-facing application traffic.

NET-044.prerequisites: Layer-2 network access to the target broadcast segment. A tool capable of sending crafted ICMPv6 Router Advertisement packets (rtadvd, THC-IPv6's fake_router6, or Scapy). Written authorization for active L2 attack traffic, since this can disrupt legitimate hosts' IPv6 connectivity.
NET-044.whatItIs: IPv6 lets any device on a network announce itself as the default router and DNS server, using messages that aren't authenticated in any way. A rogue device that sends out one of these announcements more convincingly than the real router can get neighboring devices to silently start treating it as their gateway — putting the attacker in a full man-in-the-middle position for all their IPv6 traffic, even on networks the organization thinks of as 'IPv4-only.'
NET-044.rootCause: This IPv6 auto-configuration system was designed for a trusted local network with no way to verify which device is actually allowed to announce itself as the router. Unlike IPv4, where protections against rogue address-assignment servers are common, the IPv6 equivalent protection is frequently never turned on — often because organizations assume they're 'IPv4-only' and don't realize their devices are already listening for and acting on these IPv6 announcements by default.
NET-044.impact: A successful SLAAC takeover gives the attacker a full on-path position for every dual-stack host that accepts the rogue advertisement, enabling traffic interception, credential capture on any unencrypted protocol, and selective manipulation of DNS responses via the rogue RDNSS option. Because many organizations do not actively monitor or defend their IPv6 address space to the same degree as IPv4, this attack path frequently persists as blind spot even in otherwise well-hardened networks.
stepsToIdentify: Passively capture traffic on the target segment for ICMPv6 Router Advertisement messages to establish the legitimate router's advertised prefix, preference, and lifetime values as a baseline.
Confirm whether switch-level RA-Guard, DHCPv6 Guard, or equivalent first-hop security features are configured on access ports, since their absence is the direct enabler of this attack.

Check whether in-scope hosts are dual-stack (IPv6 enabled) even where the organization considers its network 'IPv4-only,' since default OS behavior typically enables and prefers IPv6 automatically once a valid RA is received.
With authorization, send a single, clearly-scoped test RA advertising a distinguishing test prefix and confirm via a monitored test host whether it is accepted, without yet redirecting real traffic.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes active Neighbor Discovery/RA-based attacks, since this can degrade or redirect IPv6 connectivity for every host on the segment, not just a nominated target.
Use fake_router6 (or equivalent) to advertise a rogue default route and, optionally, a rogue Recursive DNS Server (RDNSS) option pointing at an attacker-controlled resolver.
Confirm a nominated test host adopts the rogue configuration by checking its IPv6 routing table and DNS resolver settings after the RA is received.
Position a listener/relay (e.g., NDPMon-adjacent tooling or a simple IPv6 forwarding setup) to intercept and relay the test host's IPv6 traffic transparently, demonstrating full on-path capability.

Stop actively advertising the rogue RA promptly after capturing proof-of-concept evidence, and confirm affected hosts revert to the legitimate router once real RAs resume, to avoid extended service disruption.

examplePayloads.label: Advertise a rogue default IPv6 router with THC-IPv6
Advertise a rogue router with a rogue DNS server via Scapy
examplePayloads.command: sudo python3 -c "from scapy.all import *; send(IPv6(dst='ff02::1')/ICMPv6ND_RA()/ICMPv6NDOptRDNSS(dns=['fe80::badd:dns'])/ICMPv6NDOptSrcLLAddr(lladdr='<attacker-mac>'), loop=1, inter=5)"

examplePayloads.label: Passive baseline capture of legitimate RAs

variants: DHCPv6 spoofing as a related but distinct attack surface where stateful DHCPv6 is in use instead of pure SLAAC, allowing rogue DHCPv6 server responses.

RA flooding as a denial-of-service variant, where large volumes of RAs with distinct prefixes overwhelm client address-configuration and neighbor-cache resources rather than establishing a clean MITM position.
mitigation: Enable RA-Guard (and DHCPv6 Guard where stateful DHCPv6 is used) on all access-layer switch ports, permitting Router Advertisements only from ports connected to legitimate infrastructure routers.

Deploy IPv6 Source/RA validation consistently wherever IPv4 DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection are already deployed, since organizations frequently harden the IPv4 path while leaving the IPv6 path completely open.
Explicitly disable IPv6 on hosts and network segments that genuinely have no IPv6 use case, rather than leaving it enabled-by-default and unmonitored 'just in case'.
Monitor for unexpected Router Advertisement sources using NDP/RA monitoring tooling (e.g., ramond, NDPMon) and alert on RAs originating from non-router-designated ports.

NET-045.prerequisites: Network access to the target TLS service. nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script or testssl.sh for cipher-suite enumeration.
NET-045.whatItIs: The target's encrypted connection (TLS) supports a mode that completes the full handshake — including verifying the server's identity — but applies zero actual encryption to the data itself. Any connection using this mode sends its data in plain, readable text despite looking, on the surface, like a legitimate secure connection.
NET-045.rootCause: This mode exists in the encryption standard purely for testing and diagnostics, letting developers check protocol compatibility without encryption overhead getting in the way. Its presence on a live, production server is almost always an accident from a broad, unreviewed list of allowed options — there's essentially no legitimate reason for it to be there in production.
NET-045.impact: A client that negotiates (or is forced, via a downgrade attempt, to negotiate) a NULL cipher suite transmits data in complete cleartext, readable by anyone with passive network-path visibility, while the connection still superficially presents as "secured by TLS" at the protocol level — this can be particularly deceptive since automated tooling or a cursory review checking only "is TLS in use" might not catch that the actual negotiated cipher provides no confidentiality at all.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the target TLS service's supported cipher suites, specifically flagging any NULL-encryption variant (`NULL-SHA`, `NULL-MD5`, or similarly named).
Confirm whether a NULL cipher suite can actually be successfully negotiated in practice.
Where negotiable, capture a test connection using the NULL cipher suite and confirm the application data is indeed transmitted in cleartext despite the TLS handshake completing normally.
Where NULL cipher suites are offered, confirm whether they are reachable via a normal client negotiation or only via an explicitly-crafted client hello, since this affects real-world exploitability.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cipher-suite enumeration and, if demonstrating impact, a connection test against the target TLS service.
Enumerate supported cipher suites and confirm NULL variants are present.
Attempt to establish a connection explicitly requesting a NULL cipher suite and confirm successful negotiation.
Capture the resulting session and confirm the application data is plaintext despite the completed TLS handshake.
Document the confirmed NULL-cipher-suite support and the demonstrated cleartext data exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate cipher suites including NULL variants
Comprehensive TLS configuration scan flagging NULL ciphers
Explicitly attempt to negotiate a NULL cipher suite

variants: NULL cipher suite supported alongside strong, properly-encrypted options (an attacker must force its selection) versus, in a severe misconfiguration, being accepted as the server's negotiated default for a specific client request.

NULL-encryption cipher suites (integrity-only, no confidentiality) are sometimes intentionally negotiated by monitoring/DLP middleboxes — auditing for this variant specifically catches infrastructure that silently downgrades confidentiality for inspection purposes.
mitigation: Remove all NULL cipher suites from the server's TLS configuration entirely — there is no legitimate production use case justifying their inclusion.
Adopt a current, well-vetted TLS cipher-suite configuration baseline rather than a broad, unreviewed cipher list.
Periodically re-scan TLS configuration after any server software update, since a default configuration reset can sometimes reintroduce broader cipher support than intended.

NET-046.prerequisites: An on-path network position between a target client and the web services it accesses (an ARP-spoofing/rogue-AP position, per the related findings). SSLstrip or a modern equivalent (bettercap's HSTS-bypass module) for intercepting and rewriting HTTPS links to HTTP.
NET-046.whatItIs: This is a classic interception technique: an attacker positioned between a victim and a website intercepts the victim's very first, unencrypted request (like typing a bare address with no 'https://'), and quietly rewrites every secure link in the response to an insecure one before passing it along. The victim's browser never actually establishes a real secure connection to the real site — it just talks to the attacker over an insecure connection the whole time, while the attacker separately maintains the real secure connection to the actual website.
NET-046.rootCause: A lot of people connect to websites by typing a bare address or clicking an old link with no 'https://' specified, which the browser can't know in advance needs to be secure — creating a brief, exploitable window on that very first request. If the browser hasn't previously been told to always use HTTPS for that specific site, an attacker positioned in the middle can keep the entire session downgraded indefinitely by continuing to rewrite every link back to the insecure version.
NET-046.impact: A victim's entire browsing session for the targeted site can be silently downgraded to HTTP, exposing credentials, session cookies, and all page content to the attacker's interception — this technique remains effective specifically against sites lacking HSTS (or a browser that hasn't yet cached that site's HSTS policy), representing a serious practical MITM risk despite HTTPS being nominally available on the target site.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target site's HSTS configuration status (per the related, dedicated HSTS finding) — SSL-stripping is only practically exploitable against a site lacking HSTS or preload-list inclusion.
With authorization, position on-path for a nominated test client's browsing session and run an SSL-stripping tool.

Observe whether the test client's browser silently continues over HTTP for the targeted site without any certificate warning (since no HTTPS connection to the real server is ever actually attempted by the victim's browser in this scenario).

Confirm whether the test client's browser has previously cached an HSTS policy for the target domain (from a prior direct visit), which would prevent the downgrade from succeeding despite the site's own current lack of the header.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes on-path SSL-stripping testing against a nominated test client's connection to the target site.
Position on-path (via an authorized ARP-spoofing/rogue-AP setup) for the test client.
Run the SSL-stripping tool and have the test client initiate a bare-domain-name request to the target site.
Confirm the resulting session remains downgraded to HTTP throughout, and capture a benign, non-sensitive proof-of-concept credential/session-cookie value as evidence.
Document the confirmed downgrade and its dependency on the target site's HSTS-absence, cross-referencing the dedicated HSTS finding as the underlying enabling condition.

examplePayloads.label: Position on-path and run SSLstrip against the test client's traffic
examplePayloads.command:
sslstrip -l 8080
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --destination-port 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080

examplePayloads.label: Modern alternative with bettercap, including HSTS-bypass techniques
examplePayloads.command: bettercap -iface eth0 -eval 'set http.proxy.sslstrip true; http.proxy on; set arp.spoof.targets <test-client-ip>; arp.spoof on'

variants: Classic SSL-stripping against a site with no HSTS at all (fully effective) versus against a site with HSTS but relying only on the header (not preload-list inclusion), where the downgrade still succeeds on the victim's very first-ever visit before any HSTS header could have been cached.
Stripping applied broadly across all HTTPS links in a session versus a more surgical, single-page-targeted downgrade to avoid detection.
mitigation: Deploy HSTS with a long `max-age` and `includeSubDomains` on every HTTPS service, per the dedicated HSTS finding's guidance.
Submit the domain to browser HSTS preload lists, closing the gap that HSTS's header-based mechanism alone can't cover on a victim's first-ever visit.
Encourage users to navigate via bookmarked or explicitly-HTTPS links rather than bare domain names where practical, as a secondary, less-reliable behavioral mitigation.

Address the underlying on-path-positioning vector (ARP spoofing, rogue AP) as the root enabler, since HSTS closes the specific downgrade window but doesn't prevent the attacker from achieving an on-path position in the first place.

NET-047.prerequisites: Network access to the target HTTPS/TLS service. openssl or curl for retrieving and inspecting the presented certificate's issuer field.
NET-047.whatItIs: The service presents a certificate it generated itself, rather than one issued by a recognized, publicly trusted authority. This causes every standard browser or tool to show a warning or outright reject the connection — and worse, it trains users and administrators to just click through these warnings out of habit, which weakens the protective value of that warning everywhere, not just for this one service.
NET-047.rootCause: A self-signed certificate is the quickest way to get encryption working without going through the process of getting one properly issued, and it sometimes gets used as a temporary stopgap during setup that's never actually replaced. It's also sometimes deliberately kept on internal-only services under the assumption that warnings there don't matter — which ignores the broader habit it trains people into.
NET-047.impact: Beyond the immediate connection warnings/failures, the most significant risk is behavioral: once users or automated systems are trained to bypass certificate warnings or disable certificate validation entirely for this specific self-signed service, that same bypassed configuration or habituated behavior often extends to genuinely malicious certificate-validation failures elsewhere, directly enabling a MITM attack against a completely different, properly-certificate-secured service that the same user/system also accesses.
stepsToIdentify: Connect to the target service and retrieve the presented certificate.
Confirm the certificate is self-signed (issuer matches subject) or issued by a CA not present in standard trust stores.
Assess how many users/systems interact with this service and whether any documented guidance instructs them to bypass the resulting certificate warning or disable validation entirely.

Where automated systems/scripts are found configured to skip certificate validation specifically to accommodate this service, flag this as a compounding, more severe finding given the broader risk it represents.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes certificate inspection against the target service.
Retrieve the certificate and confirm its self-signed/untrusted-issuer status.
Document any evidence of users/systems being instructed or configured to bypass the resulting validation failure.
Assess and document the broader behavioral/technical risk this creates for the organization's certificate-validation practices as a whole.

examplePayloads.label: Retrieve and inspect the certificate's issuer/subject fields
Confirm via curl and check for a validation failure
examplePayloads.command: curl -v https://<target-hostname>/ 2>&1 | grep -i 'self signed\|unable to get local issuer'

variants: Self-signed certificate on an internal-only tool (lower immediate risk, but still a behavioral-conditioning concern) versus on a customer-facing or broadly-accessed internal service (higher risk given wider exposure to the conditioning effect).

Self-signed certificate alone versus combined with evidence that automated tooling has been explicitly configured to disable certificate validation entirely to work around it — the latter being a materially more severe, compounding finding.
mitigation: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a properly-trusted CA (a public CA for internet-facing services, or the organization's own internal CA distributed to all relevant internal client trust stores for internal-only services).
Never configure any client or automated system to bypass certificate validation as a workaround; fix the underlying certificate/trust-chain issue instead.

Where an internal CA is used, ensure its root certificate is properly and consistently distributed to every client trust store that needs to validate against it, rather than relying on ad hoc, per-user bypass configuration.
Periodically audit for self-signed certificates across the environment as part of routine TLS-configuration scanning.

NET-048.prerequisites: Network access to the target HTTPS/TLS service. nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers or a dedicated CRIME-detection script, and the ability to trigger a request whose body reflects an attacker-influenceable value alongside a secret (a cookie/token) to test practical exploitability.
NET-048.whatItIs: The target's encrypted connection has a specific compression feature turned on that, separate from any regular web-page compression, creates a subtle side-channel: because compression shrinks repeated patterns of data, an attacker who can inject content alongside a secret value (like a login cookie) into that same compressed stream can gradually guess the secret one character at a time, just by watching how the compressed size changes.
NET-048.rootCause: This particular compression feature was deprecated specifically because of this weakness, but a server or library that hasn't been updated or reconfigured may still have it turned on. Unlike decisions made at the application level, this setting is often controlled by a lower-level library default that an application developer might not even realize is there.
NET-048.impact: An attacker capable of injecting chosen content into requests alongside a victim's session cookie (typically via a separate vector, such as getting the victim to visit an attacker-controlled page that issues cross-origin requests) can incrementally recover the secret cookie value through the compression-ratio side channel, potentially achieving session hijacking without ever needing to defeat the TLS encryption itself directly.
stepsToIdentify: Scan the target TLS service for compression support at the TLS protocol level specifically (distinct from HTTP-level gzip/deflate, which is a separate, generally-safe practice on its own).

Where TLS-level compression is confirmed enabled, assess whether the application's request-handling pattern would realistically allow an attacker to inject chosen content into the same compressed context as a sensitive cookie/token (a necessary precondition for practical CRIME exploitation).
Where the precondition is met, and with authorization, attempt a proof-of-concept extraction of a test cookie value using the compression-ratio side-channel technique.
Check whether the affected service also supports HTTP-level compression (a related but distinct BREACH-class issue), since both stem from the same underlying compression-oracle weakness.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes TLS-compression testing and, where the precondition is met, a full CRIME proof-of-concept extraction against a nominated test session.
Confirm TLS-level compression is enabled on the target service.
Set up a proof-of-concept attacker-controlled page capable of issuing repeated, chosen-content cross-origin requests to the target alongside the test session's cookie.
Run the byte-by-byte compression-ratio extraction technique against the test session's cookie value and confirm successful recovery.
Document the confirmed TLS-compression support and, if demonstrated, the successful secret-extraction proof of concept.

examplePayloads.label: Check for TLS-level compression support
Confirm via a manual TLS handshake inspection in Wireshark

variants: TLS-level compression enabled but the application's request pattern doesn't realistically allow the attacker-content-injection precondition (a valid finding, but with limited practical exploitability demonstrated) versus a confirmed, fully practical CRIME extraction scenario.

The related HTTP-level variant (as opposed to TLS-level CRIME) is BREACH, which exploits HTTP response body compression rather than the TLS compression layer itself, and requires a separate, distinct test.
mitigation: Disable TLS-level compression entirely on the server; this is a straightforward, low-disruption configuration change with essentially no legitimate reason to retain it given the well-understood risk.

Where HTTP-level (application-layer) compression is separately used, be aware this is a distinct and generally safer practice, but avoid combining it with sensitive data reflected alongside attacker-influenceable content in the same response body, since a related side-channel (BREACH) can affect HTTP-level compression under similar conditions.
Keep TLS libraries current, since modern defaults have moved away from enabling TLS-level compression at all.

NET-049.prerequisites: Network access to the target TLS service. nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script (which includes a renegotiation check) or a dedicated tool for testing insecure renegotiation specifically.
NET-049.whatItIs: The target's encrypted connection allows an older, insecure way of renegotiating (restarting) the handshake in the middle of an existing connection, with no cryptographic link tying the renegotiated session back to the original one. An attacker who can open a connection to the server — without needing to actually be logged in yet — can splice a real, legitimate user's request into that connection through renegotiation, tricking the server into processing the victim's authenticated request as if it were a continuation of the attacker's own unauthenticated session.
NET-049.rootCause: The original design for renegotiating a TLS connection had no way to verify that the renegotiated session genuinely belonged to the same original connection — a fix was later introduced to cryptographically bind the two together, but a server that hasn't been updated to require that fix (often kept that way for compatibility with older clients) remains vulnerable to this splicing trick.
NET-049.impact: An attacker can prepend their own, attacker-chosen request to a connection, then allow a victim's legitimate, authenticated request to be spliced in via renegotiation, resulting in the server executing the combined request stream as if the attacker's initial content and the victim's subsequent authenticated content were part of the same, single authorized request — depending on the application protocol (HTTP being the most commonly affected), this can enable request smuggling/injection into an authenticated session.
stepsToIdentify: Test the target TLS service for support of insecure (pre-RFC 5746) renegotiation using an SSL/TLS-scanning tool with renegotiation-check capability.
Confirm whether the server requires the secure-renegotiation extension (RFC 5746) or permits a renegotiation handshake without it.
Where insecure renegotiation is confirmed supported, assess the specific application-protocol context (typically HTTP) for realistic exploitability of the request-splicing technique.
Confirm whether the server supports secure renegotiation (RFC 5746) as an available but unused option, versus lacking the capability entirely, since this affects the concrete remediation step.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes insecure-renegotiation testing and, if demonstrating impact, a request-splicing proof of concept against the target service using a nominated test session.
Confirm insecure renegotiation support via the scanning tool.
Where feasible, demonstrate the request-splicing technique by prepending a chosen request and allowing a test client's subsequent authenticated request to be spliced in via renegotiation.
Document the confirmed insecure-renegotiation support and any successful splicing demonstration.

Report the finding as low practical severity if renegotiation is disabled entirely rather than insecurely enabled, since disabled renegotiation is not vulnerable to this specific attack despite appearing in a similar scan category.

examplePayloads.label: Check for insecure renegotiation support
examplePayloads.command: nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p443 <target-ip>  # includes a renegotiation-support field in output

examplePayloads.label: Comprehensive TLS scan flagging insecure renegotiation

variants: Insecure renegotiation supported alongside secure renegotiation (an attacker must force the insecure path) versus insecure renegotiation being the server's only supported mode.
Splicing exploited against an HTTP-based application specifically versus a different application-layer protocol running over TLS with its own request-boundary semantics.
mitigation: Update the TLS server software/library to a version supporting and requiring RFC 5746 secure renegotiation, rejecting any renegotiation attempt that doesn't include the proper cryptographic binding.

Where legacy client compatibility genuinely requires supporting insecure renegotiation temporarily, disable renegotiation entirely instead (many current server configurations simply disable renegotiation outright as the simpler, equally effective fix).
Keep TLS libraries current, since this vulnerability class has been comprehensively addressed in modern, well-maintained TLS implementations for many years.

NET-050.prerequisites: Read/administrative access (or knowledge from documentation review) of the target's backup infrastructure and storage location. Where testing black-box, network/file-system access to a discovered backup file/location for direct inspection.
NET-050.whatItIs: The organization's backup process — for databases, whole servers, or configuration files — produces backup files with no encryption at all applied to them. That means the complete contents of whatever got backed up, including any credentials or personal data present in the original system, sit in plain, readable form wherever those backups are stored.
NET-050.rootCause: Backup processes are often built with reliability and fast restoration as the main priorities, treating encryption as an optional extra that gets skipped unless a specific policy explicitly requires it. Since backup files get accessed and reviewed far less often than live production systems, an unencrypted backup can sit unnoticed for a very long time, even after everything else in the organization has been properly secured.
NET-050.impact: Anyone who gains access to a backup file/archive — through a misconfigured backup-storage location's access controls (overlapping with the general publicly-accessible-storage finding class), a stolen backup tape/drive, or a compromised backup-management system — obtains the complete plaintext contents of whatever was backed up, often representing an even broader and more complete data-exposure risk than compromising the live production system directly, since backups frequently retain historical data long after it's been deleted/rotated from the live system.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the organization's backup processes and their configured encryption settings (or lack thereof) via documentation/configuration review.

Where accessible, directly inspect a sample backup file/archive to confirm whether its content is genuinely plaintext/readable, versus merely appearing so due to file-format structure without actually being unencrypted.
Assess the backup-storage location's own access controls (a local file share, a cloud storage bucket, physical media) to determine the realistic population that could access the unencrypted backup.
Determine the backup-retention period, since a longer retention window compounds the data-exposure risk of any single unencrypted backup being accessed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes backup-file inspection and content-extraction testing against the target backup infrastructure.
Access a representative backup file/archive via its identified storage location.
Extract and inspect its content to confirm the presence of plaintext sensitive data.
Document the specific backup process, storage location, and the sensitive data categories confirmed present and unencrypted.

examplePayloads.label: Inspect a sample backup file's format/encryption status
Extract and search backup content for sensitive data patterns

variants: Database/application-data backups lacking encryption (direct sensitive-data exposure) versus full VM/system-image backups (potentially exposing an even broader scope, including OS-level credentials and configuration).

Unencrypted backup stored in an otherwise access-controlled location (moderate risk, contingent on that access control holding) versus stored in a location with its own separate access-control weakness (a compounding, more severe combined finding).
mitigation: Enable encryption for all backup processes, using a properly-managed key (per the general key-management guidance) separate from the backup storage location itself.
Apply the same access-control rigor to backup-storage locations as to production data, since backups often represent an equally or more complete copy of sensitive data.

Define and enforce a backup-retention policy balancing genuine business/compliance need against the compounding risk of retaining unencrypted (or even encrypted but very old) sensitive data indefinitely.

Periodically test backup-restoration procedures in addition to verifying encryption status, ensuring the security improvement doesn't inadvertently break the organization's actual disaster-recovery capability.

NET-051.prerequisites: Network access to the target TLS service. nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script or testssl.sh for comprehensive cipher-suite enumeration.
NET-051.whatItIs: The target's encrypted connection supports weak, outdated encryption methods — old, broken ciphers, ones with a small enough key that they can be practically cracked, or deliberately weakened options originally created to satisfy old export regulations — alongside or instead of strong, modern options.
NET-051.rootCause: Broad, permissive encryption settings tend to build up over time, as a server gets configured for maximum compatibility with older clients — without anyone going back later to trim that list down once support for those older clients genuinely isn't needed anymore. That leaves weak options available to any client, or attacker, that specifically asks for them.
NET-051.impact: An attacker able to force or take advantage of a weak-cipher-suite negotiation can, depending on the specific algorithm, practically decrypt captured traffic (RC4's biases enable practical plaintext recovery given sufficient samples), exploit a birthday-bound collision attack (Sweet32 against 3DES/Blowfish), or trivially break an export-grade cipher — undermining the confidentiality the TLS connection is meant to provide.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the target's supported cipher suites using a comprehensive TLS-scanning tool.
Flag any RC4, single-DES/3DES, or export-grade cipher suite still offered.
Confirm whether the weak cipher can actually be negotiated in practice (a client explicitly requesting it) versus only appearing in a broad list a modern client would never select by default.
Where a specific, named vulnerability (Sweet32 for 3DES) applies, assess practical exploitability given the connection's realistic traffic volume.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cipher-suite enumeration and, if applicable, exploitation testing against the target service.
Enumerate cipher suites and confirm weak options are present and negotiable.

Where a specific attack (Sweet32, RC4 biases) applies, assess and document practical exploitability, escalating to an actual proof-of-concept only where genuinely feasible within the engagement's scope and time budget.
Document every weak cipher confirmed and its specific, named vulnerability where applicable.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate cipher suites flagging weak options
Comprehensive TLS scan with named-vulnerability flagging
Explicitly attempt to negotiate a weak cipher suite

variants: RC4 support (keystream-bias-based plaintext recovery) versus 3DES/Sweet32 (birthday-bound collision attack, requiring substantial captured traffic volume to be practical) versus export-grade ciphers (trivially breakable given their deliberately weakened design).
Export-grade and 40/56-bit ciphers represent a more severe variant of general weak-cipher findings, since they're breakable in real time rather than merely below modern strength recommendations.
mitigation: Remove all weak cipher suites (RC4, single-DES/3DES, export-grade) from the server's TLS configuration, retaining only current, strong AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305).
Adopt a current, well-vetted TLS cipher-suite configuration baseline (Mozilla's SSL Configuration Generator or equivalent).
Periodically re-scan TLS configuration after any server software update to catch configuration regressions.

NET-052.prerequisites: Access to a domain-joined test account and a Kerberos-capable environment (Active Directory). Impacket's tooling (GetUserSPNs.py for Kerberoasting, or a direct check of supported encryption types) and hashcat for offline cracking of any recovered RC4-encrypted ticket material.
NET-052.whatItIs: Active Directory's login system (Kerberos) still allows an older, weaker encryption type for service tickets, instead of exclusively using the newer, stronger option. This weaker encryption is specifically what makes a well-known attack called 'Kerberoasting' practical — since a ticket encrypted this way is derived weakly enough from a service account's password that it can often be cracked offline.
NET-052.rootCause: This older encryption type was kept around for compatibility with old systems that can't handle the newer, stronger option. Unless it's explicitly turned off, it stays available as an option — and many organizations never revisit this setting even long after every genuinely old system that needed it has been retired.
NET-052.impact: Any authenticated domain user can request a service ticket (Kerberoasting) for any service account with a registered Service Principal Name, and if that ticket is issued using RC4-HMAC, the resulting ticket material can be cracked offline at high speed to recover the service account's actual password — since service accounts are frequently provisioned with weak or infrequently-rotated passwords and often hold significant privilege, this is one of the most common and effective privilege-escalation techniques in real-world Active Directory environments.
stepsToIdentify: Query Active Directory's domain/group-policy configuration for the `msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` setting on service accounts, and the domain-wide Kerberos encryption-type policy.

With authorization, use a standard, low-privilege domain test account to request service tickets for accounts with registered SPNs (Kerberoasting) and inspect the encryption type of the returned tickets.
Where RC4-HMAC tickets are obtained, assess practical crackability against a representative wordlist within the engagement's time budget.

Cross-reference which specific service accounts are affected and their privilege level, since a Kerberoastable, RC4-encrypted, highly-privileged service account represents the most severe instance of this finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes Kerberoasting and offline password-cracking testing using a designated, low-privilege domain test account.
Enumerate service accounts with registered SPNs and request their service tickets using the test account's credentials.
Confirm the returned tickets' encryption type and identify any using RC4-HMAC.
Attempt offline cracking of the RC4-encrypted ticket material against a representative wordlist.
Where a service-account password is recovered, validate it with a minimal, authorized check and document the account's privilege level as the impact evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate Kerberoastable accounts and request their tickets
Offline-crack a recovered RC4-encrypted (etype 23) ticket
Check the domain's supported Kerberos encryption-type policy
examplePayloads.command: Get-ADDomain | Select-Object -ExpandProperty KerberosEncryptionType  # PowerShell, with authorized domain read access

variants: RC4-HMAC enabled as a supported (but not sole) encryption type, giving an attacker the ability to request the weaker ticket type regardless of AES also being available, versus RC4-HMAC being the domain's effective default for accounts without an explicit, stronger encryption-type restriction configured.

Golden-ticket-adjacent risk: hosts still supporting RC4-HMAC for Kerberos also remain viable targets for older, well-documented ticket-forging techniques that specifically rely on the weaker encryption type being negotiable.
mitigation: Disable RC4-HMAC support at the domain level (setting `msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` to AES-only) once all genuinely legacy systems requiring RC4 have been identified and remediated/decommissioned.

Enforce strong, long, randomly-generated passwords for every service account, or migrate to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) which use automatically-rotated, high-entropy passwords resistant to offline cracking regardless of encryption type.
Monitor for Kerberoasting-indicative behavior (a burst of service-ticket requests for many distinct SPNs from a single account in a short window) as a detection signature.
Periodically audit and remediate service-account password strength/rotation practice as an ongoing Active Directory hygiene process.

NET-053.prerequisites: Physical access to a switch port protected by 802.1X. A second, small network device capable of acting as a hub/bridge (a cheap unmanaged switch, or a purpose-built bridging device like a LAN Turtle) to place between an already-authenticated device and the network jack.
NET-053.whatItIs: A network port that requires proper login before granting access continues to trust everything coming through that same port once one legitimate device has already logged in — without checking that traffic is still only coming from that one device. An attacker can plug a cheap network splitter in between the legitimate device and the wall, and piggyback their own device onto that already-authenticated connection, getting network access without ever logging in themselves.
NET-053.rootCause: A lot of these login-protected ports authenticate the port itself (or just the first device seen) rather than continuously checking that every single bit of traffic is still coming from that same, originally verified device. Stricter settings that would catch a second device sneaking in do exist on many switches, but a lot of deployments default to the more permissive, single-device mode that doesn't.
NET-053.impact: An attacker with brief physical access to insert a hub between an authenticated device and its jack gains full network access piggybacking on that device's authentication, without needing any 802.1X credential of their own — this is a purely physical-layer attack that entirely bypasses the network-layer authentication control 802.1X is meant to provide.
stepsToIdentify: Review the switch's 802.1X port-configuration mode (single-host, multi-host, multi-auth, multi-domain) to determine whether it's designed to detect/reject a second device's traffic on an already-authenticated port.
With authorization, physically insert a test hub/bridge between an already-authenticated test device and its network jack.
Connect a second test device to the same hub and attempt to obtain network access through it.
Confirm whether the second device successfully gains network access piggybacking on the first device's authenticated port state.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes this physical-insertion test against a nominated test port/device.
Insert the test hub/bridge between the authenticated test device and its jack.
Connect a second test device to the hub and attempt network access.
Confirm whether the second device's traffic is accepted despite not having independently authenticated.
Document the switch's port-authentication mode and the confirmed bypass technique.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm network access on the piggybacking device without independent 802.1X authentication
examplePayloads.command: dhclient eth0 && ip addr show eth0

examplePayloads.label: Check the switch's configured 802.1X host mode (where administrative access is available)
examplePayloads.command: show authentication sessions interface <interface>  # on a Cisco-style device, with authorization

variants: Piggybacking via a simple unmanaged hub (broadcasts all traffic, simplest to detect via unusual MAC-count anomalies) versus a purpose-built, more surreptitious bridging device designed to more carefully mimic single-device behavior.

MAC Authentication Bypass (MAB) fallback — where 802.1X falls back to MAC-based authentication for non-802.1X-capable devices — inherits all the weaknesses of simple MAC spoofing, effectively reintroducing the bypass the 802.1X deployment was meant to close.
mitigation: Configure 802.1X switch ports in multi-auth or multi-domain mode (rather than single-host/multi-host mode), which independently authenticates every distinct MAC address seen on the port rather than trusting the port as a whole once one device has authenticated.
Enable port-security features (limiting the number of distinct MAC addresses permitted per port, and alerting on violations) as a complementary control.
Physically secure or monitor accessible network jacks in public/semi-public areas where this attack is most feasible to execute undetected.
Periodically audit switch 802.1X configuration modes across the estate, since the more permissive default modes are commonly left unchanged unless specifically hardened.

NET-054.prerequisites: A network position on the same local Ethernet segment as the target. Scapy, arpspoof (dsniff suite), or Ettercap for crafting and sending forged ARP packets.
NET-054.whatItIs: The protocol that maps network addresses to physical device addresses on a local network has zero built-in verification — any device can claim to own any address, and most computers will just believe and remember whatever they're told, with no check at all. An attacker can claim to be the network's gateway, tricking every other device into routing its traffic through the attacker first.
NET-054.rootCause: This protocol was designed for a small, fully trusted local network with no adversarial devices in mind, and that assumption has never really been updated in the protocol itself. The real defenses against this live at the switch level, not in the protocol itself.
NET-054.impact: A successful ARP-spoofing attack gives the attacker a durable, transparent man-in-the-middle position over all traffic between the victim and whatever IP was spoofed (typically the default gateway, capturing all of the victim's outbound internet/inter-VLAN traffic) — this is one of the most foundational and broadly-enabling local-network attacks, since it's the prerequisite on-path position for numerous other findings in this domain (DNS spoofing, SSL stripping, session hijacking).
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target network segment lacks Dynamic ARP Inspection or an equivalent switch-level protection.
With authorization, send a forged ARP reply to a nominated test victim claiming to own the default gateway's IP address.
Confirm the test victim's ARP cache updates to associate the gateway's IP with the attacker's MAC address.
Confirm the attacker now receives the victim's traffic destined for the gateway, demonstrating the established MITM position.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active ARP-spoofing against a nominated test victim on the target segment.
Send forged ARP replies to the test victim (and, for a full bidirectional MITM, to the gateway as well) associating the attacker's MAC with the gateway's IP.
Confirm the resulting traffic redirection through the attacker's position.
Demonstrate impact via a benign passive-capture proof of concept, and enable IP forwarding to maintain victim connectivity throughout the test (avoiding an inadvertent denial-of-service).
Document the confirmed spoofing success and restore normal ARP state (or wait for cache expiry) once the finding is proven.

examplePayloads.label: Perform ARP spoofing with arpspoof (dsniff suite)
Bidirectional ARP spoofing with Ettercap for a full MITM position
Craft a forged ARP reply manually with Scapy
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from scapy.all import *
send(ARP(op=2, pdst='<victim-ip>', hwdst='<victim-mac>', psrc='<gateway-ip>'))
"

variants: One-directional spoofing (only the victim's cache is poisoned) versus full bidirectional spoofing (both victim and gateway are poisoned, establishing a complete, transparent MITM in both traffic directions).
ARP spoofing used purely for traffic interception versus as the enabling precursor for a chained attack (DNS spoofing, SSL stripping, session hijacking documented elsewhere in this domain).
mitigation: Deploy Dynamic ARP Inspection on network switches, which validates ARP packets against a trusted binding table (typically built from DHCP snooping records) and drops any ARP reply that doesn't match a legitimate, known IP-to-MAC binding.

Use static ARP entries for especially critical hosts (the default gateway) on high-value endpoints, understanding this doesn't scale broadly but can be a targeted mitigation for specific critical systems.
Deploy network segmentation to limit the population of hosts sharing a broadcast domain with any given set of sensitive endpoints, reducing the pool of potential on-path attackers.
Monitor for ARP-spoofing-indicative traffic patterns (gratuitous ARP floods, conflicting IP-to-MAC mappings) as a detection signature.

NET-055.prerequisites: Network access to the target TLS service, and an on-path or JavaScript-injection position capable of causing a victim's browser to make many chosen-plaintext requests (typically requiring a separate vector, such as a malicious/compromised page the victim visits). A TLS-scanning tool to confirm TLS 1.0/CBC-cipher support as the underlying precondition.
NET-055.whatItIs: An older version of TLS encryption has a specific weakness in how it encrypts data in blocks — using a predictable starting value instead of a genuinely random one for each message. Combined with an attacker's ability to get a victim's browser to make many requests (through malicious script code on a page the victim visits), this lets the attacker slowly recover encrypted content, like a login cookie, byte by byte.
NET-055.rootCause: This older version of TLS had a design flaw in exactly how it handled this predictable starting value — a flaw that was fixed in later versions. A server still supporting this older version remains theoretically exposed, though actually pulling off this attack in the real world takes considerably more effort than most other findings in this list.
NET-055.impact: Where successfully exploited, an attacker can incrementally recover encrypted content (most valuably, a session cookie) from a victim's TLS 1.0/CBC-mode connection, potentially enabling session hijacking — though the practical attack requires both a chosen-plaintext-injection capability (typically via a separate, already-achieved compromise such as a malicious ad network or a MITM position serving injected JavaScript) and specific client/server conditions that limit how commonly this is practically exploited in current environments.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target TLS service still supports TLS 1.0 with CBC-mode cipher suites, the necessary underlying precondition for BEAST.

Assess whether the client population realistically includes browsers still vulnerable to BEAST (most current browsers have implemented client-side mitigations such as 1/n-1 record splitting, which closes the practical exploitability even where the server-side TLS 1.0/CBC precondition remains).

Given the primarily historical nature of this finding today, prioritize documenting it as a legacy-protocol-support issue (overlapping with the general weak-protocol-version finding) rather than necessarily pursuing full exploitation, unless a specific, unusual client population genuinely remains vulnerable.
Check the affected client population's TLS stack versions, since BEAST specifically requires a client using TLS 1.0 with a CBC cipher suite and no 1/n-1 record splitting mitigation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes TLS 1.0/CBC-mode configuration testing against the target service.
Confirm TLS 1.0 with CBC-mode cipher support via a TLS-scanning tool.

Where full exploitation is genuinely in scope and a vulnerable client population is confirmed to exist, document the additional attacker-position/injection requirements needed as a real-world precondition rather than treating the server-side configuration alone as sufficient evidence of practical, demonstrated exploitability.
Document the confirmed legacy protocol/cipher support as the primary finding, noting BEAST specifically as the historical, named rationale for remediation priority.

Report the finding as largely historical/informational if the affected clients are confirmed to be modern browsers with client-side mitigations already in place, while still recommending TLS 1.0/CBC removal server-side.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm TLS 1.0 with CBC-mode cipher support
Explicitly test TLS 1.0 negotiation

variants: Server-side TLS 1.0/CBC support alone (the necessary but not sufficient precondition) versus a genuinely demonstrated, full exploitation chain including a chosen-plaintext-injection capability against a vulnerable client.

The related RC4-fallback mitigation some administrators historically deployed against BEAST (recommending RC4 over vulnerable CBC suites) merely traded one weak cipher family for another (RC4's own statistical biases), rather than a genuine fix.
mitigation: Disable TLS 1.0 (and SSLv3) entirely, requiring TLS 1.2 or 1.3 as the minimum supported version — this single change closes the BEAST precondition completely regardless of any other factor.
Prefer AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) which aren't affected by the CBC-mode weakness BEAST exploits, as the modern, comprehensive fix.

Keep browser/client software current, since major browsers have independently implemented client-side mitigations against this specific attack even where a server still offers the vulnerable configuration.

NET-056.prerequisites: Control of (or a test environment simulating) an autonomous system with BGP peering capability, and knowledge of the target's announced IP prefixes. A BGP-monitoring/looking-glass service (RIPE RIS, BGPStream, or a commercial route-monitoring tool) for detection-side testing rather than active route injection, which should never be performed against real, production internet routing outside of an isolated lab environment.
NET-056.whatItIs: The protocol that routers across the entire internet use to announce 'I know how to reach this address range' has no built-in way to verify that whoever's making an announcement is actually authorized to. An attacker who controls (or has compromised) a piece of internet routing infrastructure can announce that they know how to reach a victim's address range — and if other networks accept and spread that announcement, traffic meant for the victim gets misdirected to the attacker instead.
NET-056.rootCause: This routing system was designed assuming a cooperative network of trusted operators, relying on informal trust relationships between network operators rather than a comprehensive, universally-adopted cryptographic verification system. A newer verification system does exist to fix this, but it's still not deployed everywhere across the internet — so an unverified, false announcement can often still be accepted and spread.
NET-056.impact: A successful BGP hijack can redirect traffic destined for the victim organization's IP address space to the attacker's network, enabling large-scale traffic interception, denial of service (if the hijacked traffic is simply dropped rather than proxied), or, in a sophisticated attack, a MITM position allowing the attacker to intercept and even re-inject the traffic toward its legitimate destination after inspection — this is a network-wide, potentially internet-scale impact rather than one confined to a single organization's own infrastructure.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether the target organization has deployed RPKI Route Origin Authorization (ROA) records for its announced IP prefixes, which allows RPKI-validating networks to reject an unauthorized hijack announcement.

Use a BGP-monitoring/looking-glass service to review the organization's current and historical route-announcement data for any anomalous, unexpected origin-AS announcements that might indicate a past or ongoing hijack.
Assess whether the organization has any active BGP-monitoring/alerting capability of its own, or is solely reliant on third-party researchers/services to eventually notice and report an anomaly.

This finding is assessed primarily through passive monitoring-data review rather than active route injection, since actively announcing a hijacked route against real production internet routing infrastructure is never appropriate outside of a fully isolated lab/simulation environment.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope limits this assessment to passive BGP-monitoring-data review and RPKI/ROA configuration verification — active route hijacking against real internet infrastructure is out of scope for any standard engagement.
Query RPKI validation status for the organization's announced prefixes via a public RPKI-validator tool.
Review historical BGP route data for the organization's prefixes via a looking-glass/BGP-monitoring service for any past anomalous announcements.
Document the organization's current RPKI/ROA deployment status and any historical hijack-indicative anomalies found, as the primary evidence and deliverable for this finding.

examplePayloads.label: Check RPKI validation status for an announced prefix
Review historical route-announcement data via a BGP-monitoring service

variants: A full-prefix hijack (announcing the exact same prefix, which is subject to normal BGP route-preference tie-breaking) versus a more-specific sub-prefix hijack (which routing protocols inherently prefer regardless of AS-path length, making it a more reliably successful hijack technique).

Route leaks resulting from a misconfigured route-optimizer or multi-homed customer network (unintentional) present the same routing-integrity risk as a deliberate hijack, and are actually the more common real-world occurrence.
mitigation: Create and publish RPKI Route Origin Authorization (ROA) records for all of the organization's announced IP prefixes, enabling RPKI-validating networks worldwide to automatically reject unauthorized hijack announcements.
Work with upstream transit providers to ensure they perform RPKI-based route filtering (Route Origin Validation) on received announcements.
Deploy active BGP-monitoring/alerting (via a commercial service or a public monitoring platform's API) to detect anomalous announcements involving the organization's prefixes promptly.
Maintain an incident-response runbook specifically for a suspected BGP hijack, including contact procedures for upstream providers and BGP-monitoring services.

NET-057.prerequisites: Read/administrative access (or documentation review) of the organization's BGP router configuration, specifically its prefix-filtering policy applied to routes received from and announced to BGP peers.
NET-057.whatItIs: The organization's routers don't properly check that the routing announcements they accept from (or send to) other networks actually make sense for that specific partner — accepting or forwarding routes without validating they fall within the expected range. Unlike a deliberate hijack, this usually causes an accidental mistake somewhere else on the internet to get accepted and spread further by the organization's own network, adding to broader internet routing instability.
NET-057.rootCause: Properly filtering these routing announcements requires building and maintaining an explicit, up-to-date list of exactly which routes should legitimately come from each specific partner network — an ongoing task that sometimes gets skipped in favor of a simpler, broader 'accept everything' setup, especially at smaller or less experienced network operators.
NET-057.impact: Without prefix filtering, the organization's network can inadvertently accept and further propagate an accidental (or malicious) route leak from a peer, contributing to broader internet routing instability, and separately, the organization's own network becomes a less discriminating, easier vector for a route leak or hijack originating elsewhere to propagate further than it otherwise would if properly-filtering networks existed throughout the path.
stepsToIdentify: Review the organization's BGP router configuration for explicit prefix-filter (or RPKI-based Route Origin Validation) policy applied to each configured peering session.
Where administrative access allows, confirm whether any peering session is configured to accept routes without any filtering restriction at all.

Cross-reference the organization's actual current routing table against what would be expected given its documented peering relationships, looking for any anomalous, out-of-place route that prefix filtering should have rejected.

Cross-reference the leaked prefix against the organization's actual allocated address space to confirm the leak is a genuine misconfiguration rather than an intentionally-advertised, legitimately-owned block.
exploitationSteps: This finding is assessed primarily through configuration review rather than active exploitation, since deliberately triggering a route leak against real production routing infrastructure is not an appropriate testing action.
Confirm scope authorizes BGP configuration review for the target organization's routers.
Review prefix-filter policy configuration for each peering session.
Document any peering session found lacking adequate prefix filtering, and any evidence in the current routing table suggesting a filtering gap has already been exploited (accidentally or otherwise).
Report the specific leaked prefix and the ASN it was leaked to, since remediation requires a routing-policy change (explicit prefix-list/filter) on the specific BGP session involved.

examplePayloads.label: Review a BGP peering session's configured prefix-filter policy (Cisco-style device, with authorization)
Cross-reference the current routing table against expected peer prefixes

variants: Missing filtering on routes received from a peer (accepting an accidental/malicious leak) versus missing filtering on routes announced to a peer (propagating the organization's own routes more broadly than intended, a related but distinct configuration gap).

AS-path prepending manipulation, where a leaked route is made to appear less attractive via path length rather than more attractive, can still redirect a meaningful subset of traffic depending on the specific peering relationships involved.
mitigation: Implement explicit, maintained prefix-filter lists for every BGP peering session, permitting only the specific, expected prefix ranges legitimately associated with that peer.
Deploy RPKI-based Route Origin Validation to automatically reject announcements failing cryptographic origin verification, reducing reliance on manually-maintained filter lists alone.

Participate in industry best-practice frameworks (such as MANRS, Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security) which provide established guidance and community accountability for this class of routing hygiene.
Periodically audit peering configuration for filtering-policy completeness as peering relationships change over time.

NET-058.prerequisites: A Bluetooth/BLE-capable adapter with monitor/sniffing support (Ubertooth One, or an nRF52-based sniffer). Tooling for the specific vulnerability class being tested (InternalBlue for BlueBorne-class issues, the KNOB proof-of-concept scripts for the key-negotiation downgrade). Written authorization for active Bluetooth/BLE testing.
NET-058.whatItIs: Bluetooth-capable devices in scope are still vulnerable to well-known, publicly disclosed Bluetooth flaws — one family that allows an attacker to take over a device with zero interaction and without even needing to be paired with it, and another that lets an attacker force the encryption used during pairing down to something so weak it can be cracked in seconds — because these devices haven't received the manufacturer's patch fixing these specific issues.
NET-058.rootCause: One of these flaw families came from bugs across multiple different vendors' Bluetooth software, while the other comes from a design flaw in how classic Bluetooth negotiates encryption strength, with no protection against that negotiation being tampered with. Both require a manufacturer patch to actually fix, and devices — especially older or rarely-updated ones — that never get that patch stay exposed indefinitely.
NET-058.impact: BlueBorne-class vulnerabilities can, on an unpatched device, enable an attacker within Bluetooth range to achieve remote code execution or establish a MITM position without any pairing or user interaction required at all; KNOB allows an on-path attacker to force weak encryption onto a Bluetooth session and then brute-force the resulting low-entropy key in real time to decrypt or inject into the session — both represent severe, proximity-based compromise vectors for any unpatched device carrying either vulnerability.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory Bluetooth-capable devices in scope and check their firmware/OS versions against the published BlueBorne and KNOB advisory lists for confirmed-vulnerable versions.
With authorization, attempt the specific proof-of-concept technique for a suspected-vulnerable device (an InternalBlue-based BlueBorne check, or the KNOB key-length-downgrade proof of concept).
Confirm whether the specific vulnerability is practically exploitable against the identified device/firmware combination.

Prioritize devices carrying genuinely sensitive functionality (a smart lock, an industrial BLE sensor, a wireless keyboard used for administrative access) for deeper testing given their elevated real-world impact.
