exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active Bluetooth/BLE vulnerability testing against nominated test devices.
Identify the specific vulnerability class applicable to each test device's confirmed vendor/firmware version.
Run the appropriate proof-of-concept technique (BlueBorne-class exploitation via InternalBlue, or the KNOB key-negotiation downgrade attack) against the nominated test device.
Confirm the resulting impact (code execution, MITM position, or successful low-entropy key brute-force) via a benign, non-destructive demonstration.
Document the exact device, firmware version, vulnerability class, and confirmed exploitation outcome.

examplePayloads.label: Inventory Bluetooth device firmware versions for cross-referencing against advisories
examplePayloads.command: hcitool inq  # discover nearby devices; cross-reference vendor/model against BlueBorne/KNOB advisory lists

examplePayloads.label: BlueBorne-class proof-of-concept testing via InternalBlue
examplePayloads.command: python3 internalblue_cli.py  # connect to a compatible adapter and run the relevant BlueBorne-class check module

examplePayloads.label: KNOB key-negotiation downgrade proof-of-concept (research toolkit, authorized lab use only)

variants: BlueBorne-class remote-code-execution/MITM vulnerabilities (requiring no pairing at all) versus KNOB's encryption-downgrade-then-brute-force technique (requiring an on-path position during the pairing/connection process).

Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) GATT-level attacks — exploiting weakly-protected characteristic read/write permissions on a paired device — represent a related but architecturally distinct attack surface from the classic BR/EDR pairing-downgrade vulnerabilities.
mitigation: Apply vendor firmware/OS patches addressing BlueBorne-class CVEs and KNOB (CVE-2019-9506) across all Bluetooth/BLE-capable devices.
Where firmware allows, enforce a minimum acceptable encryption key length and reject connections negotiating below it.
Disable Bluetooth/BLE entirely on devices that don't require it, reducing the attack surface regardless of patch status.
For high-security environments, treat unpatched or unpatchable Bluetooth-capable devices as requiring physical/network isolation until remediated.

NET-059.prerequisites: Network access to a switch port on the target's wired network segment where CDP (Cisco Discovery Protocol) or LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol) frames are being exchanged. Wireshark or a purpose-built CDP/LLDP listening tool for passive capture.
NET-059.whatItIs: Network devices automatically broadcast detailed information about themselves — hostname, model, software version, network configuration — to anything plugged into the same switch, meant to help with legitimate network troubleshooting and mapping. There's no check on who's allowed to receive these broadcasts.
NET-059.rootCause: This broadcasting happens automatically and continuously by design, to support genuine network management — with no way to authenticate or restrict who's allowed to listen in. Anyone plugged into the same switch port passively picks up exactly the same detailed information a legitimate network admin's own tools would use.
NET-059.impact: An attacker with physical or logical access to a switch port receives detailed network-topology and device-version information with zero active probing required, directly aiding further attack planning — a disclosed switch model/firmware version can be cross-referenced against known CVEs, and VLAN/topology information helps an attacker understand and navigate the internal network structure for lateral-movement planning.
stepsToIdentify: Connect a test device (with physical-access authorization) to a representative switch port and passively capture CDP/LLDP traffic for an observation window.
Document the specific information disclosed — device hostname, model, firmware version, VLAN/native-VLAN configuration.
Assess whether CDP/LLDP is enabled uniformly across all switch ports (including general-access, non-management ports) versus restricted to trusted inter-switch/management links only.
Cross-reference any disclosed device model/firmware version against known CVEs as a potential further-escalation lead.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes passive CDP/LLDP capture at the target facility's network jacks.
Connect a test device to a representative jack and capture CDP/LLDP traffic for an agreed observation window.
Document every information field disclosed via the captured advertisements.
Cross-reference any disclosed version information against known vulnerabilities as supporting evidence for the finding's escalation potential.

examplePayloads.label: Passively capture CDP/LLDP traffic
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 'ether proto 0x2000 or ether dst 01:80:c2:00:00:0e' -w cdp_lldp_capture.pcap

examplePayloads.label: Parse and display captured CDP/LLDP advertisement content

variants: CDP/LLDP enabled on general-access, user-facing switch ports (higher risk, since any connecting device receives the disclosure) versus restricted to trusted inter-switch/management links only (lower risk, appropriate use).

LLDP's richer, more structured information model (compared to Cisco-proprietary CDP) can disclose additional detail — including precise port descriptions and system capabilities — making it a marginally higher-value reconnaissance target where both protocols are enabled.
mitigation: Disable CDP/LLDP on all user-facing, general-access switch ports, retaining it only on trusted inter-switch/management links where its topology-discovery function is genuinely needed.

Where LLDP must remain enabled more broadly for legitimate interoperability reasons (e.g. VoIP phone auto-configuration via LLDP-MED), restrict the specific information fields advertised to the minimum necessary.
Periodically audit CDP/LLDP configuration across the switch estate to catch any port where it's inadvertently left enabled beyond its intended scope.

NET-060.prerequisites: Network access to a Cisco switch with the Smart Install client feature enabled (TCP port 4786). The Smart Install Exploitation Tool (SIET) or an equivalent purpose-built tool.
NET-060.whatItIs: A Cisco feature meant to let brand-new switches automatically fetch their initial setup listens on a specific network port with zero authentication at all. An attacker who can reach that port on a switch with this feature turned on can pull the switch's configuration (which can include credentials), completely overwrite its settings or boot image, or force it to restart — all without ever providing a password.
NET-060.rootCause: This feature was designed for a narrow, trusted moment — a brand-new switch reaching out for its very first setup — and was never meant to stay reachable indefinitely on a switch that's already fully deployed and in production. But it's turned on by default on eligible devices, and it's easy to just never remember to turn it off once initial setup is done.
NET-060.impact: An attacker can extract a switch's configuration (potentially exposing credentials, SNMP community strings, or other sensitive configuration data), replace its configuration or boot image with an attacker-controlled one, or trigger a reload — collectively representing a complete, unauthenticated compromise path for any affected switch, with direct consequences for the availability and integrity of the network infrastructure it supports.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for TCP port 4786 (Smart Install) across the target's switch infrastructure.
For each discovered instance, use a Smart Install-specific tool to confirm the client is genuinely responsive to unauthenticated protocol messages.
Attempt a benign, read-only configuration-extraction request to confirm practical exploitability without altering the switch's actual configuration.
Check the switch's Smart Install client status (director-mode vs. client-mode) via the show vstack config command, since only client-mode switches with no configured director are exploitable.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes Smart Install interaction testing against the target switch — given the potential for a full configuration overwrite or reload, this needs explicit, cautious authorization and an agreed, read-only-only test scope unless a destructive test is specifically and separately authorized against a genuinely disposable test switch.
Confirm the Smart Install client is reachable and unauthenticated on the target switch.
Perform a read-only configuration-extraction request only, avoiding any configuration-modification or reload action against a production switch.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated access and the specific configuration data (if any) extracted as evidence.
Report the specific switch models/software versions confirmed in client-mode with Smart Install enabled, recommending the feature be disabled entirely where a director is not genuinely in use.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for the Smart Install port across the switch estate
Use SIET to confirm unauthenticated Smart Install access and extract configuration (read-only)

variants: Read-only configuration extraction (information-disclosure risk) versus configuration/boot-image overwrite or forced reload (a far more severe, availability- and integrity-impacting variant, appropriate only for testing against a genuinely disposable test switch with explicit authorization).

A related Smart Install variant abuses the feature not to exfiltrate configuration but to push a fraudulent configuration/IOS image directly to the switch, achieving a persistent compromise rather than a one-time information-disclosure event.
mitigation: Disable the Smart Install client feature entirely (`no vstack` in Cisco IOS configuration) on every switch once its initial zero-touch provisioning is complete — there is no legitimate reason to leave it enabled indefinitely in a production network.
Where Smart Install must remain enabled for ongoing provisioning workflows, restrict network reachability of port 4786 to only the designated Smart Install director via an access control list.

Apply vendor-recommended patches addressing specific Smart Install CVEs, as several distinct vulnerabilities (beyond the basic lack-of-authentication design issue) have been disclosed for this feature over time.
Include Smart Install status explicitly in routine network-device hardening audits, since it's a well-known, high-impact finding when present.

NET-061.prerequisites: A network position with passive traffic-visibility on the target segment (a shared hub/switch span port, or an authorized on-path position via a separate ARP-spoofing finding). Wireshark or tcpdump for capture and content extraction.
NET-061.whatItIs: One or more older protocols for web browsing or email are still in active use on the network with no encryption applied at all — meaning login credentials and message content for whichever protocol is affected travel across the network in fully readable, plain text.
NET-061.rootCause: These protocols all predate the modern expectation of encryption by default, and while most current setups default to the encrypted version, a specific older service, client, or integration can still be configured to use the plain, unencrypted version — often for compatibility with an old system that doesn't support encryption, or simply because nobody's revisited the setting since it was first configured.
NET-061.impact: Anyone with passive network-path visibility can capture and read credentials and full message/page content in cleartext for the affected protocol — for mail protocols specifically, this typically includes both the authentication credential and the full content of every message sent/received during the capture window, representing a substantial and ongoing data-exposure risk for as long as the cleartext configuration remains in use.
stepsToIdentify: Identify which of these protocols are in active use across the target network, distinguishing genuinely cleartext deployments from properly STARTTLS/implicit-TLS-secured ones.
With authorization, passively capture traffic for each identified cleartext protocol during a representative usage window.
Extract and confirm the presence of plaintext credentials and/or message content in the capture.
Assess the scope of affected users/systems and the sensitivity of the content typically exchanged via the cleartext protocol.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes passive traffic capture for the identified cleartext protocol(s) on the target network segment.
Capture traffic during a representative window covering normal use of the affected protocol.
Extract plaintext credentials and/or content from the capture as impact evidence.
Document the specific protocol, the scope of affected traffic, and the confirmed sensitive-data exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Capture and filter for cleartext HTTP traffic
Extract cleartext credentials from a captured IMAP/POP3/SMTP session
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r mail_capture.pcap -Y 'imap or pop or smtp' -T fields -e imap.request.command -e pop.request.command -e smtp.req.command -e data

examplePayloads.label: Extract objects (files) transferred over cleartext HTTP

variants: Cleartext HTTP for a web application (exposing session cookies and form-submitted credentials) versus cleartext mail protocols (exposing mail-account credentials and full message content) — both share the same missing-encryption root cause across different application protocols.
Legacy protocol used by a small, identifiable set of systems/users versus broadly, organization-wide, affecting the finding's overall severity/scope.
mitigation: Migrate every identified cleartext protocol to its encrypted equivalent — HTTPS for HTTP, and STARTTLS or implicit TLS (IMAPS/POP3S/SMTPS) for the respective mail protocols — with no unencrypted fallback permitted.
Disable the unencrypted protocol variant entirely at the server/service level once all clients have been migrated, rather than leaving it available indefinitely for backward compatibility.
Audit for any remaining legacy client/system requiring the unencrypted protocol and plan its remediation/replacement rather than accommodating it indefinitely.
Include cleartext-protocol detection in routine, periodic network traffic security audits.

NET-062.prerequisites: A network position on the same local segment as a target DHCP server (identical prerequisite conditions to the related rogue-DHCP/race-condition findings). Yersinia or a scripted DHCP-request-flooding tool, and, for the spoofing half, dnsmasq or a similar rogue DHCP server implementation.
NET-062.whatItIs: An attacker floods the network's address-assignment service with a rapid stream of fake requests, each pretending to come from a different made-up device, until it runs out of addresses to hand out. Once that happens, real devices trying to join the network can't get an address at all — and the attacker can then set up their own fake address-assignment service to step in and serve those stranded devices instead, taking full control over their network settings.
NET-062.rootCause: The address-assignment protocol has no way to verify or limit who's asking for an address — any device can request an essentially unlimited number of addresses just by claiming a different identity each time. Combined with no protection stopping a rogue address-assignment service from stepping in afterward, the whole attack chain is fairly easy to pull off on an unprotected network.
NET-062.impact: Legitimate clients are denied network connectivity once the DHCP pool is exhausted, and if the attacker's rogue DHCP server then services the resulting unmet demand, every client that obtains a lease from it can be configured with an attacker-controlled gateway/DNS server, establishing a durable, segment-wide man-in-the-middle position for every affected client simultaneously.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target segment lacks DHCP snooping and, ideally, port-security/rate-limiting on DHCP-request traffic.
With authorization, send a bounded flood of DHCP requests using rotating spoofed source MAC addresses and monitor the target DHCP server's remaining pool capacity.
Confirm whether the legitimate pool can be exhausted within the test's bounded scope.

Where authorized, follow up by standing up a rogue DHCP server and confirming a nominated test client (whose original lease request now goes unserved by the legitimate, exhausted server) obtains a lease from the rogue server instead.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes DHCP-starvation testing against the target server/segment, with a tightly bounded approach given the direct denial-of-service impact on legitimate users during the test.
Send a bounded flood of spoofed-MAC DHCP requests and monitor the legitimate server's pool exhaustion.
Where authorized to demonstrate the full attack chain, stand up a rogue DHCP server and confirm a nominated test client obtains a malicious lease from it.
Stop the starvation flood promptly and release the consumed leases (or wait for their expiry) once the finding is proven, restoring normal service to the segment.
Document the confirmed pool-exhaustion feasibility and, if demonstrated, the successful rogue-server takeover.

examplePayloads.label: Perform a bounded DHCP starvation attack with Yersinia
examplePayloads.command: yersinia dhcp -attack 1  # DHCP starvation mode, run for a bounded, agreed duration

examplePayloads.label: Monitor the legitimate DHCP server's remaining pool capacity
examplePayloads.command: show ip dhcp pool  # on the DHCP server/router, with administrative access and authorization

examplePayloads.label: Stand up a rogue DHCP server once the legitimate pool is exhausted

variants: Starvation alone (a denial-of-service impact) versus starvation followed by rogue-server takeover (compounding into a full man-in-the-middle position for every subsequently-served client).

DHCPv6 starvation (exhausting the IPv6 address pool rather than IPv4) is a distinct variant requiring its own detection and mitigation, since many organizations that hardened IPv4 DHCP snooping have not extended equivalent protections to DHCPv6.
mitigation: Deploy DHCP snooping on network switches, which both rate-limits DHCP traffic per port and prevents any unauthorized rogue DHCP server response from being accepted, addressing both halves of this attack chain.
Apply port-security (limiting the number of distinct source MAC addresses accepted per switch port) to directly prevent the rapid-MAC-rotation technique starvation depends on.
Monitor DHCP server pool-utilization metrics with alerting on abnormally rapid depletion as a detection signature.
Size DHCP address pools with reasonable headroom above expected legitimate demand, understanding this raises the bar for a starvation attack without eliminating the underlying vulnerability.

NET-063.prerequisites: A network position on the same local segment as the target hosts, on a network with IPv6 enabled (even if IPv6 isn't the organization's primary/intended addressing scheme) but lacking DHCPv6 Guard. mitm6 (from the fox-it toolset) and, typically paired for full exploitation, ntlmrelayx (from Impacket).
NET-063.whatItIs: Windows computers prefer IPv6 over IPv4 by default and will actively ask for IPv6 network settings, even on a network the organization never deliberately set up for IPv6 at all. Since no legitimate answer ever comes (because there's no real IPv6 setup), an attacker running a specific tool can answer those requests instead, making itself the network's IPv6 DNS server — and from there, redirect certain lookups toward itself to intercept and relay Windows login attempts.
NET-063.rootCause: Windows's default preference for IPv6, combined with the near-universal lack of protection against fake IPv6 address-assignment responses, means that even organizations with zero deliberate IPv6 setup are still effectively running an unprotected IPv6 service on every network segment — simply because there's no legitimate service there to compete with an attacker's fake one.
NET-063.impact: This technique reliably yields NTLM credential-relay opportunities in a huge proportion of real-world Windows Active Directory environments, since it requires no prior foothold beyond basic network access and exploits a default OS behavior most organizations have never specifically considered or hardened against — relayed NTLM authentication can frequently be used to gain administrative access to other systems on the network, making this one of the most impactful and commonly successful internal-network attack techniques in practice.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target network segment has IPv6 enabled on client hosts (the Windows default) but no legitimate DHCPv6 server and no DHCPv6 Guard protection deployed.
With authorization, run mitm6 on the segment and observe whether Windows test hosts begin soliciting and accepting the attacker's spoofed IPv6/DNS configuration.
Confirm whether WPAD or other auto-discovery DNS queries from the test hosts are redirected to the attacker's position as a result.
Assess whether relayed NTLM authentication (via a chained ntlmrelayx setup) could reach a target service with a meaningful privilege level, to correctly scope real-world impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active mitm6/NTLM-relay testing against nominated test hosts on the target segment.
Run mitm6 to begin responding to DHCPv6 solicitations and redirecting DNS for the test hosts.
Chain the redirected traffic into ntlmrelayx, targeting a nominated test service to relay any captured NTLM authentication attempt.
Confirm the resulting relayed-authentication access achieved against the test service.
Document the confirmed technique and the resulting access, then stop the tooling promptly to restore normal network behavior for the affected segment.

examplePayloads.label: Run mitm6 to begin the DHCPv6 spoofing and DNS-redirection attack
Chain redirected traffic into an NTLM relay targeting a nominated test service

variants: Basic DHCPv6-spoofing-driven DNS redirection alone (an information-gathering/positioning step) versus the full chain combined with NTLM relay to a target service, achieving concrete unauthorized access.

Relay targeted at LDAP/LDAPS (commonly used to add a rogue computer account or extract directory information) versus at another NTLM-authenticating service depending on what's reachable and valuable in the specific environment.
mitigation: Deploy DHCPv6 Guard on network switches, providing the IPv6 equivalent of DHCPv4 snooping to prevent unauthorized DHCPv6 servers from being accepted.
Disable IPv6 entirely on network segments/hosts where the organization has no deliberate IPv6 deployment, removing the underlying exposed surface if IPv6 isn't genuinely needed.
Enable SMB signing and LDAP/LDAPS channel-binding/signing requirements domain-wide, which prevents relayed NTLM authentication from being usable even if the DHCPv6-spoofing positioning step succeeds.
Disable NTLM authentication entirely in favor of Kerberos-only authentication where the environment's application compatibility allows, removing the relay target altogether.

NET-064.prerequisites: Network access to a target TLS service (typically HTTPS) that shares its private key with another service on the same or a related host still supporting SSLv2. openssl or a DROWN-specific scanning tool for confirming SSLv2 support on the shared-key service.
NET-064.whatItIs: If the same encryption key is shared between a modern, properly secured website and any other service — even a completely different one — that still supports a very old, fundamentally broken version of encryption, an attacker can use that old, broken service as a tool to gradually decrypt a captured, otherwise-secure session from the modern website, without directly attacking the modern website at all.
NET-064.rootCause: This ancient encryption version has serious, well-documented weaknesses, and any service still supporting it becomes an exploitable weak point for the shared key — regardless of how well-configured the modern service using that same key otherwise is. The problem isn't really in the modern service at all — it's that the key is shared with something far less secure.
NET-064.impact: An attacker can decrypt captured, modern TLS sessions from the properly-configured HTTPS service by exploiting a completely different, SSLv2-supporting service that happens to share the same private key — this makes DROWN a particularly insidious finding since scanning the HTTPS service in isolation would show a perfectly modern, well-configured TLS setup, while the actual vulnerability lies in an easily-overlooked, shared-key sibling service.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all services (across all hosts) sharing the same TLS private key/certificate as the target HTTPS service — commonly a mail server, an FTP-over-TLS service, or another web server on a different port/host using the identical certificate.
Test each identified shared-key service specifically for SSLv2 support, since this is the actual vulnerable component even if the primary HTTPS service itself has no legacy protocol support at all.

Where SSLv2 support is confirmed on any shared-key service, assess practical DROWN exploitability given the specific SSLv2 implementation's characteristics (some DROWN variants require additional implementation-specific conditions beyond bare SSLv2 support).
Check whether the vulnerable SSLv2-supporting service shares its private key with any other, otherwise-modern TLS service, since DROWN's cross-protocol attack specifically depends on key reuse.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes DROWN-related testing across every service sharing the target's TLS private key, not just the primary HTTPS service itself.
Enumerate every service sharing the same key/certificate.
Test each for SSLv2 support.

Where a vulnerable, shared-key SSLv2-supporting service is confirmed, assess and, where genuinely feasible within scope, demonstrate the decryption-oracle technique against a captured test HTTPS session.
Document the specific shared-key service found vulnerable and its relationship to the primary, otherwise well-configured HTTPS service.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate services potentially sharing the same certificate/key
examplePayloads.command: openssl x509 -in target_cert.pem -noout -fingerprint  # compare fingerprints across every service using the same certificate

examplePayloads.label: Test a shared-key service (e.g. a mail server) for SSLv2 support
Dedicated DROWN vulnerability scanner

variants: General DROWN (requiring roughly 2^50 SSLv2 connection attempts, computationally significant but feasible for a well-resourced attacker) versus special DROWN variants affecting specific, additionally-vulnerable OpenSSL versions that reduce this to a far more practical attack.

The cross-protocol variant — where any server sharing the same private key as an unrelated SSLv2-enabled server elsewhere (a shared certificate across multiple hosts) becomes vulnerable even if that specific server itself has SSLv2 fully disabled.
mitigation: Disable SSLv2 entirely on every service across the environment, with no exceptions — there is no legitimate reason to retain SSLv2 support anywhere in a current environment.

Never reuse a TLS private key/certificate across services with different security-configuration postures; issue distinct certificates/keys per service where their hardening levels might otherwise diverge.
Audit the full inventory of services sharing any given TLS key as part of routine certificate-management practice, not just the primary, most visible service using it.

NET-065.prerequisites: Network access to the target's CUPS (Common Unix Printing System) service, typically port 631. nmap and curl, or a CUPS-specific exploitation module for the relevant CVE (multiple CUPS RCE vulnerabilities have been disclosed, most notably the 2024 cups-browsed IPP-related vulnerability chain).
NET-065.whatItIs: A print-server system is directly reachable over the network — instead of being limited to the local machine or a trusted internal segment — and it's running a version with a known, serious flaw that lets an attacker run their own commands on it, triggered simply by how the service auto-discovers network printers.
NET-065.rootCause: This service's printer-discovery feature was built for convenience and automatic discovery, and it didn't properly check certain values coming from that discovery process before using them in a way that could lead to running commands. That risk is made worse by the service commonly being left reachable well beyond the local-machine-only access it actually needs for legitimate use.
NET-065.impact: An attacker able to reach the exposed CUPS/`cups-browsed` service can, depending on the specific CVE chain and version, achieve remote code execution on the host running the vulnerable service — given how widely CUPS is deployed by default on many Linux distributions (often without administrators realizing it's running and network-reachable at all), this represents a broad, high-impact vulnerability class when unpatched instances are found exposed.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for CUPS services (port 631, and the related UDP discovery port) across the target's network range.
For each discovered instance, determine the exact CUPS/`cups-browsed` version via its banner/version-disclosure behavior.
Cross-reference the identified version against the specific, disclosed CVE chain(s) affecting CUPS/`cups-browsed` remote printer-discovery handling.
Confirm whether the service is reachable from beyond localhost (a necessary precondition for remote exploitation of the network-facing vulnerability chain).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes exploitation testing against the identified vulnerable CUPS instance.
Confirm the exact vulnerable version and reachability from a remote test position.

Use the published proof-of-concept/exploit technique for the specific CVE chain to attempt a benign, non-destructive code-execution demonstration (writing a uniquely-named marker file, rather than a destructive payload).
Confirm successful code execution and document the exact CVE chain, version, and demonstrated impact.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for CUPS services and their reachability
Determine the CUPS/cups-browsed version via banner disclosure
Apply the published exploit proof-of-concept for the identified CVE chain
examplePayloads.command: # use the specific, publicly-documented PoC matching the confirmed CUPS/cups-browsed version and CVE chain identified

variants: The 2024 cups-browsed IPP-attribute-based RCE chain specifically, versus other, separately-disclosed CUPS vulnerabilities (privilege-escalation or information-disclosure issues) affecting different components of the CUPS stack.

A related but distinct CUPS-adjacent finding involves the `cups-browsed` service accepting and processing print-queue definitions from any host on the network without the RCE component, still enabling a phantom-printer social-engineering angle even where the RCE itself is patched.
mitigation: Apply vendor patches addressing the specific CUPS/cups-browsed CVE chain immediately upon disclosure, given the severity and breadth of affected default Linux installations.

Restrict CUPS/cups-browsed network reachability to localhost only, or a tightly-scoped trusted internal segment, disabling the remote printer-discovery/browsing functionality entirely where it isn't genuinely required.

Disable the `cups-browsed` service entirely on any host that doesn't need automatic network-printer discovery, since many server/workstation deployments have no genuine need for this convenience feature at all.
Include CUPS/print-service exposure explicitly in routine external and internal vulnerability scanning, since it's a commonly-overlooked, often-unintentionally-running service.

NET-066.prerequisites: Network access to the target's etcd (client API, typically port 2379) or ZooKeeper (typically port 2181) service. curl for etcd's HTTP-based API, or the zkCli.sh client for ZooKeeper.
NET-066.whatItIs: A backend service that stores shared configuration and coordination data for a cluster of servers (commonly used with things like Kubernetes) is reachable over the network with no login required at all. Anyone who finds it can read — and often even change — the entire cluster's configuration, which frequently includes credentials and security keys stored in plain, readable text.
NET-066.rootCause: These coordination services are built mainly for communication between machines inside the same cluster, and are often deployed with authentication turned off entirely, under the assumption that just being on a private network is protection enough. That assumption breaks down the moment the service ends up reachable more broadly than the cluster's own internal, trusted communication path.
NET-066.impact: Anyone who reaches an unauthenticated etcd instance can read the complete Kubernetes cluster state, including secrets (unless separately encrypted at rest) — this is one of the most severe possible Kubernetes-related findings, since etcd access effectively grants the ability to read every credential the cluster manages and, with write access, to directly manipulate cluster state (creating new, malicious workloads, or altering RBAC policy) bypassing the Kubernetes API server's own access controls entirely.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for etcd/ZooKeeper service ports across the target's network range.
For each discovered instance, attempt to query it without providing any authentication credential.
Where access succeeds, enumerate a sample of stored keys/data to assess sensitivity (Kubernetes secrets, application configuration) without performing a bulk extraction.
For etcd specifically, check whether at-rest encryption for secrets has been separately configured, which would meaningfully reduce (though not eliminate) the impact of unauthenticated read access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated interaction with the discovered coordination-service instance.
Attempt to list and read a representative sample of stored keys/data without authentication.
Where etcd secrets are found stored in plaintext, extract a minimal, representative sample as impact evidence rather than a bulk dump.
Where write access is also confirmed unauthenticated, demonstrate this with a benign, clearly-labeled test key write/delete rather than modifying any genuine cluster state.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated access, its read/write scope, and the specific sensitive data categories found.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for etcd/ZooKeeper service ports
Query etcd for cluster keys without authentication
Query ZooKeeper for cluster state without authentication

variants: Read-only unauthenticated access (severe information-disclosure risk, especially where Kubernetes secrets are stored unencrypted) versus write access also unauthenticated (a materially more severe, cluster-integrity-compromising finding).

etcd specifically, given its direct role storing Kubernetes secrets, versus ZooKeeper, which more commonly stores configuration/coordination state that may be less directly credential-laden depending on the specific application using it.
mitigation: Require client-certificate-based (mutual TLS) authentication for etcd, and enable authentication with strong ACLs for ZooKeeper, in every deployment.

Restrict network reachability of these coordination services to only the specific cluster nodes that genuinely need to communicate with them, never exposing them to general internal network segments or the internet.
Enable Kubernetes' etcd at-rest encryption for secrets as defense in depth, so even a future unauthenticated-access gap doesn't directly expose plaintext credentials.

Include coordination-service exposure explicitly in routine cluster/infrastructure security audits, since these services are foundational, high-impact, and easy to overlook relative to more visible, user-facing application components.

NET-067.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Docker Engine API, typically TCP port 2375 (unencrypted) or 2376 (TLS, but potentially still unauthenticated depending on configuration). curl or the Docker CLI configured to interact with a remote, exposed daemon.
NET-067.whatItIs: A tool used to manage containers on a server exposes its remote control interface with no login required (and sometimes no encryption either). Anyone who finds it can issue commands to create and run containers however they want — including one that mounts the entire host machine's file system, giving them full control over the underlying server.
NET-067.rootCause: This remote management feature was built to support legitimate remote administration, but turning it on without requiring a login removes any protection at all. Since the underlying service runs with full administrative rights on the machine, any command sent through this interface carries that same level of access.
NET-067.impact: An attacker who reaches an unauthenticated Docker API can launch a new container with the host's filesystem bind-mounted in, obtaining full root-level access to the underlying host — this is functionally equivalent in severity to a direct, unauthenticated root shell on the host, and represents one of the most severe and immediately, trivially exploitable findings in any environment where it's present.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for the Docker API port(s) across the target's network range.
For each discovered instance, attempt to query the API without providing any authentication credential.
Where access succeeds, enumerate running containers and images to confirm the scope of accessible information without launching any new container yet.
Confirm the specific configuration (port 2375 unencrypted, or 2376 with TLS but no client-certificate authentication actually enforced).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes interaction with the discovered, unauthenticated Docker API, including launching a new, clearly-labeled test container.
Query the API to confirm unauthenticated access and enumerate existing containers/images.
Launch a new container with the host's root filesystem bind-mounted, using a minimal, benign base image.
From within the launched container, confirm host-level filesystem access as proof of the escalation.
Remove the test container immediately after confirming the finding, and document the exact API endpoint, its configuration, and the demonstrated host-compromise impact.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for the Docker API port
Query the Docker API without authentication to confirm access
Launch a container with the host filesystem bind-mounted (test/authorized use only)

variants: Fully unauthenticated, unencrypted API on port 2375, versus TLS-enabled port 2376 with authentication nominally configured but a weak/default client-certificate check that's still effectively bypassable.

The related Docker socket-mount variant — where a container is given direct access to the host's `/var/run/docker.sock` — grants equivalent host-level control through a completely different exposure path than the network-reachable remote API.
mitigation: Never expose the Docker Engine API without strong, mutual TLS client-certificate authentication — the plain, unauthenticated port 2375 configuration should never be used in any network-reachable deployment.
Restrict network reachability of the Docker API to only the specific, trusted management hosts that genuinely need remote access, never exposing it broadly or to the internet.
Where remote container management is needed, prefer a properly-authenticated, purpose-built orchestration API (Kubernetes with its own RBAC) over direct, raw Docker Engine API exposure.
Include Docker API exposure explicitly in routine external and internal vulnerability scanning, given the severity and simplicity of this finding when present.

NET-068.prerequisites: Network access to the target's exposed Git (typically port 9418 for the git:// protocol, or an exposed `.git` directory over HTTP) or SVN service. git and curl, or GitTools/dumpster-diving scripts for reconstructing a repository from an exposed `.git` directory.
NET-068.whatItIs: A source-code management service is reachable with no login required, letting an attacker download the entire project — including its full history. That history often still contains things that were removed from the current version of the code but never actually deleted from the past record, like old hardcoded passwords or sensitive files.
NET-068.rootCause: Sometimes this kind of service gets set up for internal convenience with no login added. More commonly in practice, a web server accidentally serves up the project's hidden version-history folder alongside the actual website, because nobody added a rule blocking public access to that hidden folder.
NET-068.impact: Full repository reconstruction grants an attacker the complete source code and commit history of the application, including any credentials, API keys, or sensitive comments ever committed at any point in the repository's history — even if since removed from the current codebase, this content remains fully present and extractable in historical commits, often representing years of accumulated technical detail and potential secrets in one convenient package.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for the raw Git daemon protocol port, and separately, probe web servers for an accessible `.git` directory (a request to `/.git/HEAD` returning valid Git-object content rather than a 404).
Where an exposed `.git` directory is found, attempt to reconstruct the full repository using a purpose-built tool.
Search the reconstructed repository's full history (not just the current HEAD) for hardcoded secrets/credentials using a secret-scanning tool.
For an exposed SVN service, similarly attempt to enumerate and check out the repository without authentication.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes repository reconstruction/extraction from the discovered exposed source-control endpoint.
Reconstruct the full repository (via git clone for a raw daemon, or via a `.git`-directory-extraction tool for an exposed web-accessible directory).
Search the complete history for hardcoded secrets and sensitive comments/files.
Document every discovered secret/sensitive item and its location in the repository history, without further using or distributing the extracted source code beyond what's needed as evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Probe for an exposed .git directory on a web server
Reconstruct a repository from an exposed .git directory
Search the full repository history for hardcoded secrets
Clone from a raw, unauthenticated Git daemon service

variants: Web-server-exposed `.git` directory (the most common real-world instance) versus a genuinely unauthenticated raw Git daemon service.
Repository content limited to genuinely non-sensitive code (lower impact) versus containing hardcoded secrets/credentials in its history (a severe, compounding finding).
mitigation: Configure the web server to explicitly deny access to dot-prefixed directories (`.git`, `.svn`, `.env`) as a standing, mandatory hardening rule for every deployed application.
Deploy applications via a build/artifact pipeline that excludes source-control metadata entirely from the deployed artifact, rather than deploying directly from a `git clone`d working directory.
Disable any raw, unauthenticated Git/SVN daemon protocol service; require authenticated access (SSH-based Git, or an authenticated HTTPS Git server) for any genuinely-needed remote repository access.
Add automated secret-scanning across full repository history as a standing practice, remediating any historically-committed secret regardless of whether the repository itself is ever exposed.

NET-069.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Jenkins (or equivalent CI/CD) instance, typically port 8080. A web browser or curl for testing unauthenticated access.
NET-069.whatItIs: A build-automation tool used for deploying software is reachable with no login required, or lets anyone perform far more than they should — viewing build configurations, triggering builds, or worst of all, using a built-in scripting feature meant only for administrators that lets anyone run their own code directly on the server. Build configurations frequently contain embedded credentials for source code, cloud infrastructure, and deployment systems.
NET-069.rootCause: These tools tend to get set up with a strong focus on just getting builds and deployments working, and proper login/permission protections sometimes get deprioritized or left at an overly permissive default — especially for something that started out meant only for internal, trusted use but later ended up reachable more broadly than planned.
NET-069.impact: Jenkins instances are extraordinarily high-value targets given their typical role orchestrating access to source control, cloud infrastructure, and deployment credentials across an organization's entire software delivery pipeline — unauthenticated or under-authorized access, especially reaching the Script Console, provides both a direct code-execution foothold on the Jenkins server itself and a springboard to every credential/system the CI/CD pipeline is configured to touch, making this one of the most consequential possible findings in a modern software organization.
stepsToIdentify: Identify Jenkins/CI instances in scope via port/service scanning or a distinctive login page/API endpoint.
Attempt to access the instance without authentication and assess what's visible/accessible (build history, job configurations, credentials store).
Specifically test whether the Script Console (`/script`) is reachable without authentication or by a low-privilege/anonymous user.
Where job configurations are accessible, review them for embedded credentials or connection strings to other systems.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated/low-privilege interaction with the discovered Jenkins instance, including a benign Script Console proof of concept if reachable.
Attempt unauthenticated access and document what's visible.

Where the Script Console is reachable, execute a benign, non-destructive Groovy script (e.g. printing the server's hostname) to confirm code-execution capability without performing any destructive or data-exfiltrating action.
Where job configurations expose credentials, validate their scope with a minimal, read-only check rather than a broader action.
Document the confirmed access level and the resulting scope of exposure/code-execution capability.

examplePayloads.label: Check for unauthenticated Jenkins access via its API
Test Script Console reachability with a benign proof-of-concept script
Review a job's configuration for embedded credentials

variants: Fully unauthenticated instance (severe, immediately exploitable) versus authentication present but with an overly permissive anonymous/low-privilege default role still granting Script Console or credential-viewing access.
Read-only exposure (viewing job configurations/credentials) versus full code-execution capability via the Script Console — the latter being categorically more severe.
mitigation: Require authentication for all access to the Jenkins instance, with no anonymous role granted beyond, at most, minimal read access to explicitly non-sensitive information.
Restrict Script Console access to a small, explicitly-designated administrator group, never to general authenticated users let alone anonymous ones.

Store credentials used by CI/CD jobs in Jenkins's own Credentials Manager (or an external secrets-management integration) rather than embedded directly in job configuration, and restrict which jobs/users can access which stored credentials.
Restrict network reachability of the Jenkins instance to internal/VPN-only access, and apply the same security scrutiny to CI/CD infrastructure as to any other high-value, credential-adjacent system.

NET-070.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Kubernetes API server (typically port 6443) or Kubelet API (typically port 10250). curl and kubectl configured to interact with the discovered, potentially-unauthenticated endpoint.
NET-070.whatItIs: The main control system for a Kubernetes cluster, or the agent running on an individual server in that cluster, is reachable without properly requiring login — either anonymous access is allowed with overly broad permissions, or a specific interface is left open without requiring a certificate or token. This lets an attacker look at cluster resources, read stored secrets, or, in the worst case, directly run commands inside containers on that server.
NET-070.rootCause: Getting login and permissions right across a Kubernetes cluster requires careful, correct configuration in several different places at once, and a gap in any one of them — particularly the per-server agent, which some setups have historically left open to anonymous access by default — can grant direct, unauthenticated access to serious cluster or server-level functionality.
NET-070.impact: Unauthenticated API-server access can expose the complete cluster resource inventory including secrets (credentials, tokens, TLS keys) across every namespace the anonymous role can reach; unauthenticated Kubelet API access on a specific node allows direct command execution inside any pod running on that node via the `exec` endpoint, providing a direct path to container compromise and, from there, potential further lateral movement into the cluster or underlying infrastructure.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for the Kubernetes API server and Kubelet API ports across the target's network range.
For each discovered endpoint, attempt to query it without providing any authentication credential.
Where API-server access succeeds, enumerate accessible namespaces/resources and check specifically for secret-reading capability.
Where Kubelet API access succeeds, enumerate running pods on that node and test the `exec` endpoint's reachability for command execution.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated interaction with the discovered Kubernetes API/Kubelet endpoint, including a benign command-execution proof of concept via the Kubelet if reachable.
Query the endpoint without authentication and document the accessible resource scope.
Where secrets are readable, validate a minimal, representative sample's sensitivity without a bulk extraction.
Where the Kubelet `exec` endpoint is reachable, execute a benign, non-destructive command (e.g. `id` or `hostname`) inside a nominated test pod to confirm code-execution capability.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated access, its scope, and the demonstrated impact.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for the Kubernetes API server and Kubelet ports
Query the API server without authentication
Query the Kubelet's read-only API for pod inventory on the node
Execute a benign command inside a running pod via the Kubelet exec endpoint

variants: Unauthenticated API-server access (broader, cluster-wide resource/secret exposure) versus unauthenticated Kubelet API access (node-scoped, but providing direct command-execution capability inside running containers).
Read-only Kubelet API (port 10255, information-disclosure risk) versus the full Kubelet API (port 10250) with anonymous authentication enabled, providing full command-execution capability.
mitigation: Disable anonymous authentication on both the Kubernetes API server and every node's Kubelet, requiring proper client-certificate or bearer-token authentication for all access.
Apply least-privilege RBAC policy to any anonymous/unauthenticated role that must remain enabled for a specific, narrow legitimate reason, never granting broad read/write access by default.

Restrict network reachability of both the API server and Kubelet ports to only the cluster's own internal control-plane/node communication paths, never exposing them to general network segments or the internet.
Follow the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark's authentication and RBAC hardening guidance comprehensively across every cluster component.

NET-071.prerequisites: Network access to the target's out-of-band server-management web interface (Dell iDRAC, HPE iLO, or an equivalent BMC web UI), typically on a dedicated HTTPS port. A web browser or curl for testing default credentials and reachability.
NET-071.whatItIs: A server's remote hardware-management interface — letting an administrator remotely power-cycle it or access its console even when the OS is off — is reachable from a much broader part of the network than intended, sometimes even directly from the internet. This finding specifically covers the web interface's own exposure, and commonly, that it's still using its default or weak login credentials.
NET-071.rootCause: These management interfaces are built for convenient remote server administration, but that same convenience becomes a serious risk if the interface isn't deliberately kept on its own separate, restricted management network. A server set up without careful thought about which network its management port is actually connected to can end up far more broadly reachable than the administrator realizes — and its default password is easy to overlook among all the other setup steps for a new server.
NET-071.impact: Anyone who reaches the management interface with a valid (often still-default) credential gains complete, OS-independent control over the physical server — power cycling it, mounting arbitrary virtual media (potentially booting an attacker-supplied OS image), and full remote console access — this bypasses every security control the host OS itself might have entirely, since the BMC operates at a privilege level below and independent of the operating system.
stepsToIdentify: Identify out-of-band management interfaces in scope via port/service scanning or a distinctive login page.
Assess the interface's network reachability scope — confirm whether it's genuinely isolated to a dedicated management network or reachable more broadly.
Attempt login with the documented vendor default credential for the identified product.
Where default credentials fail, assess whether any other weak-credential or known-CVE vector applies to the specific firmware version in use.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes default-credential login testing against the identified management interface.
Attempt login with the vendor default credential.

Where successful, document the scope of access achieved (power control, virtual media, console) via a benign, non-destructive action rather than actually power-cycling or reconfiguring a production server.
Document the confirmed network-exposure scope and credential weakness.

examplePayloads.label: Identify the management interface and attempt default-credential login
examplePayloads.command:
curl -sk https://<target-ip>/ | grep -i 'iDRAC\|iLO'
curl -sk -X POST https://<target-ip>/data/login -d 'user=root&password=calvin'  # example Dell iDRAC default

examplePayloads.label: Confirm reachability scope from an external vantage point

variants: Management interface reachable only from an internal network position with a default credential still active (severe, but requiring prior network access) versus directly internet-facing (critical, since these interfaces have been repeatedly found exposed at scale in internet-wide scans historically).

Web-interface default-credential access alone versus combined with the separately-documented IPMI protocol-level weaknesses (cipher-suite-0, RAKP hash disclosure) providing an additional, independent access path.
mitigation: Change default administrative credentials on every out-of-band management interface immediately upon deployment.
Isolate management-interface network connectivity to a dedicated, access-controlled out-of-band management network/VLAN, never leaving it reachable from general-purpose segments or the internet.
Keep management-controller firmware current, since these interfaces have their own separate history of disclosed CVEs beyond just credential weaknesses.

Include out-of-band management interfaces explicitly in routine asset inventory and vulnerability-scanning scope, since they're sometimes overlooked as "not really part of the server" during security review.

NET-072.prerequisites: Network access to the target's message-queue management console (RabbitMQ's management UI, typically port 15672; Kafka's associated management tooling or an exposed JMX/Kafka Manager interface). A web browser or curl for testing default credentials and unauthenticated API access.
NET-072.whatItIs: A message-queue system's management console is reachable over the network with its well-known default login still active — or with no login required at all — giving an attacker visibility into queued messages, connected systems, and the ability to send or read messages directly.
NET-072.rootCause: These management interfaces are convenient operational tools that are sometimes left with default settings in place — commonly, a default account's original 'local access only' restriction gets loosened to allow remote management, without also changing its default, well-documented password to match.
NET-072.impact: An attacker with management-console access can inspect message content flowing through the queue (potentially exposing sensitive business data or even credentials passed as message payloads), publish forged messages that downstream consumers will process as legitimate, or disrupt the messaging system's availability by deleting queues/exchanges — the specific impact depends heavily on what the message queue is used for within the broader application architecture.
stepsToIdentify: Identify message-queue management interfaces in scope via port/service scanning.
Attempt login with documented default credentials for the identified broker (RabbitMQ's `guest`/`guest` being the most common).
Where successful, enumerate queue/exchange names and, where safe to do so, inspect a sample of message content for sensitivity.
Assess whether unauthenticated message publishing is also possible, which would represent a more severe, message-forgery-enabling finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes default-credential login and message-inspection testing against the target message-queue console.
Attempt login with the documented default credential.
Enumerate queues/exchanges and inspect a minimal, representative sample of message content for sensitivity, without consuming/removing production messages that legitimate consumers still need.
Where authorized, demonstrate message-publishing capability with a benign, clearly-labeled test message to a designated test queue rather than a production one.
Document the confirmed credential weakness and the resulting scope of access.

examplePayloads.label: Attempt login with RabbitMQ's default guest credential
Inspect a sample of messages in a discovered queue (non-destructive peek)

variants: RabbitMQ's specific default `guest` credential exposed remotely (a well-documented, common misconfiguration) versus a more general absence of authentication on a different broker's management tooling.

Read-only access (inspecting queue content) versus write access (publishing forged messages or deleting queues/exchanges), the latter being materially more severe for message-integrity-dependent applications.
mitigation: Change all default broker credentials immediately upon deployment, and disable the default account entirely where the broker supports it.
Restrict the default account (RabbitMQ's `guest`) to localhost-only access as intended, creating distinct, properly-credentialed accounts for any genuinely remote management need.
Restrict network reachability of the management console/API to internal/VPN-only access.
Apply TLS to the message-queue's client/management-console communication where genuinely sensitive data traverses it.

NET-073.prerequisites: Network access to the target's network-connected printer or other IoT device's administrative web interface. A web browser or curl for testing default credentials.
NET-073.whatItIs: A network printer or similar smart device's admin webpage is still reachable using the manufacturer's default login, giving full administrative control — including, on a lot of modern devices, access to stored scan or fax history, network settings (sometimes including stored WiFi credentials), and the ability to update the device's firmware.
NET-073.rootCause: Network printers and similar smart devices generally get far less security attention than core computers and servers, and default login credentials — which are publicly documented in the manufacturer's own manual — commonly never get changed, since the device's admin panel isn't usually thought of as security-sensitive, despite how much sensitive functionality many modern devices actually have.
NET-073.impact: An attacker with default-credential access can reconfigure the device (potentially redirecting scan-to-email/network-share functionality to an attacker-controlled destination, capturing scanned documents), extract stored credentials the device uses for its own network-share/email integration, access stored fax/scan job history that may contain sensitive documents, or push a malicious firmware update in the most severe scenario.
stepsToIdentify: Identify network-connected printers/IoT devices in scope via port/service scanning or a distinctive administrative-interface login page.
Attempt login with the documented vendor default credential for the identified device/model.
Where successful, review the device's configuration for stored credentials (scan-to-network-share, scan-to-email SMTP authentication) and stored job history.
Assess whether the device's firmware-update mechanism is also accessible and whether it validates update-package authenticity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes default-credential login testing against the identified device.
Attempt login with the vendor default credential.
Review configuration for stored credentials and job history as impact evidence, without altering the device's genuine production configuration.
Document the confirmed default-credential access and the resulting scope of sensitive data/functionality exposed.

examplePayloads.label: Identify the device's administrative interface and attempt default-credential login
examplePayloads.command:
curl -sk https://<target-ip>/ -o device_login_page.html
# then attempt login via the web UI with the vendor-documented default credential for the identified model

examplePayloads.label: Check for stored scan-to-network-share credentials in the device configuration (where accessible post-login)
examplePayloads.command: # review the device's network/scan-destination configuration pages for embedded, stored authentication credentials

variants: Default credential still active on a low-functionality standalone printer (moderate risk) versus on a full-featured MFC with scan-to-network-share/email and stored credential integration (higher risk given the broader stored-data/credential exposure).

IoT devices exposing an unauthenticated local web-management UI (rather than a raw network protocol) represent a related but distinct variant, often carrying additional client-side vulnerabilities (XSS, CSRF) layered on top of the base exposure.
mitigation: Change default administrative credentials on every network-connected printer/IoT device immediately upon deployment.
Restrict network reachability of device administrative interfaces to a dedicated, access-controlled management VLAN rather than a general-purpose office network.
Regularly audit and rotate any credentials stored on the device for its own network-share/email integration.

Include network-connected printers/IoT devices explicitly in the organization's asset inventory and routine vulnerability-scanning/patching cycle, rather than treating them as out-of-scope peripherals.

NET-074.prerequisites: Network access to the target Windows host's RPC endpoint mapper (TCP 135) and associated dynamic RPC ports. rpcclient, Impacket's rpcdump.py, or nmap's msrpc-related scripts for enumeration.
NET-074.whatItIs: A Windows computer's remote-management communication system is reachable from a much broader part of the network than intended, letting an attacker see what remote services are available on it and, depending on which specific ones are exposed, potentially interact with sensitive Windows management functionality that should really only be reachable from trusted administrative systems.
NET-074.rootCause: This remote-management system is a core part of how Windows computers manage each other and is turned on by default on nearly every Windows machine — so what actually determines whether it's dangerously exposed is the network segmentation and firewall rules around it, not usually a misconfiguration in the feature itself.
NET-074.impact: An attacker who can reach RPC/DCOM services beyond an intended trust boundary gains a rich reconnaissance surface (enumerable interface/service lists revealing what's running on the host) and, depending on which specific RPC-exposed service is reachable and its own credential requirements, a potential path to remote service manipulation or other Windows-management functionality that significantly aids further lateral-movement attempts within the environment.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for the RPC endpoint mapper port and enumerate registered interfaces/services on the target host.
Assess whether this reachability is consistent with the intended network-segmentation design (e.g. should this host's RPC surface be reachable from the tester's current network position at all).
For any specific, sensitive RPC-exposed service found (remote service control, WMI), assess its own independent authentication requirement.
Cross-reference against related, more specific findings (SMB null sessions, weak RPC-dependent service configurations) that might compound this general exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes RPC/DCOM enumeration against the target host.
Enumerate registered RPC interfaces/services via the endpoint mapper.
Document the specific services discovered and assess whether their reachability from the current test position is consistent with intended network segmentation.
Where a specific, sensitive service is found reachable with insufficient independent authentication, escalate testing toward that specific, more targeted finding.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate RPC endpoint mapper interfaces
Enumerate via rpcclient with a null session (cross-reference the SMB null-session finding)
nmap-based RPC/DCOM enumeration

variants: RPC endpoint mapper reachable but individual services still requiring proper authentication (a network-segmentation finding, lower direct severity) versus a specific exposed service also lacking adequate authentication of its own (a compounding, more severe combined finding).

The related DCOM-specific variant (as opposed to general MSRPC exposure) has been the vector for several high-severity remote code execution vulnerabilities (e.g., the 2022 DCOM hardening changes), making version/patch-level identification specifically important here.
mitigation: Restrict network reachability of RPC/DCOM (and the dynamic port range it uses) to only trusted administrative network segments via host-based and network firewall rules, rather than leaving it broadly reachable across general-purpose segments.
Apply the principle of least privilege and network segmentation consistently, treating RPC/DCOM reachability as equivalent in sensitivity to direct administrative access.
Disable or restrict specific RPC-exposed services that aren't genuinely needed on a given host, reducing the overall exposed surface.
Monitor for anomalous RPC/DCOM connection patterns as a detection signature for reconnaissance or lateral-movement attempts.

NET-075.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Redis (TCP 6379) or Memcached (TCP/UDP 11211) service. redis-cli or a raw netcat connection for interaction testing.
NET-075.whatItIs: A fast, in-memory data-storage service (used for caching or quick lookups) is reachable over the network with absolutely no login required. Anyone who finds the exposed port can read, change, or delete all the data stored in it directly.
NET-075.rootCause: Both of these tools were originally built to run on a fully trusted, internal-only network, with no real expectation that a login would be strictly necessary. While one of them has since added an optional password feature, it's not turned on by default — a deployment that doesn't specifically turn it on, and that's reachable from more than just the local machine, leaves the data completely open to anyone who can reach it.
NET-075.impact: Anyone who reaches an unauthenticated Redis/Memcached instance can read all cached/stored data directly (which frequently includes session tokens, cached API responses containing PII, or application-level cached credentials), and with write access, can inject malicious cached values, and for Redis specifically, several well-documented techniques exist to escalate this data-store access into full remote code execution on the underlying host (via Redis's `CONFIG SET`/module-loading capabilities, or writing a malicious SSH key/cron entry to a reachable filesystem path).
stepsToIdentify: Scan for Redis/Memcached ports across the target's network range.
Attempt to connect and issue a basic command without providing any authentication.
Where access succeeds, enumerate a sample of stored keys/data to assess sensitivity.

For Redis specifically, assess whether the further RCE-escalation techniques (writing an SSH key, using `CONFIG SET dir`/`dbfilename` to write a webshell to a reachable web root) are practically feasible given the specific deployment context.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated interaction with the discovered Redis/Memcached instance, including a benign RCE-escalation demonstration if the specific Redis technique is in scope.
Connect without authentication and enumerate a representative sample of stored keys/data.

Where Redis RCE escalation is authorized and the deployment context allows it, demonstrate a benign, non-destructive code-execution proof of concept (writing a uniquely-named marker file) rather than a destructive payload.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated access and any further escalation achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Connect to Redis without authentication and confirm access
Enumerate stored keys
Redis RCE escalation via SSH key write (authorized test only)
examplePayloads.command:
redis-cli -h <target-ip> config set dir /root/.ssh/
redis-cli -h <target-ip> config set dbfilename authorized_keys
redis-cli -h <target-ip> set poc_key "

<test-ssh-public-key>

"
redis-cli -h <target-ip> save

examplePayloads.label: Connect to Memcached without authentication and confirm access

variants: Read-only unauthenticated access (information-disclosure risk) versus write access enabling malicious cache poisoning or, for Redis, the further RCE-escalation techniques.

Instance reachable only from an internal network position (moderate-to-high) versus directly internet-facing (severe, and historically a very common source of real-world Redis compromise given how frequently this exact misconfiguration has been found exposed at internet scale).
mitigation: Set a strong `requirepass` value for Redis, and enable authentication for Memcached where the deployed version/protocol supports it (SASL-based auth for newer Memcached versions).

Bind the service to localhost or a specific, internal-only interface rather than all network interfaces, and restrict network reachability via firewall rules regardless of authentication configuration as defense in depth.
For Redis specifically, disable or rename dangerous commands (`CONFIG`, `FLUSHALL`, `EVAL`) via the `rename-command` directive where the application's genuine functional need allows it.
Never expose these data-store services directly to the internet under any circumstance.

NET-076.prerequisites: Network access to the target's HashiCorp Consul (typically port 8500) or Nomad (typically port 4646) API/UI. curl for testing unauthenticated access.
NET-076.whatItIs: A backend service used to manage and discover other services across a cluster (things like Consul or Nomad) is reachable over the network with no login required at all. Anyone who finds it can see the full list of running services, read stored configuration data (which often includes application secrets), and — if writing is also unprotected — register fake services or run their own workloads directly on the cluster.
NET-076.rootCause: Both of these tools commonly ship with access controls turned off by default in many setup guides, prioritizing quick and easy setup over security. That default often never gets revisited once the cluster goes into real use, especially for internal-only tooling that doesn't get the same scrutiny as customer-facing systems.
NET-076.impact: Unauthenticated access exposes the organization's complete internal service topology and any secrets stored in Consul's key-value store, and, where write/scheduling access is also unauthenticated, allows an attacker to register a malicious service (potentially redirecting other services' service-discovery lookups to an attacker-controlled endpoint) or, for Nomad, submit and run an arbitrary, attacker-controlled workload directly on the cluster's compute resources.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for Consul/Nomad API ports across the target's network range.
Attempt to query the API without providing any authentication credential.
Where access succeeds, enumerate the service catalog and, for Consul, the key-value store contents for sensitive data.
Where authorized, test whether write access (service registration for Consul, job submission for Nomad) is also unauthenticated.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated interaction with the discovered Consul/Nomad instance, including a benign write-access demonstration if applicable.
Query the API without authentication and enumerate the service catalog/key-value store.
Document any sensitive data found in the key-value store as impact evidence.
Where write access is confirmed unauthenticated, demonstrate this with a benign, clearly-labeled test service registration or Nomad job, then remove it immediately.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated access and its read/write scope.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for Consul/Nomad API ports
Query Consul's service catalog without authentication
Query Consul's key-value store for stored configuration/secrets
Query Nomad's job list without authentication

variants: Read-only unauthenticated access (severe information-disclosure risk, especially for Consul's KV-stored secrets) versus write/scheduling access also unauthenticated (a materially more severe, cluster-integrity-compromising finding for Nomad specifically).

Nomad's separate, less commonly audited API (distinct from Consul's) can expose the same class of unauthenticated cluster-control risk even in environments where Consul itself has already been hardened, since the two are frequently deployed together but secured independently.
mitigation: Enable and enforce ACLs on both Consul and Nomad in every deployment, with a default-deny policy requiring explicit token-based authorization for any access.

Restrict network reachability of these control-plane APIs to only the specific cluster nodes/services that genuinely need to communicate with them, never exposing them to general internal network segments or the internet.

Avoid storing genuinely sensitive secrets directly in Consul's key-value store without additional encryption; prefer a dedicated secrets-management integration (Vault) for credential material specifically.
Include service-mesh/orchestration control-plane exposure explicitly in routine infrastructure security audits.

NET-077.prerequisites: Network access to the target's syslog service (typically UDP/TCP 514) or a centralized log-management service's ingestion/query endpoint. netcat for testing unauthenticated log submission, and a log-query client/API tool if a query interface is also exposed.
NET-077.whatItIs: A system that collects log messages from across the network accepts incoming logs (and sometimes lets people search stored ones) with no check on who's sending them. An attacker can inject fake log entries — to bury real evidence of an attack in noise, or frame someone else — or, if searching is also unprotected, just read the organization's collected logs directly.
NET-077.rootCause: Older logging protocols have no built-in way to verify who's actually sending a log message. And a centralized logging platform's intake is sometimes left open to accept logs from anywhere for flexibility, without any network restriction or a more secure, authenticated way of shipping logs actually being enforced.
NET-077.impact: An attacker can inject forged log entries to manipulate the aggregated log record (undermining incident-response and forensic-investigation reliability), and where query/read access is also unauthenticated, can directly read potentially sensitive information contained in aggregated logs across the entire monitored estate — both outcomes significantly undermine the organization's detection and investigative capability, which is a particularly severe consequence given how much other security tooling depends on log integrity/availability.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for syslog/log-management service ports across the target's network range.
Attempt to submit a forged, clearly-labeled test log message without authentication.
Confirm whether the forged message appears in the centralized log store, indicating unauthenticated ingestion.
Where a query interface is also exposed, attempt unauthenticated log-data retrieval and assess the sensitivity of accessible content.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes unauthenticated log-injection and query testing against the target syslog/log-management service.
Submit a clearly-labeled, benign test log message without authentication.
Confirm the test message's ingestion into the centralized log store, where feasible to verify.
Where query access is also unauthenticated, retrieve a minimal, representative sample of stored log data as impact evidence.
Document the confirmed unauthenticated ingestion and/or query access.

examplePayloads.label: Submit a forged, clearly-labeled test syslog message without authentication
Query a centralized log-management service's ingestion/search endpoint without authentication

variants: Unauthenticated ingestion only (log-forgery risk) versus unauthenticated query/read access also present (a compounding, more severe information-disclosure finding).

Classic UDP syslog specifically (inherently unauthenticated by protocol design) versus a modern log-management platform's ingestion API left open due to a specific configuration gap rather than an inherent protocol limitation.
mitigation: Restrict network reachability of the syslog/log-ingestion service to only the specific, expected source hosts via firewall rules, rather than accepting submissions from any source.
Where feasible, use an authenticated, encrypted log-shipping mechanism (TLS-based syslog, or an authenticated agent-based log forwarder) rather than classic, unauthenticated UDP syslog.
