Require authentication for any log-query/search interface, restricting access to authorized security/operations personnel only.

Monitor for anomalous log-source patterns (log messages claiming to originate from a hostname that shouldn't be submitting to this particular receiver) as a detection signature for injection attempts.

NET-078.prerequisites: Network access to the target's Telnet service (TCP 23) or a serial-over-IP console-server product's management interface. A Telnet client, and a web browser/curl for console-server-specific management interfaces.
NET-078.whatItIs: A device that provides remote, network-based access to another device's physical console port — commonly used for managing network or industrial equipment remotely — is reachable using an old, insecure remote-access protocol, or with weak or default login credentials, exposing full console-level control over whatever's connected on the other end.
NET-078.rootCause: This old remote-access protocol sends everything, including passwords, in plain readable text, and has no modern security features at all — yet it's still used on older equipment and some console-access products for simplicity. These products are also sometimes left with their default credentials in place, since they're seen as secondary supporting equipment rather than something security-sensitive.
NET-078.impact: Console-level access to whatever device is connected via the serial link provides complete, OS/application-independent control — for a network device, this means full administrative configuration access; for an industrial control system, this can mean direct access to safety-critical or process-control functionality — and because Telnet itself is unencrypted, any credential used to access the console server (or the connected device's own console-level authentication) is exposed to passive interception as well.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for Telnet services and known console-server product web-management interfaces across the target's network range.
Attempt connection/login with documented default or weak credentials for the identified device/product.
Where console-server access is achieved, enumerate which downstream devices are reachable via the serial-console ports it manages.

Assess the sensitivity of the specific downstream device(s) reachable, since a console server connected to a critical network switch or industrial controller represents a far more severe finding than one connected to a low-criticality device.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes Telnet/console-server login testing against the target service.
Attempt login with default/weak credentials.

Where successful, document the scope of console-level access achieved and the criticality of any downstream connected device, without performing any disruptive configuration change against a production system.
Document the confirmed access and its criticality.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for Telnet services
Attempt Telnet login with a bounded set of default/weak credentials
Identify and attempt login to a console-server web management interface

variants: Telnet directly exposed on a network device's own management interface (a legacy-protocol-support finding) versus a dedicated serial-over-IP console server providing indirect access to one or more downstream devices, potentially multiplying the impact across every device it manages.

Serial-over-IP console servers used for legacy industrial/OT equipment access represent a higher-impact variant of generic Telnet exposure, since the reachable console often has direct physical-process control rather than just a general-purpose shell.
mitigation: Disable Telnet entirely wherever SSH is available as an alternative for network-device management access.
Change default credentials on any console-server product immediately upon deployment.
Restrict network reachability of Telnet services and console-server management interfaces to a dedicated, access-controlled management network.

Include console-server infrastructure and any Telnet-still-enabled devices explicitly in routine network hardening audits, since they're sometimes treated as secondary/supporting infrastructure and overlooked.

NET-079.prerequisites: Network access to the target Windows host's WinRM service (typically port 5985 for HTTP, 5986 for HTTPS). Evil-WinRM or PowerShell's native `Enter-PSSession`/`New-PSSession` cmdlets for interaction testing.
NET-079.whatItIs: A built-in Windows feature for remote administration is reachable over the network without proper restrictions on who can reach it, or an account that has access to it has a weak or default password. Either way, this lets an attacker open a full, interactive remote command session on that machine.
NET-079.rootCause: This is a genuinely powerful, legitimate remote-administration feature that's turned on by default on many modern Windows servers — and its security depends entirely on two things: whether the network actually restricts who can reach it, and whether the accounts allowed to use it have strong passwords. A gap in either one creates a direct path for remote access.
NET-079.impact: An attacker who authenticates to an exposed WinRM service (via a compromised or weak/default credential) gains a full, interactive PowerShell session on the target host with whatever privilege level that account holds — this is functionally equivalent to a remote administrative shell, providing a direct path to further lateral movement, credential harvesting, or persistence within the environment.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for WinRM ports across the target's network range.
Assess whether WinRM reachability is consistent with the intended network-segmentation design (should this host's WinRM service be reachable from the current test position at all).
Where authorized, attempt authentication using a bounded, agreed set of weak/default credential candidates for a nominated test account.
Confirm the resulting session's privilege level if authentication succeeds.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes WinRM connectivity and, where applicable, credential-testing against the target host.
Confirm WinRM reachability from the current test position.
Where authorized, attempt authentication with a bounded, agreed credential set.
Where successful, establish a session and confirm the resulting privilege level with a benign, non-destructive command.
Document the confirmed network-exposure scope and any credential weakness identified.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for WinRM ports
Attempt a WinRM session with Evil-WinRM using test/bounded credentials
Native PowerShell WinRM session establishment

variants: WinRM reachable from an unintended, broader internal network scope with strong credentials still required (a network-segmentation finding) versus combined with weak/default/reused credentials providing a direct, practical exploitation path.

WinRM configured over HTTP (rather than HTTPS) compounds the exposure with a cleartext-credential-transmission risk on top of the base unauthenticated-reachability finding, effectively combining two distinct weaknesses in one misconfiguration.
mitigation: Restrict network reachability of WinRM to only the specific, trusted administrative source hosts/jump-boxes that genuinely need remote-management access, via host-based and network firewall rules.
Enforce strong, unique credentials and, where feasible, certificate-based or Kerberos-only authentication for WinRM rather than relying on password-based local-account authentication.
Apply the principle of least privilege to which accounts have WinRM/remote-administration rights on any given host.
Monitor for anomalous WinRM connection patterns as a detection signature for lateral-movement attempts.

NET-080.prerequisites: Network access to the target TLS service and an on-path position capable of manipulating the TLS handshake (an authorized ARP-spoofing setup, or a lab test environment). nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script for confirming export-grade RSA cipher-suite support, and a FREAK-specific testing tool/script.
NET-080.whatItIs: Some servers still support an old, deliberately weakened form of encryption originally required by outdated export regulations. Combined with a once-common bug in client encryption software that would silently accept this weak option even when it wasn't asked for, an attacker positioned between the two can force the connection to downgrade to this weak encryption, then crack the resulting weak key in a matter of hours using cloud computing — recovering everything sent over that connection.
NET-080.rootCause: This deliberately weak encryption option was built specifically to comply with old export rules, using keys small enough to be crackable. Combined with client software that historically had a bug letting it slip into using this weak option even without asking for it, this created a specific and exploitable chain of two separate flaws working together.
NET-080.impact: Where both the server-side (export-grade cipher support) and client-side (the specific library bug) preconditions are met, an on-path attacker can force a connection down to an easily-factorable RSA key strength and fully decrypt the session — while the client-side precondition has been broadly patched in the years since FREAK's 2015 disclosure, the server-side configuration weakness (retaining export-grade cipher support at all) remains a meaningful hardening gap worth identifying and remediating regardless of current client-population patch status.
stepsToIdentify: Scan the target TLS service for export-grade RSA cipher-suite support.

Where confirmed, assess the realistic client population's patch status for the specific library-level FREAK vulnerability, understanding that this significantly affects real-world exploitability today versus the underlying server misconfiguration existing regardless.

Document the server-side export-cipher-suite support as the primary, actionable finding, since this is fully within the organization's own control to remediate immediately regardless of client-side patch status elsewhere.
Check whether the server's OpenSSL version predates the FREAK fix, since FREAK requires the server to support export-grade RSA cipher suites even if not offered by default to standard clients.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes export-cipher-suite testing and, where a genuinely vulnerable client population is confirmed, a controlled on-path downgrade demonstration against the target service.
Confirm export-grade RSA cipher-suite support via the scanning tool.
Where a specific, confirmed-vulnerable client is available for testing, demonstrate the downgrade-then-factor technique in a controlled, authorized environment.
Document the confirmed export-cipher support as the primary finding, noting any successfully demonstrated full exploitation chain as additional, compounding evidence.
Report the finding as largely historical against modern clients (which reject export-grade ciphers by default), while still recommending the server-side export-cipher support be removed.

examplePayloads.label: Check for export-grade RSA cipher-suite support
Comprehensive TLS scan flagging FREAK-relevant configuration

variants: Export-grade cipher support alone (the necessary server-side precondition, fully remediable by the organization) versus a genuinely demonstrated full FREAK exploitation chain requiring an additionally-vulnerable client library.

The related Logjam-adjacent export-cipher variant specifically targeting RSA (rather than DHE) export ciphers is what FREAK itself technically refers to, distinguishing it from the DHE-focused Logjam finding despite their shared 1990s export-restriction origin.
mitigation: Remove all export-grade cipher suites from the server's TLS configuration entirely — there is no legitimate reason to retain them in any current deployment.
Adopt a current, well-vetted TLS cipher-suite configuration baseline that excludes all historically export-grade and other deliberately-weakened cipher options.
Keep client-side TLS libraries/browsers current, addressing the client-side half of the original FREAK vulnerability independently of the server-side remediation.

NET-081.prerequisites: A network position with passive traffic-visibility on the target segment. Wireshark or tcpdump for capture and content extraction.
NET-081.whatItIs: A file-transfer service in scope is used without any encryption, meaning both the login credentials and the entire contents of every transferred file travel across the network in plain, readable text.
NET-081.rootCause: This file-transfer protocol predates any expectation of built-in encryption. Even though secure, modern alternatives have existed for a long time, the plain version is still sometimes used for old integrations that were never updated, often because nobody's revisited that specific setup since it was first configured.
NET-081.impact: Anyone with passive network-path visibility can capture and read FTP credentials and complete file-transfer content in cleartext — for a service handling any genuinely sensitive file transfer (financial data exports, PII-containing reports, credential files), this represents a direct, substantial, and ongoing data-exposure risk for as long as the plaintext protocol remains in use.
stepsToIdentify: Identify FTP services in scope (TCP 21) and confirm whether any of them lack FTPS support (versus separately confirming SFTP, a different protocol/port entirely, is used instead for genuinely secure transfers).
With authorization, passively capture FTP traffic during a representative usage window.
Extract and confirm the presence of plaintext credentials and file content in the capture.
Assess the sensitivity of the specific files typically transferred via the affected FTP service.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes passive traffic capture for the identified FTP service.
Capture traffic during a representative window covering a normal login and file transfer.
Extract plaintext credentials and file content from the capture as impact evidence.
Document the specific service, its typical usage pattern, and the confirmed sensitive-data exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Capture FTP traffic for credential and content extraction
Extract plaintext credentials from the capture
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r ftp_capture.pcap -Y 'ftp.request.command=="USER" or ftp.request.command=="PASS"' -T fields -e ftp.request.arg

examplePayloads.label: Extract transferred file objects from the FTP-data-channel capture

variants: Plain FTP used for genuinely low-sensitivity, public file distribution (lower real-world risk despite the technical finding) versus used for internal, sensitive business data transfer (higher risk).
Plain FTP as the sole available protocol on the service versus offered alongside an FTPS option that clients simply aren't configured to use.
mitigation: Migrate all FTP usage to FTPS or, preferably, SFTP, disabling plain FTP entirely once clients have been migrated.
Where legacy client compatibility is cited as a barrier to migration, treat this as a prioritized technical-debt item given the severity of ongoing cleartext credential/data exposure.
Audit for any remaining plain-FTP-dependent integration and plan its remediation/replacement rather than accommodating it indefinitely.

NET-082.prerequisites: Administrative access to a target network appliance (a router, firewall, or similar) sufficient to initiate a firmware update, or knowledge of the appliance's firmware-update mechanism for a black-box assessment. A genuinely-signed older firmware image for the specific device, obtained from the vendor's own historical release archive.
NET-082.whatItIs: A network device's firmware-update process doesn't stop someone from installing an older firmware version than what's currently running, and doesn't properly check that an update is both genuine and actually current — not just an old version that used to be valid. That lets someone with administrative access force the device back to a known-vulnerable older version, undoing whatever security fixes came after it.
NET-082.rootCause: The update check confirms a firmware file is genuinely signed by the vendor, but doesn't separately confirm it isn't older than what's already installed. 'Genuinely from the vendor' and 'safe to install right now' aren't the same thing — any firmware version the vendor ever signed, including old, buggy ones, will always pass that signature check.
NET-082.impact: An attacker with the ability to influence the appliance's firmware-update process (via compromised administrative credentials, a compromised management channel, or physical access) can force a downgrade to a specific older firmware version chosen because it has a known, exploitable vulnerability — then chain that reintroduced vulnerability into a full device compromise, effectively bypassing every security fix shipped since that older version.
stepsToIdentify: Review the appliance's firmware-update mechanism documentation/behavior for whether it enforces monotonic version checking independent of signature validity.
With authorization, obtain a genuinely-signed older firmware version for the specific device from the vendor's historical release archive.
Attempt to install the older, genuinely-signed firmware via the normal update mechanism and confirm whether the device accepts the downgrade.
Where the downgrade succeeds, identify a specific, known vulnerability present in that older version for potential further, separately-scoped exploitation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes firmware-downgrade testing against the target appliance, ideally against a designated test/lab unit rather than a live production device given the potential for a failed update to cause an outage.
Obtain a legitimately-signed older firmware version with a documented, known vulnerability.
Attempt to install it via the normal update mechanism and confirm the downgrade succeeds.
Where successful, demonstrate exploitation of the specific known vulnerability present in that older version as the full impact chain.
Document the exact missing version-currency check and the specific downgrade-enabled vulnerability chained.

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to install a genuinely-signed older firmware version via the normal update mechanism
examplePayloads.command: # via the device's administrative web UI or CLI firmware-upgrade command, with an authorized older firmware image obtained from the vendor's historical release archive

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the installed firmware version after the downgrade attempt
examplePayloads.command: show version  # or the device-appropriate equivalent command, with authorization

variants: Downgrade achievable via the standard administrative update interface (requiring valid admin credentials) versus via a separate, less-guarded firmware-recovery/bootloader mechanism that has its own, potentially weaker version-verification logic.

A related supply-chain variant involves an attacker with only physical/local access flashing a downgraded firmware image directly via a hardware debug/JTAG interface, bypassing any network-level firmware-signing check entirely.
mitigation: Enforce a strict monotonic version check as part of firmware installation, independent of and in addition to signature verification — reject any firmware whose version is not strictly greater than the currently-installed version absent an explicit, deliberate, separately-authorized downgrade flow.
Maintain a vendor-published or self-maintained revocation list of known-vulnerable historical firmware versions and check installation attempts against it.
Restrict administrative access to the firmware-update mechanism to the same rigor as any other highly-privileged administrative function.
Monitor for unexpected firmware-version changes on production appliances as a detection signature for an unauthorized downgrade attempt.

NET-083.prerequisites: Network access capable of reaching the target's GRE tunnel endpoint. Scapy for crafting GRE-encapsulated packets, and Wireshark for capture verification.
NET-083.whatItIs: A widely used tunneling protocol, which wraps one type of network traffic inside another for things like connecting two office sites, has no built-in authentication or encryption by default. An attacker who can reach one end of this tunnel can inject fake traffic that the other end will accept and forward as if it were legitimate — or simply read the tunnel's contents if nothing inside it is separately encrypted.
NET-083.rootCause: This protocol was designed purely to wrap and carry traffic, deliberately leaving authentication and encryption to be added separately on top if needed. A tunnel set up without that extra layer — often skipped for simplicity — has no security of its own beyond just wrapping the traffic.
NET-083.impact: An attacker who can reach a GRE endpoint can inject forged traffic that gets decapsulated and forwarded onto the tunnel's destination network, potentially bypassing network-segmentation boundaries the tunnel endpoint's own network position would otherwise enforce, and can passively read any unencrypted content the tunnel carries.
stepsToIdentify: Identify GRE tunnel endpoints in scope (protocol 47, no specific port since GRE operates directly over IP) and confirm whether IPsec or another authentication/encryption layer is applied.
With authorization, attempt to send a forged, crafted GRE-encapsulated packet to a nominated test tunnel endpoint and observe whether it's accepted and decapsulated/forwarded.
Where the tunnel carries unencrypted inner-protocol traffic, capture and confirm content readability.
Assess what network segment/resources become reachable via successful packet injection through the tunnel.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes GRE packet-injection and capture testing against the target tunnel endpoint.
Craft and send a forged GRE-encapsulated test packet and confirm whether the endpoint accepts and forwards it.
Where successful, demonstrate the resulting reachability into the tunnel's destination network via a benign, non-destructive test action.
Document the confirmed injection capability and the resulting network-segmentation-bypass impact.

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send a forged GRE-encapsulated test packet with Scapy
Capture GRE tunnel traffic to check for unencrypted inner-protocol content

variants: GRE tunnel with no protection at all (fully injectable/readable) versus GRE-over-IPsec where the IPsec layer's own configuration (per the related weak-VPN-cryptography finding) determines the actual protection level.

GRE tunnels lacking any encryption (as opposed to IPsec-protected GRE) allow full traffic interception in addition to the routing-injection risk, making an unencrypted GRE tunnel a strictly more severe finding than an encrypted one with only injection exposure.
mitigation: Apply IPsec (or an equivalent authenticated/encrypted transport) to every GRE tunnel carrying sensitive traffic or connecting to any network segment where unauthorized injection would have meaningful impact.
Restrict which source addresses are permitted to establish/send traffic to a GRE tunnel endpoint via firewall rules, as defense in depth even where IPsec is applied.
Avoid using bare, unprotected GRE for any connection where the confidentiality or integrity of the tunneled traffic matters.

NET-084.prerequisites: A network position on the same local segment as the target's HSRP/VRRP-protected default gateway. Scapy, Loki, or Yersinia for crafting forged HSRP/VRRP advertisement packets.
NET-084.whatItIs: Two protocols let multiple routers share one shared 'gateway' address for redundancy, automatically electing which router is currently active. Since the messages used for that election have either no authentication at all, or only a trivially weak, plain-text password, an attacker on the local network can send a fake message claiming to be a higher-priority router — winning the election and becoming the network's active gateway themselves.
NET-084.rootCause: Both protocols were built for convenient failover between routers that already trust each other, and their default (or commonly used) authentication is either nonexistent or laughably weak — providing basically no real barrier against a forged message. Stronger authentication options do exist for both, but they require deliberate setup and aren't always turned on.
NET-084.impact: An attacker who wins the HSRP/VRRP election becomes the segment's active default gateway, gaining a durable, protocol-level man-in-the-middle position over all traffic the segment's hosts send toward that gateway — this is a particularly severe and stable form of local-network traffic interception, since it operates at the routing-redundancy-protocol level rather than requiring the more easily-detected continuous packet injection that ARP spoofing depends on.
stepsToIdentify: Identify HSRP/VRRP in use on the target segment and confirm the authentication mode configured (none, weak cleartext, or strong MD5-based).
With authorization, craft and send a forged advertisement claiming a higher priority than the observed legitimate active router.
Confirm whether the forged advertisement wins the election, making the attacker's system the segment's active gateway.
Demonstrate the resulting traffic-interception position with a benign, non-destructive capture of test traffic.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active HSRP/VRRP election-hijacking testing against the target segment, with a bounded, carefully-monitored approach given the potential for genuine gateway-availability disruption if the test goes wrong.
Observe the current active router's advertised priority.
Craft and send a forged advertisement with a higher priority, winning the election.
Confirm the resulting active-gateway status and demonstrate the traffic-interception position via a benign capture.
Immediately restore the legitimate router's active status (stop sending forged advertisements) once the finding is proven, to avoid a genuine, extended gateway outage.

examplePayloads.label: Observe the current HSRP/VRRP advertised priority
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 'proto 112 or udp port 1985' -w hsrp_vrrp_capture.pcap

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send a forged higher-priority HSRP advertisement with Loki
examplePayloads.command: loki -i eth0  # select HSRP module, set a higher priority than observed, and launch

examplePayloads.label: Craft a forged advertisement manually with Scapy (VRRP example)
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from scapy.all import *
send(IP(dst='224.0.0.18', ttl=255)/VRRP(priority=255, addrlist=['<gateway-virtual-ip>']))
"

variants: VRRP with no authentication at all (trivially forgeable) versus HSRP with weak, cleartext plaintext-password authentication (requiring the attacker to first observe/capture the plaintext password, but still straightforward given the protocol's cleartext transmission).

The related VRRP variant (the open, multi-vendor standard equivalent to Cisco's proprietary HSRP) is subject to the identical hijacking technique and should be tested identically wherever VRRP rather than HSRP is in use.
mitigation: Configure MD5-based (cryptographic) authentication for both HSRP and VRRP wherever the router platform supports it, rather than relying on no authentication or weak cleartext passwords.
Restrict which network segments/ports can send HSRP/VRRP traffic via switch-level filtering, limiting the population of potential forgers to only the legitimate, participating routers.
Monitor for unexpected changes in the elected active router or unusual advertisement-priority patterns as a detection signature for an active hijack attempt.
Apply Dynamic ARP Inspection and general network segmentation as complementary controls reducing the broader population of potential on-segment attackers.

NET-085.prerequisites: Network access to a target TLS service running a vulnerable OpenSSL version (1.0.1 through 1.0.1f, and specific later point releases before the fix). A Heartbleed-specific scanning/exploitation tool.
NET-085.whatItIs: Heartbleed is a bug in a widely-used encryption library where a client can ask the server to 'echo back' a small piece of data, but claim the data is much larger than it actually sent. The buggy server trusts that claimed size and echoes back a chunk of its own memory instead — up to 64KB at a time — which can contain private keys, session tokens, passwords, or anything else the server happened to have in memory at that moment.
NET-085.rootCause: This came down to a straightforward but catastrophic bug: the code copied the client's claimed data size directly into a memory-read operation, without ever checking that the actual data received was really that size. A basic input-checking mistake in one of the most widely used encryption libraries on the internet.
NET-085.impact: Repeated exploitation can leak a substantial amount of server process memory over time, and because this memory can include the server's own TLS private key, session tokens, or recently-processed plaintext credentials, successful exploitation has historically enabled full private-key extraction (allowing an attacker to decrypt all past and future traffic to that server, or impersonate it) and direct session/credential theft — Heartbleed remains one of the most severe vulnerabilities ever disclosed in mainstream cryptographic software specifically because of what it could leak.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the OpenSSL version in use on the target TLS service via banner/handshake analysis, and confirm whether it falls in the vulnerable version range (1.0.1 through 1.0.1f).

Use a Heartbleed-specific scanning tool to confirm actual vulnerability, since version identification alone can be unreliable given some vendors backported the fix without changing the reported version string.
Where confirmed vulnerable, assess (with authorization) the practical impact by capturing a sample of leaked memory to characterize what kind of sensitive data is present.
Determine the precise OpenSSL version in use and cross-reference it against the narrow vulnerable range (1.0.1 through 1.0.1f) to confirm applicability before further testing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes Heartbleed exploitation testing against the target service.
Run the Heartbleed proof-of-concept/scanning tool against the target.

Where vulnerable, capture a sample of leaked memory and inspect it for sensitive content (credentials, session tokens, key material) as impact evidence, retaining only what's needed to prove the finding.
Document the confirmed vulnerability and the specific categories of sensitive data recovered from leaked memory.

Report the exact vulnerable OpenSSL version confirmed and prioritize this finding urgently given Heartbleed's well-documented history of large-scale credential and private-key exposure in real breaches.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for Heartbleed vulnerability
Dedicated Heartbleed exploitation/memory-leak tool

variants: Vulnerability confirmed present but no genuinely sensitive data recovered within the test window (still a critical finding given the demonstrated capability) versus successful extraction of private-key material or live credentials, representing the most severe possible confirmed impact.

The related, less-publicized "reverse Heartbleed" variant allows a malicious server to extract memory from a vulnerable client that connects to it, meaning outbound connections from patched-server/unpatched-client combinations deserve equal attention.
mitigation: Immediately patch OpenSSL to a fixed version — this is an urgent, critical-priority remediation given the severity and ease of exploitation.

Revoke and reissue the server's TLS certificate/private key after patching, since any prior exposure window means the original key material must be considered potentially compromised regardless of whether an actual leak was directly observed.
Force invalidation of all existing session tokens/cookies after patching and key rotation, since these may also have been exposed during any vulnerable window.
Maintain current, supported versions of foundational cryptographic libraries as an ongoing practice, given how severe a single implementation bug in this class of software can be.

NET-086.prerequisites: A network position on the same local segment as the target host and its default gateway. Scapy for crafting forged ICMP Redirect messages.
NET-086.whatItIs: A specific network message that routers use to tell a device 'hey, there's a better path for this destination' is accepted by many computers with no verification that it actually came from a real router. An attacker on the local network can send a forged version of this message, tricking a victim's computer into routing certain traffic through the attacker instead of the real gateway.
NET-086.rootCause: This message type was designed to let routers automatically help devices find better paths, but it was never built with any way to verify the sender is a genuine router. Many modern systems now restrict or ignore these messages by default, but an older or more permissively configured device may still accept a forged one.
NET-086.impact: A successful ICMP Redirect attack causes the victim to route traffic for a specific, attacker-chosen destination through the attacker's own machine instead of the legitimate path, establishing a targeted man-in-the-middle position for that specific destination without needing the broader, more detectable technique of full ARP-cache poisoning against the default gateway itself.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target host's OS/configuration accepts ICMP Redirect messages (many current OS defaults have hardened against this, so testing the actual behavior is necessary rather than assuming vulnerability).
With authorization, send a forged ICMP Redirect message to a nominated test host, claiming a better route to a chosen test destination via the attacker's own address.
Confirm whether the test host's routing table/behavior updates to reflect the forged redirect.
Demonstrate the resulting targeted traffic-interception position with a benign, non-destructive capture.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active ICMP Redirect injection against a nominated test host on the target segment.
Send a forged ICMP Redirect message directing traffic for a chosen test destination through the attacker's address.
Confirm the test host accepts the redirect and routes accordingly.
Demonstrate the resulting interception with a benign capture, then allow the redirect to time out or send a corrective redirect to restore normal routing.
Document the confirmed OS-level acceptance of forged ICMP Redirects and the resulting interception capability.

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send a forged ICMP Redirect message with Scapy
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from scapy.all import *
send(IP(src='<gateway-ip>', dst='<victim-ip>')/ICMP(type=5, code=1, gw='<attacker-ip>')/IP(src='<victim-ip>', dst='<test-destination-ip>')/ICMP())
"

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the victim's routing table reflects the forged redirect
examplePayloads.command: ip route get <test-destination-ip>  # run on the test victim host, with authorization

variants: OS accepting ICMP Redirects from any source claiming to be a router (severe, broadly exploitable) versus a more hardened OS that only accepts redirects from the already-known default gateway's address (requiring the attacker to also spoof the gateway's source address, a somewhat higher bar but still often achievable).

IPv6 ICMPv6 Redirect abuse is a distinct but analogous variant to the IPv4 finding, and is frequently overlooked specifically because IPv6 hardening lags behind IPv4 hardening in many otherwise well-secured environments.
mitigation: Disable acceptance of ICMP Redirects on all hosts where the OS supports this hardening option (`net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0` on Linux, or the equivalent registry/GPO setting on Windows), since legitimate use of ICMP Redirects is rarely necessary in a properly-designed, static network topology.

Apply the same general segmentation and Dynamic ARP Inspection controls recommended for the related ARP-spoofing finding, since they reduce the broader population of potential on-segment attackers for this technique as well.
Monitor for unexpected or high-volume ICMP Redirect traffic as a detection signature.

NET-087.prerequisites: Code-execution capability on a host behind egress filtering that still permits outbound ICMP (or another commonly-unfiltered protocol). ptunnel or icmpsh for ICMP-based tunneling, and network access from an external, attacker-controlled listener host.
NET-087.whatItIs: A protocol normally used just to test whether a device is reachable (ping) gets used instead as a hidden channel to sneak data out of the network, by encoding it into the ping messages themselves — abusing the fact that this kind of traffic is almost always allowed straight through firewalls, even in networks that otherwise carefully restrict what can leave.
NET-087.rootCause: This protocol's message content can technically carry almost any data with no restriction, and since blocking it entirely would break basic network troubleshooting, most firewall policies let it through without closely inspecting what's actually inside it — creating the same kind of hidden-channel opportunity as the similar DNS-based finding elsewhere in this list, just using a different, similarly-trusted protocol.
NET-087.impact: An attacker with code execution on an internal host, but blocked from more obvious outbound channels by egress filtering, can still exfiltrate data or maintain command-and-control communication via ICMP tunneling, since this channel is commonly permitted through even a fairly restrictive firewall policy and often receives less deep content inspection than more heavily-scrutinized protocols like HTTP.
stepsToIdentify: Review the network's egress-filtering policy specifically for whether ICMP is permitted outbound without restriction or deep content inspection.
With authorization, attempt to establish an ICMP tunnel from a test host using a standard tunneling toolkit, and measure whether it succeeds and at what throughput.
Review network-security-monitoring capability for whether ICMP traffic content/volume is inspected at all, versus being entirely unmonitored once permitted through the firewall.

Determine whether outbound ICMP is filtered at the perimeter for payload size/content, since standard ICMP echo filtering often permits ICMP entirely while still blocking the oversized or unusual payloads a tunnel requires.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes establishing an ICMP-tunneling channel from a designated test host to an attacker-controlled listener.
Set up the listener side of the tunnel on a controlled external host.
From the test host, establish the tunnel and confirm connectivity through it, measuring achievable throughput.
Demonstrate a benign, bounded data-transfer proof of concept through the tunnel.
Document whether the tunnel was detected by any monitoring in place during the test.

examplePayloads.label: Start the ICMP tunnel listener on the attacker-controlled external host
Establish the tunnel from the test host
Alternative: icmpsh for a simple reverse-shell-over-ICMP proof of concept

variants: Data-exfiltration-focused ICMP tunneling versus full interactive command-and-control (a reverse shell over ICMP).
Pure ICMP-based tunneling versus abuse of other commonly-permitted-but-under-inspected protocols (certain UDP-based diagnostic protocols) using a similar covert-channel technique.
mitigation: Apply deep packet inspection to permitted ICMP traffic where feasible, flagging unusually large or high-volume ICMP payloads inconsistent with legitimate diagnostic use.
Restrict outbound ICMP to only what's genuinely necessary (e.g. permitting it only from specific network-monitoring hosts rather than every general-purpose endpoint).
Deploy network-traffic-analysis tooling capable of detecting tunneling-characteristic patterns across ICMP and other commonly-permitted protocols, not just the most obvious ones.
Apply egress-filtering review holistically, considering every protocol permitted outbound (not just the most commonly-discussed ones like DNS/HTTP) for covert-channel potential.

NET-088.prerequisites: Network access to the target IPsec VPN endpoint configured for IKE Aggressive Mode. ike-scan for capturing the exchange, and a password-cracking tool (hashcat/John the Ripper) for offline cracking of the recovered PSK hash material.
NET-088.whatItIs: A VPN setup that uses a faster, less secure handshake mode sends a scrambled version of its shared secret password to anyone who simply starts the connection process — before they've proven who they are in any way. An attacker can just initiate the handshake, capture that scrambled value, and crack it offline, completely sidestepping any of the normal protections against repeated online login attempts.
NET-088.rootCause: This faster handshake mode trades some security for fewer round trips and better compatibility — but that tradeoff means the scrambled shared secret gets exposed to anyone who starts the exchange, before both sides have actually verified each other. The slower, more careful handshake mode doesn't have this specific problem, but the faster one is still used for compatibility with certain client setups.
NET-088.impact: An attacker can capture the PSK hash with a single, unauthenticated protocol exchange and crack it offline at whatever speed their compute resources allow, with no rate-limiting or lockout protection applying at all — if the PSK is not sufficiently long and random, this results in full recovery of the VPN's shared secret, enabling the attacker to establish their own authenticated VPN connection or, in some configurations, decrypt previously captured VPN traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target IPsec VPN endpoint is configured to accept IKE Aggressive Mode (rather than only Main Mode) for PSK-based authentication.
With authorization, initiate an Aggressive Mode exchange with the endpoint and capture the resulting hash material using ike-scan.
Attempt offline cracking of the captured hash against a representative wordlist within the engagement's time budget to assess practical PSK strength.

Where aggressive mode is confirmed, check whether the PSK is shared across multiple VPN endpoints/sites, since a single successful hash-crack could then be reused for lateral compromise of other sites.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes IKE Aggressive Mode hash capture and offline cracking against the target VPN endpoint.
Initiate the Aggressive Mode exchange and capture the PSK hash.
Attempt offline cracking against a representative, curated wordlist.
Where successful, confirm the recovered PSK by establishing a test VPN connection using it, then stop.
Document the confirmed Aggressive Mode exposure and the PSK's cracked/uncracked status within the time budget used.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the IKE Aggressive Mode PSK hash
Offline-crack the captured hash with a dedicated PSK-cracking tool
Alternative offline cracking via hashcat

variants: Aggressive Mode with a weak, dictionary-crackable PSK (fully exploitable) versus a long, high-entropy PSK (the exposure/capture step still succeeds, but offline cracking becomes computationally infeasible within a reasonable time budget).

IKEv1 Main Mode (rather than Aggressive Mode) with a pre-shared key is comparatively more resistant to offline hash capture, but still permits an active MITM to force a downgrade to Aggressive Mode on many implementations, effectively creating the same exposure via a downgrade path.
mitigation: Migrate to IKE Main Mode for all PSK-based IPsec configurations, avoiding Aggressive Mode's hash-exposure weakness entirely.

Where Aggressive Mode must remain for specific client-compatibility reasons, use a very long, high-entropy, randomly-generated PSK to make offline cracking computationally infeasible regardless of the exposure.
Prefer certificate-based authentication over PSK-based authentication for IPsec VPNs wherever the client/infrastructure supports it, removing the shared-secret cracking risk entirely.
Rotate any PSK confirmed or suspected to have been captured immediately.

NET-089.prerequisites: Network access to the target segment where IPv6 is enabled but not part of the organization's deliberate, managed addressing scheme. Standard IPv6 scanning/reconnaissance tools (nmap with IPv6 support, or the THC-IPv6 suite).
NET-089.whatItIs: Modern IPv6 networking is turned on by default on computers across the network, but the organization has no deliberate plan for managing, monitoring, or securing it. Every other IPv6-related issue in this list becomes exploitable specifically because this modern networking stack is quietly running, unmanaged and unmonitored, right alongside the organization's actual, properly managed network.
NET-089.rootCause: This modern networking stack is turned on by default in virtually every current operating system, and actually turning it off — or better, deliberately setting it up and securing it — takes a specific decision and effort that a lot of organizations never get around to. That leaves it fully functional on every computer, but completely outside the reach of firewall rules and monitoring tools that were only ever designed with the older networking stack in mind.
NET-089.impact: This finding functions as a root-cause, umbrella condition enabling several other, more specific IPv6-related findings in this domain (mitm6-based NTLM relay via DHCPv6 spoofing, MLD manipulation) — even without any of those specific techniques being separately demonstrated, the mere presence of unmanaged, unmonitored IPv6 traffic represents a blind spot in the organization's security posture, since IPv4-focused firewall rules and monitoring provide no coverage for this parallel protocol stack.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm IPv6 is enabled and functional on client/server hosts across the target network (a simple IPv6 ping/traceroute test, or reviewing host network configuration).
Confirm whether the organization has any deliberate IPv6 addressing plan, firewall ruleset, or security-monitoring coverage specifically for IPv6 traffic.

Cross-reference this finding against the more specific IPv6-related findings in this domain (DHCPv6 spoofing, MLD manipulation) to assess which specific techniques are practically exploitable as a result of this broader condition.
Assess whether IPv6 is genuinely needed for any current business purpose, or is simply an unused, unmanaged default.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through configuration/network review rather than independently exploited, since its impact is realized through the specific, separately-documented IPv6-related attack techniques it enables.
Confirm scope authorizes IPv6 reconnaissance against the target network.
Confirm IPv6 is functional and unmanaged (no deliberate addressing plan, firewall coverage, or monitoring) across representative hosts.
Document the confirmed condition and its role as the enabling precondition for the more specific, separately-tested IPv6-related findings.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm IPv6 connectivity is functional on the target segment
examplePayloads.command: ping6 -c3 ff02::1%eth0  # link-local all-nodes multicast ping to discover IPv6-active hosts

examplePayloads.label: Scan for IPv6-reachable hosts and services

variants: IPv6 enabled with genuinely no organizational awareness/use at all (the most common instance) versus IPv6 partially, informally used for some specific purpose without a corresponding, deliberate security review.

Where SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) is active alongside unmanaged/unnecessary IPv6, address privacy extensions being disabled can additionally allow long-term device tracking via a stable, hardware-derived IPv6 address.
mitigation: Make a deliberate decision to either fully disable IPv6 across the environment (where it's genuinely not needed) or to properly deploy, firewall, and monitor it with the same rigor applied to IPv4.
Where IPv6 is disabled, verify the disablement is comprehensive and doesn't inadvertently leave partial IPv6 functionality (such as DHCPv6 solicitation) still active.

Where IPv6 is deliberately kept enabled, extend firewall rules, network-segmentation policy, and security-monitoring coverage explicitly to include it, closing the blind-spot condition this finding describes.
Include IPv6 configuration status explicitly in routine network security assessments, rather than defaulting to an IPv4-only review scope.

NET-090.prerequisites: Network access to a switch port on the target's wired network segment where CDP/LLDP is active. Yersinia or a custom Scapy script for crafting forged CDP/LLDP advertisements, distinct from the passive-disclosure-focused related finding.
NET-090.whatItIs: Beyond just passively overhearing device information broadcasts (covered elsewhere), an attacker can actively send their own fake broadcasts claiming to be a legitimate device — confusing network-mapping tools that rely on these broadcasts, or, on switches that auto-assign network segments based on this information (common for phone systems), potentially tricking the switch into assigning the attacker's own device to a segment it shouldn't be on.
NET-090.rootCause: Same underlying issue as the passive version: these device-announcement broadcasts have no way to verify who's actually sending them. Any device on the network can fake being a switch, a phone, or anything else the receiving switch expects — and where the switch automatically acts on that information (like assigning a network segment), a forged broadcast can directly manipulate that automatic decision.
NET-090.impact: An attacker can disrupt or corrupt network-topology-monitoring tools that rely on CDP/LLDP data for accuracy, and, more severely, on switches using LLDP-MED for automatic VoIP VLAN assignment, can potentially spoof a VoIP-phone advertisement to have their own device automatically assigned to the (often more trusted, differently-segmented) voice VLAN, gaining network access to a segment intended only for VoIP infrastructure.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm CDP/LLDP is active on the target switch port and, specifically, whether LLDP-MED-based automatic VLAN assignment is configured.
With authorization, craft and send a forged LLDP-MED advertisement claiming to be a VoIP phone and observe whether the switch port's VLAN assignment changes accordingly.

Assess the sensitivity/trust-level of the voice VLAN (or any other automatically-assigned VLAN) relative to the segment the attacker would otherwise be confined to, to correctly scope the finding's severity.
Separately, assess whether forged advertisements disrupt or corrupt any network-topology-monitoring tooling's accuracy as a secondary, monitoring-integrity impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active CDP/LLDP spoofing against the target switch port.
Craft and send a forged LLDP-MED advertisement claiming to be a VoIP phone.
Confirm whether the switch port's VLAN assignment changes to the voice VLAN as a result.
Where successful, demonstrate the resulting network access/reachability on the newly-assigned VLAN via a benign reconnaissance action.
Document the confirmed spoofing technique and the resulting VLAN-assignment/network-access impact.

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send a forged LLDP-MED VoIP-phone advertisement
examplePayloads.command: yersinia lldp -attack 3  # or a custom Scapy-crafted LLDP-MED TLV set claiming a VoIP endpoint device type

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the resulting VLAN assignment after the forged advertisement
examplePayloads.command: ip addr show eth0  # check whether the interface received a DHCP lease/VLAN tag consistent with the voice VLAN

variants: Spoofing used to manipulate automatic VLAN assignment (a network-access-bypass impact) versus used purely to corrupt network-topology-monitoring tool accuracy (an operational/monitoring-integrity impact, generally lower severity).

CDP spoofing (announcing false neighbor information over Cisco's proprietary protocol) is functionally the vendor-specific counterpart to LLDP spoofing and warrants identical testing on any all-Cisco segment.
mitigation: Disable automatic VLAN assignment based on unauthenticated CDP/LLDP-MED advertisements, or pair it with 802.1X-based device authentication so VLAN assignment isn't solely determined by an easily-spoofed protocol advertisement.
Disable CDP/LLDP on general-access, user-facing switch ports where its topology-discovery/auto-configuration function isn't genuinely required, per the related passive-disclosure finding's guidance.

Apply port-security and 802.1X NAC as the primary access-control mechanism, treating any LLDP-MED-based VLAN convenience feature as a secondary, non-security-relevant automation rather than a trust boundary.
Monitor for unexpected or conflicting CDP/LLDP advertisements as a detection signature for active spoofing attempts.

NET-091.prerequisites: Access to cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP) with misconfigured security groups or network ACLs. Cloud provider CLI tools (AWS CLI, Azure CLI, gcloud). Understanding of cloud networking and IAAS.
NET-091.whatItIs: Cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP) use rule sets to control what network traffic is allowed in and out — and these are frequently set up too loosely, allowing traffic in from literally anywhere on the internet to sensitive ports, or just inherited from a template without ever being tightened to the specific addresses the application actually needs.
NET-091.rootCause: It's easy to open a port to the entire internet 'just for testing' and simply forget to close it back up. Combined with the fact that cloud setups often get deployed quickly without the same careful security review given to traditional infrastructure, these loose default rules tend to stick around.
NET-091.impact: Overly permissive security group rules expose services to the internet or to broader internal networks than intended, which can lead to exploitation of unpatched services, data exfiltration, or lateral movement within the cloud environment. Because cloud security-group misconfigurations are often invisible from outside the console and rarely trigger the same alerting as on-premises firewall changes, this class of exposure frequently persists undetected for months and is a leading root cause in cloud data-breach post-mortems.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all security groups / NSGs / firewall rule sets attached to in-scope cloud resources via the provider's CLI (aws ec2 describe-security-groups, az network nsg list, gcloud compute firewall-rules list).
Flag any rule permitting inbound access from 0.0.0.0/0 (or ::/0) on a sensitive port (22, 3389, database ports, management interfaces).
Cross-reference each overly-broad rule against the resource it protects to confirm the service is genuinely reachable, not just nominally exposed.
Check for security groups referencing 'temporary' or dated naming conventions, which often indicate a rule opened for testing and never closed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the rules of engagement cover the cloud account/VPC in scope, since a misconfigured security group can expose resources belonging to other tenants in a shared environment.
From an external host, attempt to connect directly to the flagged port/service to confirm real-world reachability rather than relying solely on the rule's stated intent.
Where the exposed service itself has no authentication, chain the exposure into direct data access to demonstrate full impact.
Document the minimum viable rule change (specific source CIDR, specific port) that would have prevented the exposure, for the remediation writeup.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate all security groups with 0.0.0.0/0 ingress (AWS)
Confirm external reachability of a flagged port
Azure equivalent NSG audit
examplePayloads.command: az network nsg rule list --nsg-name <nsg-name> -g <resource-group> --query "[?access=='Allow' && direction=='Inbound' && sourceAddressPrefix=='*']"

variants: Security group allowing SSH (22) or RDP (3389) from 0.0.0.0/0.
Database ports (3306, 5432, 6379, 9200) accessible from the internet due to overly permissive rules.
Egress rules configured to allow 0.0.0.0/0 outbound, allowing exfiltration if a workload is compromised.
Security groups inherited from shared/template resources without customization for the specific workload.
mitigation: Restrict security-group/NSG ingress rules to the minimum necessary source CIDR ranges — corporate VPN ranges or specific known IPs — rather than 0.0.0.0/0, for any port beyond public web (80/443).
Deploy a cloud security posture management (CSPM) tool or the provider's native equivalent (AWS Config rules, Azure Policy) to continuously detect and alert on newly-created overly-permissive rules.
Require security-group changes to go through the same change-review process as other infrastructure changes, rather than allowing ad-hoc console edits.
Periodically audit for and remove unused or 'temporary' rules that were never cleaned up after their original purpose ended.

NET-092.prerequisites: Network access to FTP servers supporting active mode (less common on modern servers; mostly legacy systems). FTP client tools. Understanding of FTP protocol variants.
NET-092.whatItIs: An older file-transfer mode requires the server to open a new connection back to the client to send data. An attacker can abuse this by asking an open file-transfer server to send data to a victim's address instead of their own — making the server connect to that victim's network on the attacker's behalf, as a way to bypass firewalls or route traffic through infrastructure the victim trusts.
NET-092.rootCause: This file-transfer mode was designed back when firewalls were rare and faking a network address wasn't really a practical concern. The protocol lets an attacker specify basically any destination address for that connection, and a lot of file-transfer servers will just go along with it, without checking that the address actually belongs to the original client.
NET-092.impact: A bounce attack allows an attacker to scan internal networks by making an open FTP server probe the target on the attacker's behalf (determining which ports are open by observing which connection attempts fail/succeed). More dangerously, if the FTP server has internal network access, it can be used to attack services on that internal network, or to deliver malicious data to internal systems that trust the source IP (the FTP server). Because the scan traffic originates from the FTP server's own trusted internal IP address, it also evades any network monitoring or firewall rules that are based on distinguishing internal from external scan sources.
stepsToIdentify: Identify FTP servers accepting active-mode PORT commands and confirm whether the server will proxy a connection to an arbitrary third-party host/port on the requester's behalf.
Test whether the FTP server itself can be instructed to connect to internal hosts not otherwise reachable from the tester's vantage point.
Check the FTP server's software version against known bounce-scan-capable implementations.

Determine whether the FTP server's control connection is reachable from external and internal segments both, since bounce-scanning value depends on what network position the FTP server itself occupies.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly covers using the FTP server as a scanning/relay pivot, since this technique probes hosts other than the FTP server itself.
Use nmap's FTP bounce scan mode to have the FTP server itself report open ports on a third host it can reach but the tester cannot.
Where internal hosts are reachable this way, document exactly which internal segment was reached through the bounce to demonstrate the network-segmentation bypass.
Report the confirmed bounce-scan capability and the specific internal targets reachable through it, recommending the FTP daemon's PORT command support be disabled or restricted as the fix.

examplePayloads.label: FTP bounce port scan via nmap
Manual PORT command test via raw FTP session
examplePayloads.command:
ftp <ftp-server-ip>
USER anonymous
PASS anonymous
PORT 10,0,0,5,0,80
LIST

variants: FTP server accepting PORT commands with arbitrary destination IPs without validation.
FTP bounce used for port scanning or reconnaissance of internal networks.
FTP bounce used to deliver malicious data to internal services that trust the FTP server's source IP.
mitigation: Disable active-mode FTP entirely and require passive mode, which does not permit the server to be instructed to connect to arbitrary third-party addresses.
Where FTP must remain active-mode for legacy compatibility, restrict the PORT command to only the IP address that initiated the control connection.
Migrate off plain FTP to SFTP/FTPS where feasible, eliminating this class of protocol-level abuse entirely.
Place any FTP server behind network segmentation so that even a successful bounce cannot reach sensitive internal hosts.

NET-093.prerequisites: Written, equipment-specific authorization covering active testing of ICS/OT protocols, since even a single malformed or unexpected write can affect a physical process — this is materially different from IT scope authorization and should name the specific outstations/registers in scope. Network access to the ICS/OT segment (often requiring a site visit or a dedicated jump host, since these networks are frequently air-gapped from general corporate access). Client OT/engineering staff available during any active write test to confirm and revert changes. Wireshark with ICS protocol dissectors, nmap, and a Modbus/DNP3 client library (pymodbus/pydnp3) or CLI tool.
NET-093.whatItIs: Protocols used to control industrial equipment (like factory or power-grid systems) were built to move sensor readings and control commands between a central control system and remote field devices, assuming the network they ran on was physically isolated and safe. Neither has any built-in login requirement or encryption — so anyone who can reach these devices on the network can read data or issue the exact same commands a legitimate operator could, with no credential check at all.
NET-093.rootCause: These protocols are decades old and were designed for physically locked-down equipment cabinets, not networks reachable from anywhere. As older, physically-isolated industrial setups moved onto standard IP networks for convenience and cost, that same trusting design carried over unchanged — while the physical isolation that used to be the actual protection was often only partly kept, or removed entirely once these systems got connected to the regular corporate network for remote monitoring.
NET-093.impact: Write access to registers or coils translates directly into control over physical equipment: pumps, valves, breakers, and motors. An attacker can force a value out of its safe operating range, disable a safety interlock, or feed the HMI false sensor readings so operators don't notice the process is out of spec until physical damage or a safety incident occurs. Because ICS uptime requirements make patching and downtime rare, these findings tend to persist for years once introduced, and the consequences — unlike most IT findings — can include equipment destruction, environmental release, or harm to people rather than just data loss.
stepsToIdentify: Passively identify ICS traffic first where possible (a SPAN/mirror port capture analyzed in Wireshark) rather than actively scanning a live production segment, since some legacy PLCs crash or fault under unexpected packets.
Where active scanning is explicitly authorized, sweep for Modbus/TCP (502) and DNP3 (20000) with nmap's modbus-discover and dnp3 NSE scripts to enumerate reachable masters and outstations.

From a passive capture, map which hosts issue write function codes (Modbus 0x05/0x06/0x0F/0x10, DNP3 Direct Operate) versus which only read, to identify the actual engineering workstations versus monitoring-only clients.

Correlate register/coil addresses seen in traffic with any available point-list or engineering documentation to understand what physical equipment each address maps to before considering any write test.

Check for any authentication layer in use — DNP3 Secure Authentication (SAv5) or Modbus over TLS — since its absence should be treated as the default expectation for legacy deployments and its presence is itself worth verifying is configured correctly.

Confirm with the client which findings may be validated with a live read-only query (e.g. one holding-register read) versus which must remain analysis-only because the process is safety-critical or cannot tolerate any additional traffic.
exploitationSteps: Treat this category as read-only-by-default: obtain explicit, equipment-specific written authorization before issuing any write function code, and have client OT staff on standby able to intervene if a test affects the physical process.
Start with a single read (e.g. a Modbus Read Holding Registers request) against a non-critical, already-identified register to confirm the endpoint responds to unauthenticated requests at all.

If a write test is explicitly authorized, select a register mapped to a low-consequence point (an indicator light or non-critical setpoint, never a safety interlock) identified during the documentation-correlation step.

Issue a single write (Modbus Write Single Register, or DNP3 Direct Operate) to that point, and have the client visually or telemetrically confirm the change registered, then immediately revert it to its original value.

Do not chain writes into an automated or repeated sequence; one demonstrated write per authorized point is sufficient evidence and avoids any risk of a stuck or repeated command affecting the process.

Document the finding as unauthenticated read and/or write capability, citing the specific register/coil addresses and function codes used, and flag any point you identified but did not test because it was safety-critical.

examplePayloads.label: Passive discovery via SPAN port capture
examplePayloads.command: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp port 502 or tcp port 20000' -w ics_capture.pcap

examplePayloads.label: Active Modbus service discovery (only if authorized for active scanning)
DNP3 service discovery (only if authorized for active scanning)
Single read-only holding-register query
Single authorized write to a pre-identified, low-consequence register (revert immediately after)
Python pymodbus read for scripted verification
examplePayloads.command: from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient; c = ModbusTcpClient('10.20.30.50'); print(c.read_holding_registers(0, 10).registers)

variants: Modbus/TCP with no authentication at all, allowing unrestricted read and write to every register the outstation exposes.
DNP3 without Secure Authentication (SAv5), where any host on the segment can issue Direct Operate commands accepted at face value.
PROFIBUS/PROFINET or EtherNet/IP deployments with the same absence of authentication, reached because the OT/IT network boundary is flatter than documented.

Corporate-to-OT network bridging via a jump host or remote-monitoring VPN that lacks its own strong authentication, giving an attacker who compromises the jump host the same protocol-level access as a local engineer.
Legacy serial-to-Ethernet gateways that translate an old serial Modbus RTU bus onto TCP without adding any of the authentication the newer protocol variants at least optionally support.
mitigation: Segment ICS/OT networks from corporate IT with firewalls that default-deny, and require any cross-boundary traffic to pass through a monitored, authenticated jump host rather than direct routing.

Deploy ICS-aware firewalls or IDS that understand Modbus/DNP3 function codes, so writes to specific critical registers can be alerted on or blocked even though the protocol itself has no authentication.
Where the field devices and infrastructure support it, enable DNP3 Secure Authentication (SAv5) or Modbus over TLS rather than the base unauthenticated protocol.
Restrict which hosts are allowed to reach protocol ports 502/20000 via ACLs at the switch/firewall level, so only the actual designated master(s) can talk to each outstation.

Keep ICS networks air-gapped from the internet entirely; where remote access is a genuine operational need, use a dedicated, monitored, MFA-protected remote-access solution rather than routing OT protocols across a general-purpose VPN.
Continuously monitor ICS traffic baselines and alert on unexpected masters, unexpected function codes, or writes outside normal operational patterns.
Maintain an accurate, current point list/asset inventory mapping registers to physical equipment, since without it neither defenders nor testers can judge which writes are safe to investigate.

NET-094.prerequisites: Network access to systems; ability to send crafted IP packets (Scapy, custom tools). Understanding of IP fragmentation, MTU, and packet handling.
NET-094.whatItIs: Very large network packets, or packets that get split into pieces during transmission, can be mishandled by network equipment — letting an attacker craft malformed, split-up packets that sneak past security tools, crash equipment, or exploit bugs in how devices reassemble them.
NET-094.rootCause: Reassembling split-up packets correctly is a genuinely tricky, historically bug-prone piece of software. Overlapping or unusually structured pieces, or oversized packets, can trigger memory bugs, incorrect filtering, or crashes in devices that don't carefully validate how those pieces fit back together.
NET-094.impact: Successful exploitation can cause denial-of-service (device crash or processing loop), or bypass of firewall rules if the firewall and downstream device reassemble fragments differently, allowing an attacker to smuggle traffic past the firewall. Where the evasion path is used to smuggle a signatured exploit past an inline IDS/IPS, the fragmentation weakness effectively nullifies the organization's investment in that detection layer for the duration of the attack.
stepsToIdentify: Send oversized and deliberately malformed/overlapping IP fragments toward in-scope hosts/security devices and observe whether they are reassembled inconsistently or cause a crash/hang.

Compare how different devices on the path (firewall, IDS, and end host) each reassemble the same fragmented packet, since a security device that reassembles differently from the end host creates a detection-evasion gap.

Check whether jumbo frames (MTU > 1500) are enabled end-to-end or only on part of the path, since an MTU mismatch between hops causes silent fragmentation/black-holing that itself is a diagnostic and DoS concern.

Test PMTUD (Path MTU Discovery) behavior by sending oversized packets with the Don't Fragment bit set and confirming whether ICMP 'fragmentation needed' responses are correctly generated and honored along the path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope permits fragmentation/DoS-adjacent testing, since malformed fragments can crash some network stacks.

Craft overlapping fragments designed to be interpreted differently by an inline IDS/IPS versus the end host, and send a signatured attack payload split across them to confirm it passes the IDS undetected.
If testing for a denial-of-service condition specifically, send a small number of malformed jumbo-frame fragments and monitor the target's stability rather than sustaining the traffic.

Where an MTU mismatch is confirmed, document the specific hop at which fragmentation/black-holing occurs as part of the operational (non-security) finding, since this often affects reliability alongside the security concern.

Report the fragment-reassembly discrepancy between security devices with a clear before/after capture showing the evaded signature, so the finding is independently reproducible by the client's own team.

examplePayloads.label: Craft overlapping IP fragments with scapy
examplePayloads.command: sudo python3 -c "from scapy.all import *; send(IP(dst='<target-ip>', flags='MF', frag=0)/ICMP()/('A'*8)); send(IP(dst='<target-ip>', frag=1)/('B'*8))"

examplePayloads.label: Fragmentation-based IDS evasion test via fragroute

variants: Teardrop attack: overlapping IP fragments with malicious offsets causing reassembly buffer overflow.
Ping of Death: oversized ICMP echo request exceeding the maximum IP packet size, causing buffer overflow.
Jumbo frame mismatch between firewall and upstream devices, causing filtering bypass.
mitigation: Ensure firewalls, IDS/IPS, and end hosts all use the same, standards-compliant fragment-reassembly policy (prefer 'first fragment wins' consistently across the whole path) to eliminate the interpretation gap attackers rely on for evasion.
Enable full packet reassembly at the perimeter (rather than inspecting fragments individually) so that inline security tooling always evaluates the same reassembled payload the end host will see.
Apply vendor patches for known fragmentation-handling crashes/hangs in network stacks, and rate-limit fragmented traffic where sustained volume is a DoS concern.

NET-095.prerequisites: Network access to systems running MVRP (Multicast VLAN Registration Protocol); Ethernet switches and ports with MVRP enabled. Tools: packet crafting (Scapy), switch CLI for MVRP configuration.
NET-095.whatItIs: A protocol that lets network devices automatically register interest in specific multicast traffic and join network segments dynamically has no authentication at all. An attacker can abuse it to register for sensitive multicast traffic or fake their way into a network segment they shouldn't have access to.
NET-095.rootCause: This protocol was designed for trusted internal networks with no built-in login or verification — like a lot of older networking protocols from that era, it assumes that physical security alone is enough protection, not any kind of logical network boundary.
NET-095.impact: An attacker can join multicast groups used by network services (e.g., group communication, redundancy protocols) and intercept traffic, or spoof membership to disrupt multicast delivery to legitimate members. In environments running redundancy or clustering protocols over multicast, forged membership can also desynchronize failover state between nodes, turning a Layer 2 protocol weakness into an availability incident.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether switch ports facing untrusted segments (guest, lobby, unmanaged areas) have MVRP/GVRP enabled and are trusted to register new VLANs dynamically.
Attempt to advertise a new VLAN via MVRP from an untrusted port and confirm whether the switch propagates it network-wide.
Enumerate which VLANs are currently registered via MVRP across the switch fabric to establish the legitimate baseline before attempting any registration test.
Check whether the switch fabric's trunk ports restrict which VLANs may be dynamically registered (VLAN pruning/allowlisting) even where MVRP itself remains enabled.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers L2 protocol testing on the physical segment in question, since this can affect VLAN topology switch-wide.
From an untrusted port, send MVRP registration frames declaring membership in a VLAN the tester should not have access to, and confirm whether traffic for that VLAN becomes reachable.
Where successful, document which additional VLANs became reachable as a result, since this can bridge a supposedly-isolated guest network into internal segments.
Withdraw the test VLAN registration immediately after confirming propagation, to avoid leaving an unintended VLAN active on the production fabric.
Report the specific switches/trunk ports through which the rogue registration propagated, since remediation is typically applied per-port rather than fabric-wide.

examplePayloads.label: Craft and send MVRP registration frames with Yersinia
Confirm resulting VLAN reachability after a successful MVRP registration

variants: MVRP enabled on access ports where end devices can abuse it.
Unencrypted/unauthenticated multicast traffic that could be disrupted or intercepted via MVRP spoofing.
mitigation: Disable MVRP/GVRP entirely on any port facing an untrusted or unmanaged segment; only enable dynamic VLAN registration between trusted core/distribution switches that genuinely need it.
Where dynamic VLAN registration is required, restrict which VLANs each participating port is permitted to register via a static VLAN-registration allowlist rather than trusting all requests.
Treat access-layer switch ports as untrusted by default: disable trunking negotiation (DTP) and dynamic protocols on any port not explicitly configured as an inter-switch link.

NET-096.prerequisites: Network access to network backup services (NDMP, backup protocols on TCP/10000+, SMB/NFS backup targets). Backup system credentials or exploitation of default credentials. Tools: backup software clients, network analysis tools.
NET-096.whatItIs: Centralized backup systems hold complete copies of servers and databases, and communicate with backup software installed across the network — often with weak or no login required on their management interface or the channel used to talk to that backup software.
NET-096.rootCause: Backup systems were historically designed to run entirely within a trusted internal network, so proper login protection was often treated as a nice-to-have rather than a real requirement. The communication channels these systems use are also frequently overlooked during general network hardening, since they're seen as purely internal, administrative traffic.
NET-096.impact: Unauthenticated access to a backup service's management port or agent interface allows an attacker to enumerate what data is being backed up, steal backup copies, or initiate restore operations that overwrite production data. If backup agents run with root/SYSTEM privileges (which they typically do), compromising an agent can lead to full-system compromise of the backed-up host. Because backups by definition contain a complete historical copy of production data — including records that may since have been deleted or rotated on the live system — this exposure can leak data the organization believed was already remediated.
stepsToIdentify: Identify backup infrastructure services (Veeam, Bacula, NetBackup, rsync-based backup agents) reachable on the network and test whether they accept connections without authentication.
Where reachable, attempt to enumerate available backup jobs/catalogs and, if unauthenticated, attempt to browse or restore a sample file to confirm real data access.

Check whether the backup service enforces role-based access separately from general network reachability, since some products bind an unauthenticated management port even when job data itself requires credentials.

Where backup credentials are used elsewhere in scope (e.g., found in a configuration file during a separate test), attempt to reuse them against the backup service to test for credential-based rather than purely network-based exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes accessing backup data, since a successful test may expose highly sensitive historical data across the entire backed-up estate.
