Connect to the exposed backup service and enumerate available backup sets/catalogs without providing credentials.
Restore or preview a single, low-sensitivity file only, sufficient to prove unauthorized data access — avoid bulk restoration, which itself can constitute an unauthorized-scope data-handling action.
Where credentials are recoverable from an unrelated finding, test them against the backup console specifically to demonstrate a realistic attack chain rather than treating each finding in isolation.
Report the specific backup sets/catalogs enumerated (by name only, not content) so the client can assess exposure scope without the report itself becoming a sensitive-data handling concern.

examplePayloads.label: Identify exposed backup service ports
Enumerate a Bacula director without valid credentials
examplePayloads.command: bconsole -c bacula-dir.conf  # attempt connection with default/blank director password

variants: Backup management port exposed without authentication on the internal network.
Backup agent communication unencrypted and unauthenticated, allowing plaintext command injection.
Backup credentials stored in plaintext in configuration files or logs on backed-up systems.
mitigation: Require strong, unique authentication for every backup agent, catalog server, and management console — never rely on network placement alone as the access control.
Place backup infrastructure on a dedicated, tightly firewalled management VLAN reachable only from the backup servers themselves, not the general production network.
Encrypt backup data both in transit and at rest, so that even a network-level exposure does not directly yield readable data.
Audit backup-service configurations for default credentials or disabled-authentication modes as a standard part of the build process.

NET-097.prerequisites: Physical or network access to network devices (routers, switches, firewalls). Device management interfaces (serial console, web UI, SSH). Knowledge of default credentials for common vendors.
NET-097.whatItIs: Network equipment — switches, routers, firewalls — ships with default login credentials or unchanged security settings that rarely get updated during setup and deployment.
NET-097.rootCause: Changing these defaults takes a deliberate configuration step that's easy to skip, and a lot of network equipment is built on the assumption that just being physically inside the data center is protection enough. Once installed, these devices often just get trusted and never revisited for a proper security review.
NET-097.impact: An attacker with network access to a compromised device can fully control it, reconfigure routing/firewall rules, exfiltrate configuration data (which often includes credentials for other systems), or pivot to manage the connected network. Device-level compromise at this layer sits upstream of every host on the segment it serves, so a single default-credential finding can translate directly into a network-wide man-in-the-middle or denial-of-service capability.
stepsToIdentify: Fingerprint network device make/model/firmware (routers, switches, APs, IoT-class network gear) via banner grabs, SNMP, or web-management-interface identification.
Attempt login to any exposed management interface (web, SSH, Telnet) using the vendor's published default credentials for that model.
Where the vendor default is unknown, check the device's serial console or physical label, since some vendors print a unique default password per unit rather than a single shared one.

Test whether the management interface enforces account lockout after repeated failed attempts, since its absence indicates the device may also be vulnerable to a slower, non-default credential brute-force.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers the specific device(s) identified before attempting default-credential login, since this directly grants administrative access if successful.
Attempt the vendor default credential set against the device's management interface.
On successful login, demonstrate impact by reviewing (not modifying) the device configuration to confirm the level of access obtained.

Where multiple devices of the same model are in scope, test the default-credential set against a small, representative sample rather than every unit, to establish the finding is systemic without exhaustively logging into each device.
Report the specific model/firmware combination and default credential confirmed, since remediation (credential rotation) needs to be applied fleet-wide, not just to the tested unit.

examplePayloads.label: Identify device vendor/model via banner and SNMP sysDescr
Attempt default-credential login against the web management interface

variants: SSH or Telnet accessible with default credentials.
HTTP management interface accessible with default credentials.
SNMP configured with default read/write communities (public, private).
Console port (serial) accessible without a password.
mitigation: Change all default credentials on network devices as a mandatory step of the initial deployment checklist, before the device is connected to a live network segment.
Disable any unused management protocol (Telnet, unencrypted HTTP admin panel) in favor of SSH/HTTPS with strong, unique credentials.
Maintain an inventory of deployed device models and firmware versions and periodically re-audit for default-credential drift (e.g., after a factory reset during troubleshooting).

NET-098.prerequisites: Network access to load balancers (Citrix NetScaler, F5 BIG-IP, AWS ALB, HAProxy, etc.). Knowledge of health-check endpoint patterns. HTTP analysis tools (curl, Wireshark).
NET-098.whatItIs: Load balancers regularly check whether backend servers are healthy by hitting a specific status endpoint — and if that endpoint is set up to reveal actual application details (like whether the database connection is working) instead of a simple yes/no, an attacker can learn about the internal state of the application just by watching how that status endpoint responds.
NET-098.rootCause: These status-check endpoints often get thrown together quickly just to satisfy the load balancer's need for a simple 'I'm alive' response, without much thought about what information ends up in that response. Developers sometimes add extra debugging details or database-connection checks to it for their own convenience, accidentally leaking information in the process.
NET-098.impact: Information leaked in health-check responses can reveal internal server names, database connection state, cloud-provider infrastructure details, or debugging hints that aid an attacker in finding application vulnerabilities. This is relatively low-impact disclosure, but when combined with other reconnaissance findings, it can accelerate a full attack. Health-check disclosure is rarely critical in isolation, but it reliably shortens the reconnaissance phase of a broader attack chain by revealing backend topology and dependency health that would otherwise require active probing to discover.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the load balancer's configured health-check endpoint (commonly /health, /status, /actuator/health) and request it directly, bypassing normal application routing where possible.
Compare the health-check response's verbosity against what an unauthenticated client should reasonably see — internal hostnames, dependency status, stack traces, or version numbers are red flags.

Check whether the same verbose health-check response is reachable both internally and via the public-facing listener, since the acceptable risk differs significantly between those two exposure levels.

Where the endpoint is framework-default (e.g., Spring Boot Actuator's /health), check for sibling endpoints (/env, /beans, /heapdump) that are commonly left enabled alongside it and carry substantially higher risk.
exploitationSteps: Request the health-check endpoint directly and record any internal infrastructure detail disclosed (backend hostnames/IPs, database connectivity status, dependency versions).
Where the endpoint reveals differing responses for healthy vs. unhealthy backend nodes, use this as a reconnaissance signal to map the backend pool's topology.

Where a sibling diagnostic endpoint (e.g., /actuator/env or /actuator/heapdump) is also reachable, escalate the finding significantly and test it as its own, higher-severity issue rather than folding it into the health-check finding.
Report the specific fields disclosed and clearly separate the low-risk 'health check is public' finding from any higher-risk sibling-endpoint exposure discovered along the way.

Cross-check the disclosed backend hostnames/IPs against any external asset inventory already built during the engagement, since this endpoint frequently reveals internal naming conventions useful for phishing pretexts.

examplePayloads.label: Request common health-check endpoint paths directly
examplePayloads.command: for p in /health /actuator/health /status /healthz; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$p: %{http_code}\n" https://<target>$p; done

examplePayloads.label: Pull verbose Spring Boot Actuator health details if exposed

variants: Health-check endpoint echoing database connection status (connected, disconnected, error reason).
Health-check endpoint including server hostname or internal DNS name in the response.
Health-check endpoint reflecting environment variables or configuration values.
mitigation: Restrict health-check endpoints to internal-only source ranges (the load balancer's own health-check probes) rather than exposing them on the public listener.
Return a minimal, generic response (200 OK / 503) to external callers, moving any detailed dependency/version information to an internal-only diagnostic endpoint.
Review all /actuator, /status, and framework-default diagnostic endpoints during hardening, since many frameworks expose these verbosely by default.

NET-099.prerequisites: Access to Windows systems running Print Spooler service (TCP/445, 135, or USB/network printing). CVE-2021-1675 (PrintNightmare) or other print spooler vulnerabilities. Tools: Metasploit, custom exploits.
NET-099.whatItIs: The Windows service that manages printing has a history of serious vulnerabilities that let an unauthenticated attacker run their own code remotely, with the highest level of system privilege available.
NET-099.rootCause: This service processes untrusted input — like print jobs and printer driver files — coming from the network, without properly validating it first. These vulnerabilities have typically involved loading files from untrusted network locations or flaws in how certain data formats get parsed.
NET-099.impact: An attacker can achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows systems running Print Spooler, leading to full system compromise and lateral movement within the network. Because Print Spooler runs as SYSTEM on affected hosts by default, successful exploitation grants the highest local privilege level available on Windows without any prior credential, making it a preferred initial-access or privilege-escalation vector in real intrusions.
stepsToIdentify: Identify Windows systems with print spooler enabled (port scanning for SMB/RPC endpoints).
Query system to confirm print spooler is running: Get-Service -Name spooler
Check Windows version and patch level to identify potentially vulnerable systems.
Attempt to connect to print spooler RPC endpoint (TCP/135, named pipe).
Test for known print spooler vulnerabilities using Metasploit or vulnerability scanners.
exploitationSteps: Identify a vulnerable Windows system running print spooler.
Craft a malicious print job or trigger print spooler vulnerability via RPC.
Exploit the vulnerability to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges.
Establish reverse shell or install persistent backdoor.
Pivot to other systems on the network using compromised system credentials.

examplePayloads.label: Metasploit PrintNightmare exploit
examplePayloads.command: use exploit/windows/smb/printnightmare_rce; set RHOSTS target; exploit

examplePayloads.label: Check print spooler status
Print spooler RPC probe
Custom print spooler exploit
Disable print spooler (mitigation)
Vulnerability scanner detection
examplePayloads.command: nessus scan target (identifies print spooler vulnerabilities)

variants: PrintNightmare variants: RCE via remote DLL loading, local privilege escalation via AddPort.
Print spooler vulnerability in print driver installation allowing arbitrary file write.
Combining print spooler RCE with credential dumping for lateral movement.
Print server compromise leading to mass compromise of all systems printing to that server.
mitigation: Apply latest Windows security patches immediately (MS21-36 patches for PrintNightmare).
If print spooler is not required, disable the service entirely.
Restrict network access to print spooler ports (135, 445) from untrusted networks.
Implement application whitelisting to prevent arbitrary DLL loading.
Monitor print spooler service for unusual behavior (unexpected DLL loads, network connections).
Use Print Server hardening guides from Microsoft; keep print drivers updated.
Monitor for PrintNightmare exploitation attempts via Windows Event Logs (Event ID 4688).

NET-100.prerequisites: Network access to internal network; knowledge of network topology and segmentation. Network analysis tools (tcpdump, Wireshark, traceroute). Understanding of VLANs, ACLs, and firewall rules.
NET-100.whatItIs: The network isn't properly divided into isolated zones, allowing traffic to flow between parts of the network that should be kept completely separate. An attacker who compromises one, less-protected part of the network can use that as a stepping stone to reach far more sensitive systems that were supposed to be isolated.
NET-100.rootCause: Proper network isolation requires carefully configured network zones, firewall rules, and access lists — and these are often left incomplete or misconfigured during the original network design, so the boundaries between different security zones never actually get properly enforced.
NET-100.impact: An attacker with access to one network segment can pivot to restricted segments (database servers, management networks, production systems) not meant to be accessible. Segmentation failures are especially damaging because they invalidate the organization's own risk model — controls and monitoring calibrated for a 'low-value' segment turn out to sit directly upstream of systems the organization believed were protected by an additional layer of isolation.
stepsToIdentify: Map network topology to identify supposed network segments and security domains.
Test connectivity between segments; attempt to route traffic across VLAN boundaries.
Enumerate systems in different segments to identify intended access restrictions.
Analyze firewall rules and ACLs for misconfigurations or overly-permissive rules.
Check whether security domain boundaries are enforced (DNS, database access, etc.).
exploitationSteps: From a compromised system in a low-security segment, attempt to reach systems in restricted segments.
Probe for network routes or gateways that allow cross-segment access.
Exploit firewall misconfigurations to send traffic to restricted segments.
Pivot using legitimate network services (NTP, DNS, Syslog) that cross segment boundaries.
Establish persistence in restricted segments by compromising systems accessible from pivoting point.

examplePayloads.command: route print (Windows) or ip route (Linux) to identify internal networks

examplePayloads.command: nmap -sn 192.168.10.0/24 (scan supposed isolated VLAN from compromised system)

examplePayloads.label: Test firewall rule boundaries
examplePayloads.command: tracert database-server (attempt to reach database segment from web segment)

examplePayloads.command: # Use compromised system as pivot to reach otherwise-blocked segments

variants: Incomplete segmentation; one restrictive rule but many exceptions and workarounds.
Implicit trust between segments; reliance on network isolation without per-system authentication.
Management network accessible from production networks, or vice versa.
Database server accessible from web tier without firewall filtering (should be restricted).
mitigation: Implement zero-trust network architecture; assume no trust between any network segments.
Use microsegmentation to isolate security domains with application-layer firewalls.
Enforce strict firewall rules between network segments; default deny all traffic.
Validate all cross-segment traffic via next-gen firewalls with deep packet inspection.
Implement network access controls (NAC) to verify system compliance before network access.
Monitor and alert on unusual cross-segment traffic or connection attempts.
Regular review and audit of network segmentation configuration.

NET-101.prerequisites: Network access to systems using NTP (UDP/123). Tools: ntpdate, custom packet crafting (Scapy). Understanding of NTP protocol and time synchronization.
NET-101.whatItIs: Servers that keep every computer's clock in sync across the organization are sometimes left with no login requirement at all. An attacker can send fake time-sync responses, tricking systems into trusting the wrong time — which matters more than it sounds, since correct time is quietly relied on for things like log accuracy, certificate validity checks, and time-based access rules.
NET-101.rootCause: This time-sync protocol has no built-in login requirement by default. A more secure option does exist, but it has to be deliberately turned on, and a lot of older setups never bothered. Time-syncing is usually treated as invisible background infrastructure rather than something security-relevant, so it rarely gets the same hardening attention as other services — and since it typically runs over a connectionless protocol, faking the sender's address is straightforward for anyone positioned nearby on the network.
NET-101.impact: Time poisoning affects logging fidelity, can cause certificate validation failures, and can disable time-based authentication codes. Because so many unrelated controls silently depend on accurate time, a successful time-poisoning attack can produce security failures in systems that have no direct relationship to NTP at all, making root-cause analysis during an incident significantly harder.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for NTP on UDP/123 and confirm whether it's reachable without authentication.
Test whether downstream systems trust and update their time from the NTP server by sending false time responses.
Check whether NTP authentication (symmetric key or NTS) is configured between clients and the server, since its absence is what makes spoofing viable.
Assess the blast radius of a successful time shift — Kerberos ticket validity, TLS certificate validity windows, and log-correlation all depend on accurate time.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers time-poisoning testing and affects systems that trust the NTP server.
Send specially crafted, spoofed-source NTP responses to a target client and observe whether it accepts and applies the false time.
Where successful, demonstrate a concrete downstream consequence — e.g., a Kerberos authentication failure due to clock skew, or a certificate appearing valid/expired outside its real window.

Cross-reference this finding with any Kerberos or certificate-validation findings elsewhere in the engagement, since a demonstrated downstream failure in either area substantially strengthens the impact narrative for NTP hardening.

examplePayloads.label: Query and confirm unauthenticated NTP is reachable
Spoof an NTP response to shift a client's clock

variants: NTP server exposed to the internet with no authentication.
Internal NTP server exposed to a broader network than intended.
mitigation: Enable NTP authentication (symmetric keys or Network Time Security/NTS) between clients and time servers so spoofed responses are rejected.
Restrict which hosts may query and be trusted by internal NTP servers, and don't expose them to the public internet unless specifically operating as a public time source.
Monitor for and alert on abrupt, large time-jumps, which are anomalous during normal operation.

NET-102.prerequisites: Network access to out-of-band management networks (IPMI, iLO, iDRAC, serial console servers). Default credentials or exploitation of weak authentication. Tools: standard management clients, Metasploit.
NET-102.whatItIs: A separate network specifically used for administering critical equipment (like remote console access) is supposed to be kept apart from the regular production network. When that separation isn't properly enforced, or login protection on it is weak, an attacker can get direct access to the management interfaces of critical infrastructure.
NET-102.rootCause: This management network is sometimes just assumed to be physically isolated or only reachable from restricted locations, without that assumption ever actually being verified with real network controls. It's often left on a flat, unsegmented network with minimal login protection.
NET-102.impact: Access to OOB management is equivalent to physical access to servers, allowing power control, console access, BIOS/firmware manipulation, or remote wipe of systems. Because OOB management interfaces typically operate below the OS layer, compromise here survives OS reinstalls and endpoint-security tooling entirely, making it one of the most persistent footholds an attacker can establish in the estate.
stepsToIdentify: Identify whether the out-of-band (OOB) management network (iLO/iDRAC/IPMI, console servers, OOB switch management VLAN) is reachable from the general production/user network rather than being physically or logically air-gapped.
Where reachable, enumerate which management interfaces are accessible and whether they enforce their own independent authentication.
Where an OOB interface is reachable, check its firmware version against known IPMI/iLO/iDRAC CVEs (e.g., the IPMI cipher-zero authentication bypass) in addition to testing default credentials.

Confirm whether the OOB network shares physical switch infrastructure with production, even if logically VLAN-separated, since misconfigured trunk ports are a common cause of 'unintentional' OOB reachability.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers the OOB network segment, since access here typically grants low-level control (power, console, firmware) over physical hosts.
From a production-network vantage point, attempt to reach and authenticate to an OOB management interface to confirm the segmentation failure is real, not just theoretical.
Document the specific path (VLAN, routing rule, or shared switch) that allows production traffic to reach the OOB segment, for the remediation writeup.
Where the IPMI cipher-zero bypass or a known firmware CVE is confirmed in addition to network reachability, treat this as a critical finding independent of whether default credentials also succeed.
Report the exact network path (switch, VLAN, or routing rule) that allowed production-to-OOB reachability, since this is the primary remediation target, more so than any single device's credentials.

examplePayloads.label: Test reachability of common OOB management ports from the production segment
Attempt authentication against a discovered OOB interface from the production segment
examplePayloads.command: curl -sk https://<oob-ip>/redfish/v1/  # or ssh <oob-ip> for IPMI/iDRAC/iLO consoles

variants: OOB network not firewalled from production, allowing pivot from a compromised production server to management.
Default or weak credentials on OOB management interfaces.
mitigation: Physically or logically air-gap the OOB management network from the production network — no routing path should exist between them.
Where a jump host is required to bridge to OOB for legitimate administration, place it under strict access control and MFA, and log every session.
Disable IPMI's cipher-zero authentication bypass and any default credentials on OOB management controllers as a standard hardening step.

NET-103.prerequisites: Network access to systems with PXE (Preboot Execution Environment) boot enabled. DHCP/TFTP server access or ability to intercept boot traffic. PXE attack tools (pxeexploit, metasploit).
NET-103.whatItIs: A network-boot feature lets computers with no hard drive load their operating system over the network at startup. Without any authentication, an attacker can intercept that boot process and swap in a malicious operating-system image, compromising the machine before it's even finished starting up.
NET-103.rootCause: This boot feature was designed for trusted internal networks with no built-in login requirement. Any device on the network can request and receive a boot image from any server offering one, with no check confirming the server or the image is actually legitimate.
NET-103.impact: Full system compromise achieved at the firmware/bootloader level, persisting across OS reinstalls and avoiding most detection mechanisms. A compromised boot image gives the attacker code execution before the operating system's own security controls (EDR, disk encryption, secure boot policy) have even loaded, making this one of the few network-based paths capable of bypassing endpoint defenses entirely.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether the network segment allows any DHCP client to receive PXE boot options (next-server, boot filename) without device authentication.
Attempt to request and download the network boot image served to legitimate clients.

Capture and inspect the legitimate boot image's contents (kernel, initrd, embedded configuration) to understand what sensitive data (credentials, keys) might already be embedded in it, independent of any rogue-server attack.
Check whether the PXE/TFTP service is reachable from network segments beyond the intended provisioning VLAN, which would allow the attack to be staged from a less-trusted vantage point than intended.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers PXE/network-boot testing on the segment.
Act as a rogue PXE/TFTP responder and confirm whether a booting client can be redirected to fetch a boot image from the tester's own server instead of the legitimate one.
Where successful, demonstrate that an attacker-supplied boot image (rather than a real payload) can be served, without actually deploying a malicious image against a production host.

Where embedded credentials or keys are found in the legitimate boot image itself, report this as a separate finding alongside the rogue-server risk, since it represents its own exposure even without an active attacker.
Report the specific network segments from which the PXE/TFTP service was reachable, to scope the remediation's segmentation requirement accurately.

examplePayloads.label: Stand up a rogue PXE/TFTP responder
Download the legitimate boot image from the real TFTP server for comparison

variants: Unauthenticated DHCP offering PXE boot with no signature verification of the bootloader or kernel.
TFTP accessible from a broader network than intended, allowing off-network PXE attacks.
mitigation: Segment PXE boot traffic to a dedicated provisioning VLAN, isolated from general client segments, and restrict which switch ports may participate.
Where supported, use secure boot / signed boot images (UEFI HTTPS Boot or signed PXE images) so a client validates the image's authenticity before executing it.
Disable PXE/network-boot options in device firmware for any host that has already been provisioned and doesn't require re-imaging on every boot.

NET-104.prerequisites: Network access to systems running VNC (Virtual Network Computing) on default ports (5900-5910). VNC client software. Tools: nmap (VNC discovery), VNC clients, custom connection scripts.
NET-104.whatItIs: A remote-desktop tool lets someone view and fully control another computer's screen, mouse, and keyboard over the network. A lot of these servers — especially older installs — are left with login completely disabled, or with a password that was set once during installation and never changed, meaning anyone who can reach the right network port gets full remote control with no login prompt at all.
NET-104.rootCause: The underlying protocol behind this tool supports a mode that skips login entirely, and several versions of the software ship with that as an easy default for use on a supposedly trusted local network. Combined with the fact that this is often set up quickly for one specific remote-support need and then forgotten about, servers end up reachable far more broadly than intended, with no password, a default one, or one chosen once for convenience and never changed.
NET-104.impact: An attacker who reaches an open VNC session has the same capability as someone physically sitting at the keyboard — they can read whatever is on screen (email, internal tools, credentials being typed by a legitimate user), exfiltrate files via drag-and-drop or a terminal, install malware or a persistent backdoor, and pivot into whatever internal systems that desktop already has access to (VPN clients, saved RDP/SSH sessions, password managers left unlocked). Because the session looks identical to a legitimate user interacting with the machine, it is also one of the harder access vectors to distinguish from normal administrative activity in logs unless VNC connections themselves are being monitored.
stepsToIdentify: Sweep the target range for the VNC port block with nmap -p5900-5910 --script vnc-info, which reports the RFB protocol version and, critically, which security types (None, VNC Authentication, TLS) the server offers without needing a password.

Where vnc-info reports security type 'None', confirm at the protocol level (not just inferred from the scan) by completing the RFB handshake with a client and observing whether a desktop appears without any password prompt.

Where VNC Authentication is offered, note that the challenge-response scheme uses DES-encoded fixed-length passwords capped at 8 characters, which is worth flagging as a legacy weakness independent of whether a specific password is guessable.

Check whether the connection can be wrapped in TLS or is tunneled over SSH (a common port-5900-only-on-localhost pattern); an unencrypted VNC session on an unswitched or wireless segment is also sniffable, which is a separate finding worth noting alongside authentication.

Where authentication is present, test a short list of common defaults appropriate to the discovered product (do not brute-force broadly without authorization) — see the 'try common default/weak VNC passwords' guidance for exact scope limits.
Cross-reference any VNC host also running RDP or SSH, since a VNC-exposed desktop with saved credentials for those services multiplies the pivot value of this single finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization covers interactive desktop access, since a successful connection here means full mouse/keyboard control of a live system, not just an information-disclosure check.
Connect with a standard VNC client (vncviewer or remmina) to the identified host:port; where security type None was confirmed, no further steps are needed to reach the desktop.

Where a password is required, attempt only the small set of vendor/product default credentials identified during discovery, respecting any account-lockout or rate-limit behavior observed, rather than an unbounded wordlist run against a live production host.

Once connected, take a screenshot and note the logged-in user/desktop context for the report, then avoid unnecessary interaction with open applications, unsaved documents, or anything that could alter the target's state.

Check for saved credentials, open password managers, or active sessions to other internal systems visible on the desktop, since this is usually the highest-value evidence of downstream impact — document what's visible rather than using it to pivot further unless that's explicitly in scope.
Disconnect cleanly and record the exact host, port, security type, and (if applicable) which default credential worked, since remediation will need the same specifics to fix the right server.

examplePayloads.label: Discover VNC services and reported security types
Confirm no-auth access at the protocol level
Attempt a short, authorized list of vendor-default passwords
examplePayloads.command: for p in password vncpass admin; do echo "trying: $p"; vncviewer -passwd <(echo $p) 10.20.30.50::5900; done

examplePayloads.label: Scoped credential check with a small, authorized list only
Metasploit VNC security-type scanner
Verify whether the session is TLS/SSH-wrapped or plaintext

variants: VNC with security type None, requiring no password at all — the most direct case, found via the RFB handshake itself rather than by guessing.
VNC Authentication in use but with a vendor default or organization-wide shared password, which functions the same as no authentication once the default is known.

Unencrypted VNC on a shared network segment, where the DES-based challenge-response and subsequent screen data can be captured and, in older implementations, recovered via known-plaintext weaknesses in the DES scheme.
VNC bound to a high, non-standard port under the assumption that obscurity is protection, discoverable with the same nmap sweep extended to a wider port range.
Multi-user/shared VNC configurations that allow simultaneous connections, letting an attacker observe a legitimate user's live session (including anything they type) without disconnecting them.
mitigation: Disable the 'None' security type outright in the VNC server configuration; require VNC Authentication or, preferably, a stronger scheme at minimum.
Prefer tunneling VNC over SSH or wrapping it in TLS rather than relying on the base RFB protocol's authentication alone, since the native password scheme is legacy and weak by modern standards.
Restrict VNC ports at the host firewall and network ACLs to a short allow-list of admin source IPs; VNC should never be reachable from the general user network or the internet.
Replace any installation-default or long-unrotated password with a strong, unique one, and track VNC credentials in the same rotation/rotation-on-departure process used for other privileged access.
Where remote desktop access is a genuine ongoing need, prefer a modern remote-access solution with MFA and centralized audit logging over bare VNC.
Log and alert on VNC connections, particularly from outside the expected admin IP range or outside business hours.
Inventory and periodically re-scan for VNC services, since these tend to be set up informally and forgotten rather than provisioned through a managed process.

NET-105.prerequisites: Network access to VoIP systems (SIP, RTP). VoIP protocol knowledge. Tools: Wireshark (SIP/RTP analysis), SIPvicious (SIP scanning), custom packet crafting (Scapy).
NET-105.whatItIs: Voice-call systems (VoIP) that transmit calls without encryption let anyone who can see that network traffic simply capture and listen in on the actual conversation.
NET-105.rootCause: Older or budget-conscious VoIP setups often skip encryption for simplicity, on the assumption that voice traffic would only ever travel over a trusted internal network. Encryption also adds some processing overhead that gets deprioritized.
NET-105.impact: Eavesdropping on phone calls leaks sensitive business or personal information discussed during calls. Beyond the individual call, systematic interception of SIP/RTP traffic across an organization can build a durable intelligence picture of internal relationships, deal negotiations, and sensitive discussions over time.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether SIP signaling and RTP media streams are transmitted in cleartext (no SRTP/TLS) on the voice VLAN.
From a position able to observe voice traffic (a compromised host on the same VLAN, or a mirrored switch port), capture a sample call setup and media stream.
Check whether SRTP (encrypted media) or TLS-protected SIP signaling (SIPS) is available as an option but simply not enforced, versus being entirely unsupported by the PBX/softphone deployment.
Determine the population of users/extensions affected — a single unencrypted trunk between sites has different risk than every desk phone on the LAN transmitting in cleartext.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes intercepting voice traffic, since this involves capturing potentially sensitive call content.
Capture SIP signaling and the corresponding RTP stream for a test call between two in-scope extensions.
Reconstruct the captured RTP stream into audio to demonstrate the real-world impact of the eavesdropping exposure.
Where SRTP/SIPS is available but not enforced, note this specifically in the finding since remediation may be a configuration change rather than requiring new infrastructure.
Securely delete the captured audio sample immediately after generating proof-of-concept evidence for the report, consistent with minimizing retention of intercepted sensitive communications.

examplePayloads.label: Capture SIP/RTP traffic on the voice VLAN
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -w voip_capture.pcap 'udp portrange 5060-5061 or udp portrange 10000-20000'

examplePayloads.label: Reconstruct captured RTP audio with Wireshark's VoIP analyzer
examplePayloads.command: wireshark -r voip_capture.pcap  # Telephony > VoIP Calls > select call > Play Streams

variants: Plaintext SIP/RTP allowing direct eavesdropping.
Encrypted SIP but plaintext RTP, leaking call content even if signaling is protected.
mitigation: Enable SRTP for media and TLS (SIPS) for signaling on all VoIP infrastructure, rather than relying on network segmentation alone.
Place voice traffic on a dedicated, properly access-controlled VLAN with port security to prevent unauthorized hosts from joining it.
Disable hub-like span/mirror ports and unmanaged switches on the voice network that could allow passive traffic capture.

NET-106.prerequisites: Access to wireless network infrastructure (guest SSID configuration). Wireless testing tools (WiFi analyzer, Wireshark with wireless capture, custom scripts).
NET-106.whatItIs: Guest WiFi networks are meant to keep visitors separate from the internal corporate network. If that separation isn't actually enforced at the network-equipment level, a guest can break out of their isolated network and reach internal systems just as easily as a real employee.
NET-106.rootCause: Properly isolating guest traffic requires specific firewall rules and network-segment settings to actually be configured on the WiFi equipment. If that setup is skipped, a guest device ends up with the same reach into the internal network as a legitimate employee's device.
NET-106.impact: Unauthenticated guests gain access to internal network resources, defeating the purpose of guest network segmentation. Guest network breakout is frequently the first step in a broader intrusion chain, since guest segments typically receive far less monitoring than the production network they end up bridging into.
stepsToIdentify: Connect to the guest wireless network and attempt to reach hosts on the internal/corporate network or other guest clients.
Test whether client-isolation (AP-enforced peer blocking) is actually enabled, not just nominally configured.

Test client isolation from multiple points within the guest network (not just a single client), since some AP implementations only enforce isolation between clients on the same radio/band, missing cross-band traffic.

Check whether guest DNS resolution is restricted to public resolvers only, or whether it can resolve and therefore route toward internal-only hostnames, which is itself an information-disclosure indicator of a segmentation gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers the guest wireless segment.
From the guest network, attempt to reach internal-only resources (internal DNS, intranet, printers) to confirm whether segmentation is enforced at the network layer, not just the SSID/branding layer.
Where client isolation is absent, attempt to reach another guest client directly to demonstrate the lateral-movement risk between guest devices.

Where reachability to internal-only resources is confirmed, attempt only a benign, low-impact interaction (e.g., a banner grab) sufficient to prove access, rather than pursuing deeper exploitation of the internal resource itself.
Report the specific internal destinations reachable from the guest network and the exact protocol/port that succeeded, to give the client a precise segmentation gap to close.

examplePayloads.label: Test reachability from guest Wi-Fi into internal ranges
Test peer-to-peer reachability between guest clients (client isolation check)

variants: Guest SSID DHCP on the same VLAN as corporate users, providing no isolation.
Firewall rules allowing guest-to-corporate access for common services (DNS, NTP).
mitigation: Enforce client isolation at the AP/controller level so guest devices cannot reach each other, and verify it functionally rather than trusting the configuration checkbox.
Place the guest SSID on a dedicated VLAN with a firewall policy that explicitly denies all routes to internal network ranges, rather than relying on Wi-Fi-layer separation alone.
Periodically re-test guest network segmentation after any network change, since routing/firewall rule changes elsewhere can silently reopen a path.

NET-107.prerequisites: Access to network infrastructure devices or ability to intercept network traffic during device provisioning. Knowledge of zero-touch provisioning protocols (Cisco ZTP, Juniper JUNOS, Arista ZTP). Custom scripts or Metasploit modules.
NET-107.whatItIs: New network devices (switches, routers) can automatically configure themselves by downloading their setup and firmware from a designated setup server the moment they're powered on. If that process isn't authenticated, an attacker can intercept it and push a malicious configuration or firmware onto the new device instead.
NET-107.rootCause: This auto-setup process works by trusting whatever server on the network claims to be the legitimate setup server, with no cryptographic way to actually verify that claim. An attacker on the same network can simply impersonate that server.
NET-107.impact: A device receives malicious configuration or firmware during provisioning, becoming compromised before even joining the network. Because ZTP-provisioned devices trust their bootstrap configuration completely, a single compromised provisioning event can be replicated automatically across every device that provisions through the same process, turning one weakness into a fleet-wide compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether a new device on the provisioning VLAN automatically trusts and executes configuration/firmware served by whatever host answers the ZTP discovery request first.
Check whether the ZTP process cryptographically verifies the provisioning server's identity or the downloaded configuration's integrity.

Determine whether the ZTP process pins to a specific, pre-registered provisioning-server identity (e.g., via a serial-number-to-server mapping at the vendor's cloud service) versus trusting the first responder on the local segment.

Check whether devices re-run ZTP on every boot or only on true factory-reset/first-boot, since ongoing re-trust on every restart significantly widens the attack window versus a one-time provisioning event.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers the provisioning VLAN/process.
Stand up a rogue ZTP/provisioning responder and confirm whether a device performing zero-touch provisioning will accept configuration from it instead of the legitimate provisioning server.
Where successful, demonstrate that arbitrary (non-malicious, lab-safe) configuration can be pushed to a freshly-provisioned device.
Where devices re-trust ZTP on every reboot, note this specifically, since it means the rogue-provisioning window recurs continuously rather than only during initial deployment.
Report which specific device models were confirmed to accept unauthenticated provisioning, since ZTP trust models frequently vary even within a single vendor's product line.

examplePayloads.label: Stand up a rogue DHCP/ZTP responder on the provisioning VLAN
Confirm the provisioned device applied the rogue configuration
examplePayloads.command: ssh admin@<newly-provisioned-device-ip> 'show running-config' # verify the config matches what the rogue server pushed

variants: ZTP over HTTP without TLS or signature verification of configuration/firmware.
DHCP option 66/67 pointing to an unauthenticated provisioning server.
mitigation: Require the ZTP process to cryptographically verify the provisioning server's identity (mutual TLS or a signed bootstrap certificate) before accepting any configuration.
Isolate the provisioning VLAN so that only the legitimate provisioning server and the new device being onboarded can communicate on it during the provisioning window.
Verify a cryptographic signature/hash on the downloaded configuration or firmware before the device applies it.

NET-108.prerequisites: External network perspective (internet-facing systems). Ability to send packets from arbitrary source IPs (requires some network control or ISP cooperation). Port scanning tools (nmap). Understanding of routing and BGP.
NET-108.whatItIs: A widely recommended best practice says networks should check that outgoing traffic actually has a source address that belongs to them, before letting it leave. Without this check, an attacker can send traffic with a completely fake source address — enabling large-scale attacks that use the organization's own network to flood someone else, appearing to come from a victim who had nothing to do with it.
NET-108.rootCause: This kind of outbound filtering has to be deliberately configured on the network's edge equipment — it isn't automatic. Without it, that equipment will forward any packet regardless of whether its claimed source address actually makes sense for where it came from, since normal routing has no built-in way to verify that.
NET-108.impact: The network can be used as a source or amplification point for DDoS attacks against external targets, and the organization could face legal liability for originating attack traffic. Beyond the immediate technical risk, being identified as a source of spoofed attack traffic can trigger upstream provider blacklisting, damaging the organization's own network reputation independent of any direct data loss.
stepsToIdentify: From a test host inside the network, attempt to send a packet with a forged source IP address that does not belong to the local subnet, and confirm whether the egress router permits it to leave the network.
Where an external vantage point is available (with authorization), send a packet spoofing the organization's own address space toward it and see if it arrives.

Where anti-spoofing is confirmed absent, check whether it is inconsistently applied — some organizations filter at the internet-facing edge but not between internal segments, leaving intra-organization spoofing still possible.

Cross-reference this finding against any amplification-protocol findings already identified (open NTP/Memcached/DNS resolvers), since egress spoofing is the specific enabler that turns those into effective attack tools.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes spoofed-source packet testing, since this is a prerequisite enabler for several other attacks (DNS/NTP amplification, cross-network attribution attacks).
Craft and send a single outbound packet with a source address outside the local subnet's legitimate range, and confirm via a monitoring host whether it was permitted to egress unfiltered.
Do not use this finding to actually launch a volumetric attack — a single confirmatory packet is sufficient evidence.

Where amplification-capable services were also found exposed elsewhere in the engagement, explicitly note in the report that this anti-spoofing gap is what would make those findings usable as an actual amplification attack, not just a standalone exposure.
Report the specific egress point(s) tested and confirmed unfiltered, distinguishing internet-facing from inter-segment spoofing if both were assessed.

examplePayloads.label: Send a single spoofed-source packet to test egress filtering
examplePayloads.command: sudo python3 -c "from scapy.all import *; send(IP(src='8.8.8.8', dst='<your-monitoring-host>')/ICMP())"

examplePayloads.label: Confirm via a second, independent monitoring host outside the local network
examplePayloads.command: # on the external monitoring host: tcpdump -i eth0 'src host 8.8.8.8' -c1

variants: No egress filtering on the network's edge, allowing any source IP in outbound packets.

Egress-only filtering gaps (this finding) are frequently paired with an equivalent ingress-filtering gap that permits obviously-spoofed inbound traffic (e.g., internal-address-space sources arriving from the internet) — both directions should be tested together.
mitigation: Implement BCP38/BCP84 ingress/egress source-address filtering at every network edge, dropping any outbound packet whose source address doesn't belong to the local address space.
Enable unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) on edge routers as a standard, low-overhead complement to explicit ACL-based filtering.
This single control meaningfully reduces the organization's ability to be used as a launch point for reflection/amplification attacks against third parties, independent of any other finding.

NET-109.prerequisites: Network access to Active Directory domain; ability to query Kerberos servers. Tools: impacket (GetNPUsers.py), Hashcat, Metasploit. Understanding of Kerberos AS-REP and pre-authentication.
NET-109.whatItIs: In Active Directory environments, a specific security step in the login process — one that normally requires proving you know the password before getting a ticket — can be turned off for individual accounts, usually for compatibility with older systems. When it's off, an attacker can request a login ticket for that account with no credentials at all, and the response they get back can be cracked offline to recover the actual password.
NET-109.rootCause: This security step is optional in the underlying login protocol, and some organizations turn it off for specific service accounts or old systems that need it. The assumption is usually that the account isn't reachable by an attacker — an assumption that falls apart the moment any part of the network gets compromised or becomes reachable to someone hostile.
NET-109.impact: Offline password cracking against service accounts or user accounts with pre-auth disabled, potentially compromising high-privilege accounts. Because AS-REP roasting requires no prior authentication or network position beyond a single unauthenticated request per account, it is one of the lowest-effort, highest-value techniques available to an attacker who has only obtained a list of valid usernames.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate domain user accounts and identify which have the 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' (UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH) flag set.
Request an AS-REP for each such account without providing a password and confirm the KDC returns an encrypted response.

Where multiple accounts have pre-authentication disabled, prioritize cracking attempts against service/admin-sounding account names first, since the value of a recovered credential scales with the account's privilege.

Cross-reference recovered account names against any password-policy information already gathered in the engagement, to set realistic expectations for offline cracking feasibility before committing significant compute time.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers Active Directory/Kerberos testing.
Request AS-REP responses for accounts with pre-authentication disabled, which the KDC will return without requiring any valid credential.
Attempt to crack the encrypted portion of the AS-REP offline to recover the account's plaintext password, then verify (do not further exploit) that it authenticates successfully.
Use a strong, curated wordlist plus rules (rather than raw brute-force) for the offline cracking attempt, given realistic engagement time constraints.

Where a password is recovered, verify it authenticates successfully via a single, minimal-impact login (e.g., an LDAP bind) rather than a broader interactive logon, and stop immediately once verified.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate and request AS-REP for pre-auth-disabled accounts
Crack the captured AS-REP hash offline

variants: Service accounts with pre-authentication disabled.
User accounts with weak passwords and pre-authentication disabled.
mitigation: Re-enable Kerberos pre-authentication for every account unless there's a specific, documented, and reviewed business reason not to.
Where pre-authentication genuinely cannot be re-enabled, enforce a very strong, long, unique password for that account, since offline cracking is the primary risk it creates.
Monitor for and alert on repeated AS-REQ requests for pre-auth-disabled accounts, which is a strong AS-REP-roasting attempt signal.

NET-110.prerequisites: Network access to LDAP directory services (typically TCP/389 unencrypted, TCP/636 TLS). LDAP query tools or custom scripts. Understanding of LDAP and Active Directory.
NET-110.whatItIs: Company directory servers (which store employee info, group memberships, and org structure) can be set up to let anyone connect and search that directory with no login at all — leaking internal organizational details that are genuinely useful to an attacker planning further attacks.
NET-110.rootCause: This anonymous access is sometimes turned on for operational convenience — like letting an email client look up someone's address without needing a login — without anyone realizing just how much internal information that ends up exposing.
NET-110.impact: Unauthenticated enumeration of users, groups, and organizational structure, aiding reconnaissance for social engineering, targeted phishing, or privilege escalation attacks. The information gathered from an anonymous LDAP bind — organizational structure, group memberships, and account naming conventions — routinely serves as the foundation for a subsequent, far more convincing spear-phishing or password-spraying campaign.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt an anonymous (unauthenticated) bind against the directory server and confirm whether it succeeds.
Where successful, enumerate what data is queryable anonymously — user objects, group memberships, and any attributes containing sensitive information.
Where anonymous bind succeeds, specifically check whether it exposes password-related attributes (pwdLastSet, userAccountControl flags) that reveal which accounts have weak or non-expiring passwords.
Test whether anonymous bind also permits enumeration of privileged/administrative groups, since this materially increases the finding's severity beyond generic user enumeration.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers directory service testing.
Perform an anonymous LDAP bind and enumerate the accessible directory tree without providing any credential.
Extract a sample of user account names and any sensitive attributes exposed, to demonstrate concrete impact (e.g., username enumeration feeding into a later password-spray attack).

Where privileged-group membership is enumerable, flag this specifically as high-value reconnaissance data and note it in the report as a direct input to a targeted, rather than generic, follow-on attack.
Limit the extracted sample to what is needed to prove the finding — avoid a full directory dump even though anonymous bind may technically permit one.

examplePayloads.label: Test and enumerate via anonymous LDAP bind
Attempt an anonymous bind and dump the full base DN tree for review

variants: Anonymous bind allowed with full directory search capability.
Anonymous bind allowed but restricted to specific attributes (less severe but still a leak).
mitigation: Disable anonymous LDAP binds entirely, requiring authenticated access even for basic directory queries.

Where a specific legitimate use case requires anonymous read access (e.g., an unauthenticated mail client address-book lookup), restrict it to only the specific attributes genuinely required, not the full directory tree.
Audit directory ACLs to ensure sensitive attributes (password hashes, security-relevant flags) are never exposed even to authenticated low-privilege accounts, as defense in depth.

NET-111.prerequisites: Network access to systems using NetBIOS (UDP/137) or LLMNR (UDP/5355). Tools: Responder, Wireshark, custom packet crafting (Scapy). Understanding of LLMNR/NetBIOS protocols.
NET-111.whatItIs: Windows networks have backup ways for computers to find each other by name when normal DNS lookup fails. An attacker on the network can jump in and answer one of these backup lookups before the real answer arrives, claiming to be whatever computer was being searched for — redirecting that traffic to themselves and potentially capturing login credentials in the process.
NET-111.rootCause: These backup name-lookup methods have no way to verify who's answering, and they just accept whichever answer arrives first. They're commonly turned on by default on Windows networks specifically as a fallback when normal DNS doesn't work.
NET-111.impact: Man-in-the-middle attacks on network traffic, particularly for SMB shares and other services that rely on hostname resolution. Combined with an NTLM relay, this can escalate to domain compromise. Because this technique captures usable NTLM hashes without any prior foothold beyond local network access, it remains one of the most reliable initial-access and lateral-movement primitives observed in real internal penetration tests and ransomware intrusions alike.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether LLMNR and NetBIOS Name Service are enabled on client hosts (both are enabled by default on Windows) and whether the network allows broadcast/multicast name-resolution traffic.
Monitor for LLMNR/NBT-NS broadcast queries generated by normal client activity (e.g., a mistyped share name) that a poisoning tool could respond to.

Determine the proportion of hosts on the segment with LLMNR/NBT-NS still enabled by default, since remediation guidance and reported severity should reflect the realistic blast radius, not just theoretical exposure.

Where possible, correlate captured hashes to specific privileged accounts (service accounts, admins) versus standard users, since cracked privileged credentials have materially higher downstream impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes credential-capture testing via name-resolution poisoning.
Run a poisoning tool to respond to LLMNR/NBT-NS broadcast queries, and capture the resulting NTLM challenge/response when a client attempts to authenticate to the tester's host.
Attempt to crack the captured NTLMv2 hash offline to recover a plaintext password, demonstrating full impact without further using the credential.

Limit the poisoning window to the minimum time needed to capture a representative sample of hashes, rather than running the attack for the full engagement duration, to limit disruption to normal name-resolution traffic.
Where NTLM relay (rather than offline cracking) is also in scope, note this as a related, higher-impact escalation path but treat it as a distinct finding requiring its own explicit authorization.

examplePayloads.label: Poison LLMNR/NBT-NS and capture NTLM hashes with Responder
Crack a captured NTLMv2 hash offline

variants: LLMNR/NBT-NS enabled on the network with no segmentation or monitoring.
NTLM relay-capable after successful LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning.
mitigation: Disable LLMNR (via Group Policy) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) on all clients, relying solely on properly-configured DNS for name resolution.
Where legacy application compatibility genuinely requires NBT-NS, restrict it to specific network segments and monitor for poisoning-tool signatures.
Enforce SMB signing so that even a captured NTLM relay attempt cannot be used for a relay-based attack, as a complementary control.

NET-112.prerequisites: HTTPS/TLS access to servers supporting DHE (Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) with weak key sizes (512-bit or 1024-bit). TLS analysis tools (testssl.sh). Significant computational resources for key factorization.
NET-112.whatItIs: This is an attack against how secure connections agree on an encryption key. By tricking both sides into using an old, deliberately weak version of that key-agreement process, an attacker can break the resulting weak key and use it to decrypt the entire connection. Cracking the weak key takes significant upfront computing effort, but once that work is done for a commonly-used setup, it can be reused against anyone else using the same one.
NET-112.rootCause: This weak, export-grade version of the key-agreement process was originally required by old export regulations. Even though those regulations have long since been lifted, many servers kept supporting this weak option anyway, just for backward compatibility.
NET-112.impact: Successful Logjam attack allows decryption of TLS traffic using the downgraded export-grade Diffie-Hellman key. Because Logjam requires the attacker to complete a costly one-time precomputation against a specific, widely-reused prime before real-time downgrade attacks become practical, its risk is concentrated on services that reuse a small number of well-known default DH groups rather than generating unique parameters.
stepsToIdentify: Test the server for support of export-grade Diffie-Hellman ciphers using testssl.sh or openssl s_client.
Identify the DH group size negotiated for standard (non-export) ciphers, since even non-export DH below 2048 bits carries meaningful risk against well-resourced attackers.
Check whether the server reuses the same DH parameters across many connections, which increases the value of precomputing an attack against that specific group.

Determine whether the server's DH parameters match the small set of common, precomputable 512-bit or 1024-bit export-grade groups specifically targeted by the original Logjam research team's precomputation.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers TLS downgrade-attack testing.
Attempt to negotiate an export-grade DHE cipher suite and observe whether the server accepts it.

Where accepted, document the effective key strength offered and reference the known precomputation-based attack against common export-grade DH groups, without needing to independently reproduce the full academic attack.
Report the specific DH group size and whether it matches a known precomputed target, recommending unique, sufficiently large parameters or migration to ECDHE as the fix.

examplePayloads.label: Test for Logjam / export-grade DHE support
Enumerate negotiated DH group size directly

variants: Export-grade Diffie-Hellman ciphers enabled on TLS services.

A closely related finding is a DHE key-exchange server that supports export-grade groups only under specific legacy-client-negotiated conditions, meaning a scan against default client behavior alone can miss the exposure that a deliberately downgraded client handshake reveals.
mitigation: Disable all export-grade cipher suites entirely on the server.
Use a Diffie-Hellman group of at least 2048 bits (or prefer ECDHE, which isn't subject to the same precomputation risk at equivalent classical security levels).
Avoid reusing default/well-known DH groups across many servers; generate unique, sufficiently large parameters where DHE is used at all.

NET-113.prerequisites: Access to TLS 1.2 connections using CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode with specific TLS versions. Ability to observe response timing or side-channel information. Computational resources for statistical analysis.
NET-113.whatItIs: This is a subtle attack against how some encrypted connections process data: the server takes a tiny bit longer or shorter to respond depending on whether encrypted data was formatted correctly. That tiny timing difference is small enough to seem irrelevant, but an attacker who measures it carefully, again and again, can use it to slowly figure out the real content byte by byte.
NET-113.rootCause: The order in which a specific older encryption setup checks data integrity versus decrypting it creates small, measurable timing differences depending on where exactly something goes wrong. This was a known flaw in an older way of combining encryption steps — one that's been fixed in the newest version of TLS, which requires a different approach specifically designed to avoid this class of problem entirely.
NET-113.impact: Partial plaintext recovery through timing analysis of many crafted TLS records. While Lucky13 requires precise timing measurement and is difficult to exploit reliably outside a lab environment, its presence indicates the server still supports legacy CBC ciphersuites that carry cumulative cryptographic risk beyond this specific attack.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the server supports CBC-mode TLS cipher suites and test for the presence of the padding-oracle timing side-channel using testssl.sh's Lucky13 check.
Assess whether the TLS library/version in use has already been patched for the constant-time MAC verification fix, since most modern stacks have.

Cross-reference the finding against the broader TLS configuration to determine whether CBC suites are actually preferred/selected in practice, or merely present in the offered list behind stronger AEAD ciphers.

Check the specific TLS library and version in use against the CVE database, since most mainstream libraries patched the underlying timing side-channel years ago even while leaving the CBC suite itself enabled.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers TLS side-channel timing analysis.
Run testssl.sh's Lucky13 module or an equivalent timing-oracle probe against the CBC cipher suites offered.

Given how difficult reliable exploitation is in practice (requiring extremely precise timing measurement over many requests), the objective in a standard engagement is to confirm exposure to the theoretical risk, not to fully reproduce plaintext recovery.

Where the library is confirmed patched against the timing side-channel, downgrade the finding's practical severity in the report accordingly, while still recommending CBC suite removal as defense-in-depth.
Report testssl.sh's raw output alongside the interpreted risk level, so the client's own team can independently verify the finding without re-running the scan.

examplePayloads.label: Test for Lucky13 exposure via testssl.sh
Cross-check the specific TLS library/version against the known Lucky13-patched release list

variants: TLS 1.0/1.1 with CBC ciphers, vulnerable to Lucky13.

The equivalent side-channel risk exists in some non-TLS protocols implementing their own CBC-mode MAC-then-encrypt scheme (certain VPN client implementations, historically), making this a protocol-design pattern to watch for beyond TLS specifically.
mitigation: Prioritize AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) over CBC-mode suites, which removes the underlying padding-oracle risk entirely rather than just patching around it.
Ensure the TLS library in use is a current, patched version, since the constant-time MAC-check fix has been standard in modern TLS stacks for years.
Where CBC suites must remain available for legacy client compatibility, confirm the specific implementation has the timing-safe padding-check fix applied.

NET-114.prerequisites: Network access to Ethernet switches; ability to generate substantial ARP traffic. Tools: Scapy, custom scripts, or tools like Yersinia. Understanding of MAC address tables (CAM tables).
NET-114.whatItIs: Network switches keep a table mapping which device (by its network address) is connected to which physical port, so they know exactly where to send traffic. If an attacker floods the switch with thousands of fake addresses, that table fills up completely — and once it's full, the switch has no choice but to start broadcasting traffic to every port at once, turning it into something anyone nearby can eavesdrop on.
NET-114.rootCause: This table only has limited space, and switches don't limit how fast new addresses can be added to it by default. An attacker can flood it with enough fake addresses to overflow it entirely. Since switches prioritize keeping traffic flowing over keeping it private, most of them fall back to broadcasting everything once the table's full, rather than simply dropping unrecognized traffic — quietly trading privacy for uptime.
NET-114.impact: Network sniffing of all traffic on the segment once the CAM is full, allowing eavesdropping on plaintext protocols and password capture. Because MAC flooding forces the switch into an insecure fail-open state rather than failing closed, an attacker can achieve broad plaintext visibility on a switched network without needing to compromise any individual host.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether the target switch enforces port security / MAC-address-limiting on access ports.

In a lab/authorized segment, flood the switch's CAM table with forged MAC addresses and observe whether the switch fails open (broadcasting all traffic, effectively acting as a hub) once the table fills.
Establish the switch's CAM table size (from vendor documentation or SNMP) beforehand to calculate how many forged MAC addresses are actually required, minimizing unnecessary traffic during the test.
After the test, verify the switch recovers to normal (learning-mode) behavior once forged entries age out, to confirm no lasting operational impact was introduced.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes CAM-table-exhaustion testing, since this can degrade switch performance for other users on the segment during the test.
Flood the switch with a large number of forged source MAC addresses to fill its CAM table.
Once the table is full, monitor traffic on the tester's own port to confirm whether the switch is now flooding frames intended for other hosts, and capture a sample as proof.

Immediately stop generating forged MAC traffic once fail-open behavior is confirmed and captured, rather than sustaining the flood, to minimize the window of degraded performance for other users on the segment.

Report the specific number of MAC addresses required to exhaust the table and the observed switch behavior (fail-open vs. fail-closed) so remediation testing can be verified against the same baseline.

examplePayloads.label: Flood the switch's CAM table with forged MACs
Confirm resulting broadcast-like behavior by capturing traffic

variants: Unprotected switch with no MAC table size limits or aging mechanisms.

A related but distinct variant is ARP table (rather than CAM table) exhaustion on the connected hosts themselves, which can produce a similar denial-of-service effect through a different resource-exhaustion mechanism.
mitigation: Enable port security on all access ports, limiting the number of learned MAC addresses per port to a small, expected number (typically 1-2).
Configure port security violation behavior to shut down or restrict the port rather than failing open to broadcast-all behavior.
Monitor switch CAM table utilization and alert on rapid, abnormal growth as an early indicator of an in-progress flooding attempt.

NET-115.prerequisites: Network access to public NTP servers; ability to send UDP packets with spoofed source IPs. Tools: Scapy, custom scripts, or ntpflood tools.
NET-115.whatItIs: An old diagnostic feature on time-sync servers lets anyone ask for a list of recently connected clients — and the response can be much bigger than the request. An attacker can abuse an exposed server with this feature enabled to flood a victim with a disproportionately large amount of traffic, and can do this across many such servers at once for an even bigger attack.
NET-115.rootCause: This diagnostic feature was built for server maintenance and used to be turned on by default in older versions of the time-sync software. It was never meant to be a core, everyday feature — but it turns a tiny request into a large response, which is exactly what makes it useful for this kind of attack.
NET-115.impact: Used as an amplification vector in volumetric DDoS attacks against external targets. Beyond the direct amplification impact on the external victim, an organization whose infrastructure is abused this way can face upstream provider action against its own connectivity for originating attack traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Identify NTP servers in scope supporting the legacy monlist command, which returns a large response relative to the tiny request that triggers it.
Calculate the amplification ratio for a single, non-spoofed monlist query against the discovered server.

Where monlist is disabled, additionally check for other amplification-capable NTP query types (e.g., certain mode-6/7 control queries) that some implementations still expose even post-monlist-hardening.
Check the NTP daemon's version and vendor advisories to determine whether the specific amplification vector observed has a known CVE and patch available.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the rules of engagement explicitly authorize reflection/amplification testing, following the same authorized-destination-only precautions as other amplification test cases — never spoof a real third-party address.
Send a single, non-spoofed monlist query and measure the resulting response size against the query size to calculate the realized amplification ratio.
Do not send spoofed-source or repeated/looped queries — a single confirmatory measurement is sufficient evidence of exposure.

Where the amplification ratio is calculated, report it alongside the specific query type used, since remediation guidance differs between disabling monlist specifically versus broader mode-6/7 restriction.
Cross-reference this finding with the BCP38/anti-spoofing finding elsewhere in the engagement, since both conditions together are what enable a real-world amplification attack, not either alone.

examplePayloads.label: Test for monlist support and measure amplification ratio
Automated scan for monlist-vulnerable NTP servers across a range

variants: Exposed NTP with monlist enabled, usable for DDoS amplification.

A related, lower-severity NTP amplification variant uses standard time-query responses (rather than monlist) which offer a smaller but still non-trivial amplification factor, and remains exploitable even after monlist has been disabled.
mitigation: Disable the monlist command entirely (disable monitor in ntp.conf), which has no legitimate modern use case and exists purely as a legacy debugging feature.
Upgrade to a current NTP daemon version (ntpd 4.2.8p3+ or chrony), which disables monlist by default.
Restrict NTP query access to expected client ranges rather than leaving it open to the entire internet.

NET-116.prerequisites: Network access to routing infrastructure; ability to send routing protocol packets (OSPF, EIGRP). Tools: Scapy, Quagga, custom routing protocol implementations. Understanding of OSPF/EIGRP protocols.
NET-116.whatItIs: Protocols that let routers inside a network automatically share information about the best paths to reach different destinations can, without authentication, let an attacker on that network inject fake routing information — redirecting traffic through a router the attacker controls.
NET-116.rootCause: Both of these protocols were designed for a trusted, internal network. Authentication is available for both, but it has to be deliberately turned on, and a lot of older setups just never did. Since these protocols trust any device on the segment that can successfully connect and start exchanging routes, whether a route gets accepted comes down purely to network reachability, not any verified identity.
NET-116.impact: Traffic destined for internal or external networks is redirected through the attacker's machine, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on a large scale. Because routing-protocol trust operates below the application layer, a successful attack here can silently redirect traffic for every downstream network that relies on the falsified route, without any of the affected endpoints showing signs of compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether OSPF/EIGRP routing-protocol authentication (MD5 or better) is enabled between routers on the segment.
Where a test host can reach a routed segment directly, check whether it can form an adjacency with a legitimate router without providing any authentication.

Determine whether the routing protocol is running in a mode susceptible to plaintext or no authentication versus MD5 (still crackable but at least present) or the stronger HMAC-SHA options available in modern implementations.

Check whether route redistribution/filtering (route maps, prefix lists) would have limited the blast radius of an injected route even if the adjacency itself succeeded, as a secondary defense-in-depth check.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes routing-protocol-level testing, since a successful attack can affect production traffic routing network-wide.
Attempt to establish a rogue OSPF/EIGRP adjacency with a legitimate router from an unauthorized host on the segment.
Where successful, inject a single low-impact test route (not a route affecting production traffic) to confirm the adjacency is genuinely trusted, then immediately withdraw it.

Where authentication is present but using a weak algorithm (plaintext or MD5), note this as a distinct, lower-severity finding from a complete absence of authentication, since the remediation and urgency differ.
Immediately withdraw any test route and confirm via a second observation that normal routing has been restored before concluding the test.

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to form a rogue OSPF adjacency and inject routes
examplePayloads.command: sudo loki  # select OSPF module, attempt neighbor establishment on the target segment

examplePayloads.label: Passively observe existing OSPF/EIGRP hello packets to confirm authentication mode before attempting adjacency
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'proto ospf or ip proto 88' -c 10

variants: No OSPF/EIGRP authentication, allowing any source to inject routing updates.
Weak MD5-based authentication, which can be cracked.
mitigation: Enable cryptographic authentication (MD5, or preferably SHA-based where supported) for all OSPF/EIGRP adjacencies, rejecting any neighbor that cannot authenticate.
Restrict which interfaces participate in the routing protocol — disable it entirely on access-layer/user-facing ports where no legitimate router should ever be attached.
Monitor for unexpected new adjacencies or routing-table changes as an operational alerting signal.

NET-117.prerequisites: Network access to Elasticsearch service (TCP/9200 default). No authentication required for exploitation of default configurations. HTTP client tools (curl, browser). Understanding of Elasticsearch REST API.
NET-117.whatItIs: A widely-used search and analytics tool, often used to store and search through logs, is exposed with no login required. Anyone who can reach it can search, read, and even change all the stored data — which often includes logs containing credentials, personal information, and security event records.
NET-117.rootCause: This tool was designed assuming internal-only use, and it has no login required by default. It frequently ends up reachable from the internet or a much broader network than intended, based on an assumption that its technical complexity alone would discourage attackers — which it doesn't.
