Enumerate offered cipher suites and confirm 3DES/64-bit block cipher support.

Document exposure against the established academic research; the attack requires an impractically large volume of same-key traffic (hundreds of GB) to be realistic, so a standard engagement confirms the exposure rather than reproducing full plaintext recovery.
Where a genuinely long-lived, high-throughput connection using 3DES is identified, flag it specifically as the realistic instance of this otherwise largely theoretical attack.

Report a clear recommendation to remove 3DES/64-bit block ciphers entirely, since modern AEAD ciphers are universally preferable and there's no compatibility case that requires retaining them on current clients.

examplePayloads.label: Test for Sweet32 (64-bit block cipher support)
Estimate realistic data-volume exposure by checking session/connection duration limits on the specific service

variants: Sweet32 against TLS versus against IPsec/OpenVPN configurations still using 3DES or Blowfish for the data channel.
Combination with automated background traffic generation (e.g., via malicious JavaScript in a MITM'd session) to accelerate reaching the birthday bound.
Legacy internal services (older VPN concentrators, embedded appliances) where 3DES remains the only supported cipher due to hardware limitations.
3DES retained specifically for FIPS-compliance reasons in some environments, requiring careful cipher suite selection to remain both compliant and hardened.
mitigation: Remove 3DES and other 64-bit block cipher suites from the TLS configuration entirely, in favor of AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Ensure any long-lived encrypted tunnel (site-to-site VPN, persistent connections) is rekeyed well before the volume threshold where birthday-bound attacks become practical.
Re-scan periodically, since legacy-compatibility settings on VPN concentrators in particular are a common place 3DES support lingers.

NET-138.prerequisites: Network reachability to the target sufficient to send TCP SYN probes and observe SYN-ACK responses; no credentials required.
NET-138.whatItIs: Some older or embedded network devices generate the starting number used to track a network connection using a predictable pattern (like a simple counter) instead of something genuinely random. That means an attacker who isn't even positioned to see the real traffic can still guess that number and inject or hijack the connection blind.
NET-138.rootCause: The original guidance for generating this starting number was weak by today's standards. While most modern systems moved to strong, effectively unguessable generation long ago, some embedded devices, older network equipment, and custom software still use overly simple, predictable methods — making this number something an attacker can guess instead of something genuinely unpredictable.
NET-138.impact: Predictable TCP sequence numbers allow an attacker to forge TCP packets and hijack TCP connections without seeing traffic, enabling injection of commands or data. Because this technique requires no visibility into the target's traffic to succeed, it remains viable even against a victim on a fully switched, non-broadcast network, distinguishing it from most other spoofing-class attacks.
stepsToIdentify: Sample a target host's initial sequence numbers (ISNs) across multiple connection attempts and assess whether they follow a predictable pattern rather than being cryptographically random.
Cross-reference the target OS/network-stack version against known historically-weak ISN generation implementations.

Where a predictable pattern is found, assess the realistic blast radius by identifying what trust relationship (e.g., IP-based authentication, a legacy rlogin/rsh-style service) could actually be exploited via successful sequence prediction.
Check whether the host is embedded/IoT-class equipment with a lightweight or outdated TCP/IP stack, since these remain the most common source of genuinely predictable ISN generation today.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers TCP-spoofing testing, since this technique attempts to inject data into a connection the tester doesn't directly control.
Sample a sequence of ISNs from the target and analyze them for predictability (nmap's ISN-sequenceability classification is a fast first check).
Where a genuinely predictable pattern is found on a legacy/embedded stack, this is now a rare finding on modern OSes — document the specific implementation and pattern observed.
Where an exploitable IP-based trust relationship is also present, note this combination specifically since sequence prediction alone has limited value without a downstream trust mechanism to abuse.
Report the specific host/stack confirmed to exhibit predictable ISNs, since this is now a rare, high-signal finding on modern infrastructure and often indicates outdated embedded firmware.

examplePayloads.label: Assess TCP ISN predictability via nmap
Compare ISN samples against a modern OS baseline for contrast

variants: ISN prediction combined with predictable IP ID sequence generation on the same weak stack, compounding spoofing feasibility.
Blind spoofing against IP-based trust relationships (legacy rlogin/rsh, certain firewall allow-rules) versus blind injection into an already-established third-party session.
Modern OS TCP stacks are essentially immune to this class of attack; the finding is almost exclusively relevant to embedded/IoT/legacy appliance TCP implementations.
Combination with source routing or other legacy IP options (where still enabled) to further ease off-path exploitation.
mitigation: Ensure the network stack in use generates cryptographically random initial sequence numbers, which is the default on virtually all current mainstream operating systems.

For any legacy/embedded device found with predictable ISN generation, prioritize a firmware update or replacement, since this is a foundational networking weakness rather than an application-layer one.

Layer TLS or IPsec on top of any connection where TCP-level spoofing risk is a genuine concern, since encryption/authentication at a higher layer neutralizes the practical impact even if ISN prediction were possible.

NET-139.prerequisites: Network reachability to UDP/69 on the target; no authentication required. Filename knowledge or a wordlist improves practical enumeration success.
NET-139.whatItIs: A simple file-transfer protocol, commonly used for network device firmware and configuration backups, has no login requirement of any kind. Where it's reachable beyond the specific management network it's meant for, anyone can read or write files on it with zero authentication.
NET-139.rootCause: This protocol was designed decades ago for simplicity in constrained network-boot scenarios, and it has no login or access-control system built in at all. Whether it's actually protected depends entirely on how carefully its file access and network reachability were set up — and misconfigurations routinely leave it exposed far beyond its intended, narrow use case.
NET-139.impact: TFTP is unauthenticated and can leak system files or configuration if exposed, or allow push of malicious files if write access is available. Because TFTP has no built-in access logging in most implementations, unauthorized read or write access frequently goes unnoticed until the resulting device misconfiguration or malicious firmware causes a visible operational failure.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for TFTP on UDP/69 and attempt to list or retrieve files without any credential, since TFTP has no authentication mechanism at all.

Where a directory listing isn't directly supported by the protocol, attempt common configuration-file names used by network devices (running-config, startup-config) that are frequently served via TFTP for backup purposes.

Where a configuration file is retrieved, check specifically for embedded enable-secret/SNMP-community hashes and note their crackability, since network-device configuration exports typically use weak/reversible obfuscation, not strong hashing.

Determine whether the TFTP service also accepts writes (not just reads), since this would allow an attacker to push a malicious configuration back to a device that later pulls it, not just exfiltrate the existing one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers TFTP access.
Attempt to retrieve common device configuration filenames from the exposed TFTP server.
Where a configuration file is retrieved, review it (without further action) for embedded credentials or SNMP community strings, which is the typical high-impact outcome of this finding.
Where write access is confirmed, do not actually upload any file to a production path — a single confirmatory write to a clearly-scoped test filename is sufficient evidence.

Report the specific credential material (community strings, enable-secret hashes) found in the retrieved configuration, since this often chains directly into the SNMP-community-string finding elsewhere in the engagement.

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to retrieve a common device config filename via TFTP
Scan for TFTP exposure across a range

variants: TFTP used for PXE network boot of workstations/servers, where a malicious boot image could compromise any device that PXE-boots from the exposed server.
TFTP exposed on the same segment as SNMP with write access, compounding the risk of a combined configuration-exfiltration-and-modification attack chain.
Vendor-specific firmware TFTP servers left reachable post-deployment rather than only during the initial device provisioning window.
TFTP root directory misconfiguration exposing files well beyond the intended configuration/firmware directory, including unrelated sensitive data on the host.
mitigation: Restrict TFTP access via ACL to only the specific management hosts that legitimately need it (e.g., a config-backup server).
Where feasible, replace TFTP with SCP/SFTP for configuration backup/restore workflows, since TFTP has no authentication or encryption at all.
Never store configuration files containing live credentials on a TFTP server without immediately rotating any credential that could plausibly have been exposed this way already.

NET-140.prerequisites: Network reachability to TCP/23 on the target; for credential capture demonstration specifically, a network position able to observe the relevant traffic or explicit coordination for a live authentication capture.
NET-140.whatItIs: An old remote-access protocol sends everything — including login credentials — in plain, readable text with zero encryption. Where it's still used to manage a device or server, anyone who can see that traffic, or simply connect to it directly, can capture credentials or interact with the exposed admin interface themselves.
NET-140.rootCause: This old protocol predates modern encrypted remote-access tools and stays enabled on a lot of network equipment, older systems, and embedded devices — either as an old leftover default, or for compatibility with older management tools — simply because nobody's explicitly turned it off in favor of a modern, encrypted alternative.
NET-140.impact: Telnet transmits all credentials and traffic in plaintext, allowing complete credential capture and session hijacking. Because Telnet sessions are often used for full device administration, credential capture here typically grants the same privilege level as the legitimate administrator, not merely read access to network traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for Telnet on TCP/23 across in-scope hosts and network devices.
Where reachable, attempt to capture a legitimate login and confirm credentials are visible in cleartext.

Where a legitimate session cannot be observed, attempt the tester's own authorized login over Telnet and confirm the credential is visible in the capture, as sufficient proof without needing to intercept a real user's session.

Check whether Telnet is the only management path, or whether SSH is also available but Telnet was simply left enabled alongside it, since the remediation (disable Telnet) is materially simpler in the latter case.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers cleartext-protocol interception testing.
Capture a Telnet session (the tester's own authorized login, or passively where a legitimate session can be observed) and confirm the credential is visible in plaintext in the capture.
Where SSH is confirmed available as an alternative, note this specifically in the report since it means remediation is a straightforward service-disable rather than requiring new infrastructure.

Report the specific hosts/devices with Telnet enabled and, where captured, confirm the credential exposure without recording or retaining the actual plaintext password beyond what's needed for the proof-of-concept screenshot.
Report a general recommendation to disable Telnet fleet-wide as part of routine hardening, given the protocol carries no legitimate secure use case on a modern network.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for Telnet exposure
Capture a Telnet session to confirm cleartext credentials

variants: Telnet enabled on network infrastructure (routers/switches) versus on general-purpose servers or embedded/IoT devices, each with different blast-radius implications.
Telnet exposed to the internet directly versus only reachable from an internal management segment.
Telnet used for a limited, non-administrative service banner (e.g., some older printers) with lower but still non-trivial information-disclosure impact.
Cleartext credential capture combined with credential reuse against SSH or web-based management interfaces on the same or other devices.
mitigation: Disable Telnet entirely on every device, replacing it with SSH for all administrative access.
Where a legacy device genuinely cannot support SSH, isolate it on a dedicated management segment with no route from general network access.
Audit device inventories periodically for Telnet re-enablement, since factory resets or firmware updates can silently restore it as a default.

NET-141.prerequisites: Network reachability to the target TLS service; no credentials required for detection. Full MITM exploitation requires a suitable network position relative to a victim client.
NET-141.whatItIs: A certificate issued by an internal, self-signed, or otherwise untrusted authority — one that's not recognized by standard browsers and tools — causes a security warning every time someone connects. Where people get used to just clicking through these warnings routinely, the whole protection that certificate checking is meant to provide against interception attacks gets seriously weakened, not just for this one service but as a habit across the whole organization.
NET-141.rootCause: The authority that issued this certificate either isn't recognized by standard browsers and operating systems at all (a private, internal authority, or a self-signed certificate), or the server isn't correctly sending all the pieces needed to build a complete chain of trust back to a recognized authority — causing the check to fail even in cases where it technically could have succeeded.
NET-141.impact: If a self-signed or internally-generated CA certificate is trusted by clients without proper validation, attackers can create valid-appearing certificates for any domain. Because certificate trust decisions cascade — a browser or client that trusts the rogue CA will silently trust every certificate it subsequently issues — a single successful forgery can be leveraged repeatedly across many future connections without re-exploitation.
stepsToIdentify: Inspect the TLS certificate chain presented by in-scope services and confirm whether the issuing CA is a publicly-trusted root or an internal/private CA not distributed to client trust stores.
Check for self-signed certificates presented on any service expected to be trusted without manual client-side exceptions.

Where an internal/private CA is found trusted by client machines, check how that trust was established (Group Policy-pushed root certificate vs. manual, ad-hoc installation) to assess whether it's a managed, intentional control or an uncontrolled exception.

Check whether the same untrusted/self-signed certificate is reused across multiple, unrelated services, since this indicates a systemic 'click-through the warning' culture rather than an isolated one-off exception.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers certificate-trust-chain review.
Retrieve and inspect the full certificate chain for each in-scope TLS endpoint, noting the issuing CA and whether it resolves to a trust anchor present in standard client trust stores.

Where clients are found to have been configured to blanket-trust an untrusted/self-signed CA, assess whether this materially weakens their ability to detect an unrelated MITM attempt using a different fraudulent certificate.

Where a managed internal CA is confirmed (Group Policy-distributed), downgrade the practical severity of this finding significantly, since it represents an intentional, controlled trust decision rather than an uncontrolled exception.

Report specifically on any ad-hoc or self-signed certificate trust exceptions found, since these are the actual security-relevant instances of this finding, distinct from properly-managed internal PKI.

examplePayloads.label: Retrieve and inspect the full certificate chain
Check whether the untrusted CA's root is present in the organization's MDM-managed trust store
examplePayloads.command: security find-certificate -a -c "<ca-common-name>" /Library/Keychains/System.keychain  # macOS example; use certutil -store Root on Windows

variants: Fully self-signed certificate with no CA chain at all versus a private/internal CA not distributed to relevant client trust stores.
Missing intermediate certificate causing chain validation failure despite a legitimately trusted root, which is typically a simple server misconfiguration to fix.
Expired or not-yet-valid certificates producing a similar warning-fatigue risk through a different root cause.

Internal CAs deliberately used for internal-only services with properly managed distribution to corporate device trust stores, representing a much lower actual risk despite superficially similar scan output.
mitigation: Use certificates issued by a publicly-trusted CA for any externally-facing service, and a properly-managed internal PKI (not ad-hoc self-signed certs) for internal-only services.
Where an internal CA is used, ensure its root is distributed to client trust stores via a managed process (MDM/GPO), rather than instructing users to manually click through a browser trust warning.
Regularly audit for expired, self-signed, or unexpectedly-issued certificates across the estate.

NET-142.prerequisites: Layer 2 access to a switch access port on a segment with an exploitable native VLAN or DTP misconfiguration; a frame-crafting tool such as Scapy or Yersinia.
NET-142.whatItIs: VLAN hopping lets a device on one network segment send traffic that reaches a different, supposedly separate segment it shouldn't have access to — either by crafting specially double-labeled network traffic, or by tricking a switch into directly negotiating a trunk connection (a link normally reserved for carrying traffic between switches).
NET-142.rootCause: One technique exploits how a switch handles a specific, commonly-used 'default' network segment — a specially crafted frame with two layered labels can trick the switch into forwarding it onto a different segment than intended. The other technique exploits switch ports left in a mode that will automatically negotiate a full trunk connection with any device that asks for one, rather than restricting that to legitimate switch-to-switch links only.
NET-142.impact: Attackers can break out of their assigned VLAN and access other network segments via double-tagging or DTP exploitation. Because VLAN hopping bypasses the Layer 2 isolation that many organizations treat as an implicit trust boundary between network zones, successful exploitation frequently exposes assumptions about 'internal-only' access that were never actually enforced at the network layer.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether the switch port the tester is connected to has DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) enabled and will negotiate trunk mode on request.
Check whether the native (untagged) VLAN configured on trunk links matches the VLAN the tester's access port is assigned to, which is the precondition for the double-tagging variant.
Where DTP negotiation succeeds, enumerate the full list of VLANs reachable via the newly-formed trunk to establish the true blast radius of the finding.

Where the double-tagging variant is tested, confirm it only works one-way (attacker-to-victim-VLAN, not bidirectional) as expected by the attack's mechanics, to avoid overstating the finding's capability in the report.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers VLAN-hopping testing on the specific switch/segment.
Attempt to negotiate trunk mode via DTP from an access port and confirm whether the switch grants it, which would expose all VLANs on that trunk.
Separately, test the double-tagging variant by sending a frame with two stacked 802.1Q tags to reach a different VLAN via the native-VLAN mismatch.
Restore the tester's port to standard access mode immediately after confirming trunk negotiation or double-tagging success, to avoid leaving the port in an unintended state.

Report the specific VLANs reached via each variant tested (DTP negotiation vs. double-tagging), since they represent independent findings with different, specific remediations (disable DTP; align native VLAN).

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to negotiate a trunk port via DTP
Craft a double-tagged frame to reach a target VLAN

variants: Classic double-tagging (blind, one-way injection) versus switch spoofing via DTP trunk negotiation (full bidirectional trunk access).
Double-tagging combined with a targeted DoS/injection payload rather than pure reconnaissance, given its blind/one-way nature.
VLAN hopping against wireless controller infrastructure where SSIDs are mapped to VLANs with similarly weak trunk boundary enforcement.
Private VLAN (PVLAN) misconfigurations that allow similar cross-segment traffic leakage through a related but distinct mechanism.
mitigation: Disable DTP on all access ports (switchport nonegotiate) and explicitly configure them as access-mode only, never trunk-negotiable.
Never use the default VLAN (VLAN 1) as the native VLAN on trunk links; assign a dedicated, unused VLAN as native instead.
Explicitly prune unnecessary VLANs from trunk links rather than allowing all VLANs by default.

NET-143.prerequisites: Layer 2 access to a segment where WPAD auto-discovery is attempted by client browsers and the 'wpad' name is not securely registered; tools such as Responder, mitm6, and ntlmrelayx.
NET-143.whatItIs: Browsers can automatically look up and use a specific network's proxy settings through an unauthenticated lookup process. Since that lookup trusts whichever device answers first, an attacker on the local network can respond with a malicious proxy configuration, routing the victim's entire web traffic — and often their login credentials — through a server the attacker controls.
NET-143.rootCause: This auto-discovery lookup has no way to verify who's answering it. Many networks either never intended to use this feature at all but still have devices configured to look for it anyway, or never registered the expected name themselves — leaving it wide open for any attacker capable of faking a DNS answer, spoofing a local name lookup, or simply registering that name first.
NET-143.impact: WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) abuse via DNS/LLMNR spoofing causes clients to route traffic through attacker's proxy, enabling MITM of all HTTP traffic. Because WPAD is enabled by default on many Windows configurations, this attack can succeed against a broad population of hosts with zero prior reconnaissance, requiring only that the attacker's machine be reachable on the local segment.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm whether clients are configured to auto-discover proxy settings via WPAD and whether the corresponding DNS name (wpad.<domain>) or DHCP option is unregistered/unclaimed.
Where unclaimed, this represents a direct vulnerability: any host on the network can register the name/respond to the broadcast and become the trusted proxy for all auto-discovering clients.

Where the WPAD name/DHCP option is unclaimed, check via DNS/WHOIS-style internal lookups whether it has ever been registered, since an org that has proactively blackholed the name is not vulnerable even though the name resolves.
Determine the proportion of the client estate with WPAD auto-discovery enabled by default (most unmanaged Windows installs), to convey realistic blast radius in the finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes WPAD-spoofing/credential-capture testing.
Respond to WPAD auto-discovery requests (via DNS, NetBIOS, or LLMNR depending on the client's resolution order) with a malicious proxy configuration.
Capture the resulting NTLM authentication attempt that clients send when connecting through the tester's rogue proxy, and attempt offline cracking to demonstrate impact.

Limit the rogue-proxy testing window to the minimum needed to capture a representative NTLM sample, then immediately stop responding to auto-discovery requests to restore normal (failed, harmless) WPAD lookups.
Report the specific resolution mechanism exploited (DNS, DHCP, or NetBIOS/LLMNR) since the remediation (registering the DNS name, disabling the DHCP option) differs by mechanism.

examplePayloads.label: Poison WPAD auto-discovery and capture NTLM credentials via Responder
Confirm the malicious proxy configuration is actually applied by the browser
examplePayloads.command: # on the victim client: check browser network settings / proxy auto-config URL currently in effect

variants: WPAD injection via DNS name-claiming (registering/poisoning the 'wpad' hostname) versus via DHCP option 252 spoofing.
Combination with mitm6 to leverage unmanaged IPv6 DNS takeover for a more reliable and broader-reaching injection on dual-stack networks.
WPAD-captured NTLM credentials cracked offline (if hashes only, rather than fully relayed live) as an alternative to real-time relay.
Proxy-based traffic interception alone (without credential capture) for browsing activity monitoring, distinct from the NTLM relay attack chain.
mitigation: Explicitly disable WPAD auto-discovery via Group Policy on all clients unless it's a deliberately deployed and DNS/DHCP-registered proxy configuration.
Where WPAD is intentionally used, register the wpad.<domain> DNS name internally to prevent it from being claimed by an unauthorized host.
Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS as a complementary control, since WPAD poisoning frequently chains through the same name-resolution fallback behavior.

NET-144.prerequisites: Network reachability to the target TLS service; full active exploitation of the Logjam downgrade additionally requires a man-in-the-middle position relative to a victim client.
NET-144.whatItIs: Some servers still use a weak, small key size for a particular key-exchange method. An attacker with enough computing power can break that specific key exchange — and because a lot of servers reuse the exact same small set of well-known values, a large amount of upfront computing effort against one commonly-used value can then be reused to break the same exchange on countless other servers.
NET-144.rootCause: Old export restrictions used to cap this key size very low for certain configurations, and many servers never removed support for that weak option even after those restrictions were lifted. Separately, a huge number of servers on the internet reuse the same small handful of standard key-exchange values, which makes large-scale precomputation against those specific values a realistic threat, even for key sizes once considered acceptable.
NET-144.impact: Weak Diffie-Hellman parameters (< 1024 bits) can be factored, allowing session key recovery and traffic decryption. Because weak DH parameters affect every session negotiated using them until the parameter set is replaced, a single weak configuration can retroactively weaken the confidentiality of previously-captured, still-stored encrypted traffic once broken.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the Diffie-Hellman group size and parameters offered across all in-scope TLS/SSH services, flagging anything below 2048 bits.
Check whether the same non-standard DH parameters are reused across multiple servers, which increases the value of precomputing an attack against that specific group.

Where a sub-2048-bit or reused group is found, check whether it matches one of the well-known, widely-reused default groups (e.g., historical Apache/OpenSSL default primes) that are the specific target of nation-state-scale precomputation, since this materially raises realistic risk.
Confirm whether the affected service supports ECDHE as an alternative that a client could select instead, since coexistence of a strong option alongside the weak one affects remediation urgency.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers TLS/SSH cryptographic-parameter review.
Enumerate DH parameters via testssl.sh (TLS) or ssh-audit (SSH) across in-scope services.
Document any sub-2048-bit or reused/well-known group as a finding, referencing the established precomputation-based attack research rather than reproducing it independently.
Where the weak DH group matches a known, widely-reused default, flag this specifically in the report given the documented feasibility of precomputed attacks against exactly such groups.
Recommend generating a unique, sufficiently large (2048-bit minimum, 3072+ preferred) DH group per organization/service, or migrating to ECDHE entirely, as the concrete remediation.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate DH parameter strength for TLS
Enumerate DH group strength for SSH

variants: Logjam-style active downgrade to export-grade (512-bit) DH versus passive risk from reused, undersized (1024-bit) static DH parameters.
Weak DH parameters in non-TLS contexts such as SSH (though SSH host key exchange algorithms differ) or IPsec/VPN configurations using classic DH groups.
Combination with Raccoon-class timing attacks on the same DHE cipher suites, compounding overall DH-related exposure on a given host.
Servers still supporting export cipher suites purely for legacy compatibility despite the underlying export restrictions having been lifted decades ago.
mitigation: Use a minimum 2048-bit DH group (3072-bit+ preferred for high-assurance environments), or prefer ECDHE where client support allows.
Avoid reusing a single well-known DH group across many servers; generate unique parameters per deployment where DHE/DH is used at all.
For SSH specifically, disable diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 and other legacy key-exchange algorithms in the server configuration.

NET-145.prerequisites: An internal network position (physical access, VPN, or a foothold obtained during the assessment); an external listener under the tester's control to receive outbound test connections.
NET-145.whatItIs: The firewall doesn't properly restrict what internal computers are allowed to connect out to — letting them reach virtually any destination on any port. Malware and attackers rely on this kind of unrestricted outbound access for calling home, stealing data, and hiding their communication inside normally-trusted protocols.
NET-145.rootCause: Firewall rules are often designed with a heavy focus on blocking incoming traffic, while outbound traffic gets left wide open by default — because properly restricting outbound connections requires understanding and explicitly allowing every single legitimate thing the organization's own software needs to reach, which is a lot more work than just allowing everything by default.
NET-145.impact: Without egress filtering (BCP38), attackers can send spoofed packets with internal source IPs from the network, enabling DDoS amplification and obstructing attribution. Beyond enabling the organization's own infrastructure to be weaponized against third parties, weak egress filtering also removes a control that would otherwise limit outbound data exfiltration from an already-compromised internal host.
stepsToIdentify: From an internal test host, attempt outbound connections on a wide range of ports/protocols to an external test listener and record which succeed.
Specifically test for unrestricted outbound access on ports commonly used for data exfiltration or C2 (arbitrary high ports, DNS, ICMP) rather than only the standard web ports.

Where broad egress is confirmed, check whether it applies uniformly to all internal hosts or only to specific segments (e.g., a DMZ vs. internal user LAN), since remediation priority should focus on the highest-risk segment first.
Test DNS-based egress specifically, since DNS is almost universally permitted outbound even in otherwise well-filtered environments and is the most common real-world exfiltration/C2 channel.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers outbound-connectivity testing.
Attempt outbound connections across a broad port range to a tester-controlled external listener and record which succeed unfiltered.

Where broad egress is confirmed, demonstrate a realistic exfiltration/C2 channel over one of the open paths (e.g., DNS or HTTPS to a tester-controlled host) as evidence, without transmitting any real sensitive data.
Where DNS-based egress is confirmed unfiltered, demonstrate a minimal proof-of-concept DNS tunnel transmitting only a benign test string, not any real or simulated sensitive data.
Report the specific ports/protocols confirmed open outbound, ranked by realistic exfiltration/C2 usefulness, to help the client prioritize egress-filtering rule changes.

examplePayloads.label: Test broad outbound port access to an external listener
examplePayloads.command: for p in 21 22 23 25 53 445 1433 3389 4444 8080 8443; do timeout 2 bash -c "echo > /dev/tcp/<external-test-host>/$p" && echo "$p open"; done

examplePayloads.label: Set up the external listener side to confirm connections

variants: Fully permissive outbound policy (allow-all) versus a partially restrictive policy that still leaves high-risk ports/protocols (DNS, ICMP, common C2 ports) open.
Weak egress filtering combined with a lack of outbound traffic inspection (no proxy/DLP), compounding both the initial C2 establishment risk and undetected exfiltration risk.
Cloud environments with overly permissive security-group egress rules mirroring the same issue in a virtualized context.
DNS-tunneling-specific exposure even where general egress filtering is otherwise reasonably restrictive, since DNS is almost universally required outbound.
mitigation: Implement default-deny egress filtering, explicitly allowlisting only the specific outbound ports/destinations business applications actually require.
Route and inspect all outbound web traffic through a proxy that enforces the allowlist and logs destinations, rather than permitting direct unrestricted outbound access.
Pay particular attention to DNS and ICMP, since both are frequently left unrestricted for operational reasons and are common tunneling/exfiltration channels.

NET-146.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection within range of the target network; hashcat or aircrack-ng with an appropriate wordlist/rule set for the offline cracking phase.
NET-146.whatItIs: WPA2's login handshake, which can be captured just by listening or forced by kicking someone off briefly, contains enough information to attempt cracking the WiFi password entirely offline — trying millions of guesses without ever touching the actual network again. If the password is weak or a common one, the attacker recovers it with zero further interaction needed.
NET-146.rootCause: WPA2 derives its actual encryption keys from one shared password — and while the underlying cryptography is sound, the entire network's security comes down to how strong that one password actually is. Since the handshake (or, with a newer technique, sometimes even a single message from the access point) provides everything needed to test password guesses offline, a weak password is fully crackable with no way for the network to slow the attacker down or notice what's happening.
NET-146.impact: Captured WPA2 4-way handshakes can be cracked offline using dictionary or brute-force attacks if the passphrase is weak. Beyond the immediate cracking risk, PSK-based Wi-Fi networks with a shared passphrase provide no per-user accountability, so a leaked or brute-forced key cannot be revoked for one user without re-keying and redistributing credentials to every legitimate device on the network.
stepsToIdentify: Monitor for WPA2 handshakes on the target network.
Capture handshakes for later cracking.
Assess the apparent passphrase strength/complexity as a proxy for offline-cracking feasibility before investing significant compute time.

Determine the estimated real-world crackability of the captured handshake by assessing passphrase complexity indicators (length, dictionary-word usage) observable from the SSID/organizational context, without actually completing a full offline crack unless separately scoped.
exploitationSteps: Identify the target network's BSSID and channel using airodump-ng, and begin capturing on that channel.

Where a natural handshake is not observed within a reasonable window, send a small, targeted number of deauthentication frames to a connected client using aireplay-ng to force reassociation and handshake capture, or use the PMKID technique to avoid client interaction entirely.
Convert the captured handshake/PMKID to a crackable format using hcxpcapngtool or aircrack-ng's native tooling.
Run an offline dictionary and/or rule-based brute-force attack against the captured material using hashcat with GPU acceleration.
Upon successful recovery, use the passphrase to authenticate to the network as a legitimate client.
Where prior traffic captures exist, use the recovered key to decrypt previously captured WPA2 traffic from any client on the network.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the WPA2 4-way handshake
Trigger a handshake via a brief targeted deauth
Crack the captured handshake offline

variants: Traditional 4-way handshake capture (requires a connecting or reconnecting client) versus the PMKID technique (requires only a single frame from the AP, no client interaction).
WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X) networks are not susceptible to this specific PSK-cracking technique, though they have their own distinct attack surface (e.g., EAP relay attacks).
WPA3-SAE's Dragonfly handshake is designed to resist offline dictionary attacks even against weak passphrases, meaningfully reducing this risk class where deployed and correctly implemented.
Guest network PSK compromise used as a stepping stone toward internal network access where guest/corporate segmentation is also weak.
mitigation: Use WPA3-Personal (SAE) where client devices support it, which is resistant to offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake in the way WPA2-PSK is not.
Where WPA2-PSK must remain in use, enforce a long, high-entropy passphrase (20+ random characters) that's infeasible to crack via wordlist/GPU attack.
Move sensitive access to WPA2/3-Enterprise with per-user certificate or credential-based authentication (802.1X) rather than a single shared PSK, eliminating the shared-secret-capture risk entirely.

NET-147.prerequisites: Network reachability to TCP/873 on the target; no credentials required for anonymous modules.
NET-147.whatItIs: A file-sync tool has a mode that can be set up with completely open, unauthenticated shared folders. Where that's reachable from an untrusted network with no login required, anyone can browse what's shared and read — or if writable, even modify — files that often include backups or entire copies of a file system.
NET-147.rootCause: This tool does support proper login protection for its shared folders, but it's often set up without that protection turned on at all — sometimes deliberately, as an overly broad convenience for internal backup automation, and sometimes just left over from an early test setup that never got locked down before being exposed more widely.
NET-147.impact: Unauthenticated rsync can leak files from the server or allow upload of malicious files if rsync is misconfigured. Because rsync is commonly used for automated backup and deployment pipelines, an exposed module can serve as a stealthy foothold that blends into legitimate, expected file-synchronization traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for rsync daemon on TCP/873 and list available modules without providing credentials.
Attempt to browse the contents of any module lacking an auth users directive.

Where a module is listable, check whether any module lacks the auth users directive specifically, versus all modules requiring authentication but simply being enumerable by name (a much lower-severity finding).
Where writable modules are found (list contains 'write' or 'rw' permission), note this distinctly since it allows file upload, not just read access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers rsync access.
List available modules and, for any unauthenticated module, perform a read-only listing/dry-run sync to confirm real data exposure without pulling the full dataset.
Where a writable, unauthenticated module is found, do not upload any file to it — confirming write capability via a dry-run (--dry-run flag) is sufficient evidence without leaving an artifact.
Report each exposed module by name along with its confirmed access level (read-only vs. read-write), since remediation is applied per-module via the auth users/hosts allow directives.
Report a general recommendation to require the auth users directive on every module by default, rather than treating authentication as opt-in per module.

examplePayloads.label: List available rsync modules
Perform a dry-run listing of an unauthenticated module's contents

variants: Anonymous rsync modules with read-only access versus modules also permitting write access, which carries substantially higher impact.
rsync daemon mode exposure versus rsync-over-SSH, which inherits SSH's authentication and is not subject to this specific finding.
rsync used for internal backup automation but inadvertently exposed to a broader network segment or the internet due to firewall misconfiguration.
rsync modules mapped to live production directories (higher impact if writable) versus static, point-in-time backup archives.
mitigation: Require authentication (auth users + a secrets file) for every rsync module, with no unauthenticated modules left as a default.
Restrict rsync daemon access via hosts allow to only the specific hosts that need it, in addition to authentication.
Prefer rsync-over-SSH for any sensitive data transfer, which adds transport encryption the bare rsync protocol doesn't provide on its own.

NET-148.prerequisites: Valid low-privilege domain credentials (or a foothold capable of unauthenticated Kerberos requests where permitted), network access to a domain controller, Impacket's GetUserSPNs.py or Rubeus, and Hashcat or John the Ripper for offline cracking.
NET-148.whatItIs: Any regular, logged-in user in an Active Directory network can request a special ticket tied to a specific service account — and that ticket is encrypted using a scrambled version of that service account's own password. The attacker takes that ticket and tries to crack it offline, with zero further contact with the network needed.
NET-148.rootCause: Active Directory allows any logged-in user to request these tickets for service accounts by design — that part isn't the bug. The real problem is that many service accounts have weak, rarely-changed passwords and use an older, weaker encryption method instead of a stronger modern one, making the extracted ticket realistically crackable within a reasonable amount of time.
NET-148.impact: Successful cracking of a service account's password can lead to lateral movement or privilege escalation, and because service accounts frequently hold elevated or administrative privileges within the domain, a cracked hash can result in full domain compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Using valid low-privilege domain credentials, enumerate all accounts with a registered SPN via Impacket's GetUserSPNs.py or PowerView's Get-DomainUser -SPN.
Request TGS tickets for each identified SPN-bearing account and export them in a crackable hash format (Hashcat mode 13100 for RC4 or 19600/19700 for AES).
Check the encryption type used for each returned ticket to identify accounts still using weak RC4-HMAC encryption, which are typically much faster to crack.
Run the extracted hashes against a targeted wordlist and rule set with Hashcat to identify weak service account passwords.
Cross-reference cracked service accounts against the domain's privilege groups (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins) to assess criticality of the exposure.
exploitationSteps: Authenticate to the domain with the available low-privilege credentials.
Run GetUserSPNs.py with the -request flag to automatically request and dump TGS tickets for all SPN accounts in Hashcat-crackable format.
Run Hashcat against the dumped hash file using an appropriate mode and a strong wordlist plus rules.
Upon cracking a service account password, authenticate as that account and enumerate its effective privileges to determine follow-on impact (lateral movement, DCSync rights, etc.).

Cracking RC4-encrypted TGS hashes with Hashcat
Using Rubeus to request and roast tickets from a Windows host

variants: Targeted Kerberoasting where only accounts with weak PASSWD_NOTREQD or old passwordLastSet dates are roasted to prioritize the highest-probability cracks.
AS-REP roasting combined in the same engagement for accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (a related but distinct technique).
Kerberoasting against Managed Service Accounts (MSAs) which are typically resistant due to long random passwords, used to demonstrate the contrast in exposure.
mitigation: Enforce long (25+ character), randomly generated passwords or migrate to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) for all SPN-registered service accounts.
Disable RC4-HMAC Kerberos encryption domain-wide and enforce AES-only encryption types for service accounts.
Monitor for anomalous volumes of TGS-REQ events (Event ID 4769) requesting tickets for multiple SPNs from a single account in a short window.
Limit service account privileges to the minimum required and avoid placing service accounts in highly privileged groups.

NET-149.prerequisites: Authenticated low-privilege domain credentials, network access to an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) Certificate Authority and its enrollment endpoints, and Certipy or Certify for enumeration and abuse of vulnerable certificate templates.
NET-149.whatItIs: Active Directory's certificate system is frequently set up in a way that lets a regular, low-privilege user request a certificate that can be used to log in as a different, often much more privileged account — or lets them specify exactly whose identity that certificate should represent. These well-documented misconfiguration patterns let an attacker turn limited access into complete control over the entire organization's network.
NET-149.rootCause: Certificate request permissions get set too loosely, combined with dangerous settings — like allowing the requester to specify whose identity the certificate represents, or not requiring anyone to manually approve the request — letting a low-privilege user request a certificate that impersonates a top-level administrator account.
NET-149.impact: Exploitation of ESC1-class or CA-configuration escalation paths can allow an attacker to obtain a certificate that authenticates as Domain Administrator or any other targeted account, leading directly to full Active Directory domain compromise without needing to crack any password hashes.
stepsToIdentify: Run Certipy's `find` command (or Certify's `find /vulnerable`) using low-privileged domain credentials to enumerate all published certificate templates and the CA's configuration.

Review the enumeration output for templates flagged as vulnerable to known ESC patterns (e.g. ESC1: client-auth EKU + enrollee-supplies-subject + low-priv enroll rights; ESC4: weak template ACL allowing template reconfiguration).
Check the CA server's own configuration for ESC6/ESC7-class weaknesses (e.g. `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` flag enabled, or weak access control on the CA object itself).

Confirm whether the identified low-privileged account genuinely has enrollment rights on the flagged template by attempting a certificate request (in a controlled, authorized manner) specifying an arbitrary SAN corresponding to a privileged account.
Document each vulnerable template/CA setting with the specific ESC classification for the report, since remediation differs per pattern.

Check certificate templates for the ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag and overly-permissive enrollment rights (e.g., Domain Users granted enroll) in addition to the specific vulnerable-template patterns already identified, since AD CS misconfiguration commonly involves multiple co-occurring issues.
exploitationSteps: Use Certipy to request a certificate from the vulnerable template, specifying the Subject Alternative Name of a target privileged account (e.g. a Domain Admin).
Use the resulting certificate to authenticate via PKINIT (Kerberos) and obtain a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) for the impersonated account.
Use the obtained TGT to access domain resources or perform a DCSync operation, confirming full domain compromise as the proof of concept in the authorized test environment.
Report each vulnerable certificate template by name along with the specific ESC (Escalation) technique class it enables, since AD CS remediation is applied per-template.

variants: ESC4: attacker with write access to a template's ACL reconfigures it to introduce the ESC1 conditions themselves.
ESC6/ESC7: CA-level misconfiguration (SAN attribute flag or weak CA object ACL) rather than a specific vulnerable template.
ESC8: NTLM relay to the AD CS HTTP enrollment endpoint (web enrollment) to obtain a certificate on behalf of a coerced machine account.
mitigation: Audit all certificate templates and remove `ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT` and client-authentication EKUs from templates available to low-privileged principals; require manager approval where subject flexibility is genuinely needed.
Restrict certificate template and CA object ACLs so only intended administrators can modify template configuration or enrollment permissions.

Disable the `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` flag on the CA unless explicitly required, and enforce HTTPS with EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on any web enrollment endpoints to prevent relay.
Regularly run AD CS auditing tooling (Certipy/PSPKIAudit) as part of routine hardening reviews and monitor certificate issuance events.

NET-150.prerequisites: A domain account (or compromised service account) holding replication rights (`DS-Replication-Get-Changes` and `DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All`) either legitimately or via prior privilege escalation, network access to a domain controller, and Impacket's secretsdump.py or Mimikatz's lsadump::dcsync module.
NET-150.whatItIs: A legitimate feature that domain controllers use to sync data with each other can be abused by anyone granted the right permission, to pretend to be a domain controller themselves — and request every user's password data, without ever touching a real domain controller directly.
NET-150.rootCause: The specific permissions that allow this kind of sync request get granted too broadly — often to service accounts used by legitimate directory-sync tools, or accidentally inherited through nested group memberships — letting an account that isn't actually a domain controller invoke this sync feature and pull out sensitive data.
NET-150.impact: Full compromise of the Active Directory domain: an attacker can extract every user's password hash (including the KRBTGT hash needed to forge Golden Tickets), enabling persistent, long-term, and effectively undetectable domain-wide access.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate which principals hold `DS-Replication-Get-Changes` and `DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All` rights on the domain object using BloodHound or PowerView (`Get-DomainObjectAcl` with a filter on the relevant extended-right GUIDs).
Cross-reference the identified principals against expected legitimate holders (Domain Controllers, Domain Admins, and known directory-sync service accounts such as Azure AD Connect's MSOL_ account).
Flag any unexpected account, group, or nested group membership holding these rights as a potential privilege-escalation and persistence risk.

Where authorized and with an account already holding these rights (e.g. via prior escalation in the same engagement), attempt a DCSync request for a low-value test account first to confirm the exposure without touching sensitive accounts.
Document the specific ACE granting the replication rights (direct grant vs. inherited via nested group) for precise remediation guidance.

Confirm the specific account or group holding Replicating Directory Changes / Replicating Directory Changes All rights is not a legitimate, intended replication principal (e.g., a real domain controller computer account) before treating the finding as a misconfiguration.
exploitationSteps: Using the account confirmed to hold replication rights, run Impacket's secretsdump.py against the domain controller specifying DCSync mode.
Extract the NTLM hash (and Kerberos keys) for the KRBTGT account and/or targeted privileged accounts as directed by the rules of engagement.

Use the extracted KRBTGT hash to demonstrate Golden Ticket forging capability in the authorized test environment as the final proof of full domain compromise, or use a targeted account's hash for a pass-the-hash proof of concept.
Report the specific account/group holding replication rights and the point at which those rights were likely granted (e.g., an overly-broad delegation), to support precise remediation.

Performing DCSync via Impacket secretsdump

variants: Abuse via a compromised Azure AD Connect / directory-sync service account that legitimately requires replication rights but has weak credential protection.
Abuse via WriteDACL/GenericAll rights on the domain object being used to self-grant replication rights before performing DCSync (a two-step escalation chain).
Targeted DCSync of a single high-value account (e.g. a specific executive or admin) rather than a full-domain dump, to reduce detection footprint.
mitigation: Restrict `DS-Replication-Get-Changes`/`-All` rights to Domain Controllers and a minimal, tightly controlled set of directory-sync service accounts, removing any unnecessary or inherited grants.
Apply tiered administration and credential protection (e.g. Protected Users group, gMSA) to any account legitimately requiring replication rights, such as directory-sync service accounts.
Enable and monitor for Directory Service Replication events (Event ID 4662 with the replication GUIDs) originating from non-domain-controller source hosts.
Rotate the KRBTGT account password (twice, per Microsoft guidance) after any confirmed or suspected DCSync exposure to invalidate any forged tickets.
